en: The Diagnosis of Mādhava:
The Characteristics of the Fivefold Diagnosis.
The Characteristics of the Fivefold Diagnosis.
Having prostrated before Śiva— the cause of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world, the gateway to heaven and liberation, and the refuge of the three realms— I shall now,
at the command of virtuous physicians, summarize [this work] by means of the words of various sages.
This *Rogaviniścaya* (Determination of Diseases), which includes the etiology and symptoms of diseases along with their complications and fatal signs, is being composed.
For physicians of small intellect who have not studied various other treatises, this alone will be sufficient for easily understanding disease.
The etiology, the premonitory symptoms, the clinical signs, the therapeutic suitability, and the pathogenesis— this fivefold knowledge of diseases is traditionally taught.
[These are further classified] by means of the occasioning cause, the causal factor, the locus, the condition, the manifestation, and the instrumental cause.

They say that the *nidāna* (etiology) is explained by various synonyms as that by which the premonitory stage (*pūrvarūpa*) is characterized; it is the disease about to arise, not yet presided over by a specific *doṣa*.
Because of its subtlety, the symptoms (*liṅga*) of diseases are unmanifest; such is their true nature. (5–6)
That very same [state] when it has reached manifestation is designated as *rūpa* (form);
it is also called *saṃsthāna* (configuration), *vyañjana* (manifestation), *liṅga* (sign), *lakṣaṇa* (characteristic), *cihna* (mark), and *ākṛti* (shape).
[It pertains to] those things that are contrary to their causes and diseases, and which produce contrary effects.
One should recognize as *upaśaya* (therapeutic suitability) that application of medicines, diet, and lifestyle which brings relief from disease; for that is known as *sātmya* (habituation).
Conversely, that which is the opposite is *anupaśaya* (non-suitability), and it is known as *asātmya* (unwholesome habituation) to the disease.
Just as a disease is produced by a specific morbid humor and its subsequent spreading, so too is its manifestation termed *saṃprāpti*, *jāti*, or *āgati*;
it is distinguished by its enumeration, variations, predominance, strength, and timing. (10)

It is divided as will be stated right here: "There are eight types of fever" (11). Regarding the various combinations of the humors (doṣas), one should determine the predominance of a disease based on whether it acts independently or dependently (12).

The specific strength or weakness [of a disease] is determined by the causes and other factors in their entirety or by their individual parts, as well as by the portions of night, day, season, and food; thus has the meaning of diagnosis (nidāna) been stated, and it will now be taught in detail. 13.
The etiology of all diseases is the vitiation of the humors (malas). The cause of that vitiation is said to be the indulgence in various unwholesome things.
Furthermore, a disease that acts as an etiological factor can also arise from another disease.
For example: from the heat of fever, blood-bile (raktapitta) is provoked;
from blood-bile, fever arises; and from both of these, emaciation (śoṣa) also occurs.
From the enlargement of the spleen (plīhā), abdominal enlargement (jaṭhara) results, and from abdominal enlargement, swelling (śotha) likewise arises. (16)
From hemorrhoids (arśas), abdominal pain and abdominal tumors (gulma) arise;
from the defects of sleeping during the day and other such causes, catarrh (pratiśyāya) arises;
from catarrh, cough (kāsa) arises; and from cough, consumption (kṣaya) is produced.
When there is a depletion of the cause of a disease, a wasting (śoṣa) also arises.
First, those are merely diseases; later, they act as causes [of other diseases].
For indeed, some disease, having become the cause of another disease, subsides.
Furthermore, one [disease] does not subside while another acts as the cause;
thus, the most difficult combinations of diseases are seen among men.
Therefore, by diligent physicians who desire eminent success, [these must be treated]. 20.
This definitive determination of fever and other diseases, which is to be known and will be explained, [is now presented]. Next, the etiology of fever (jvara-nidāna).

The fever born from the breath of Rudra, enraged by Dakṣa’s insult, is known to be eightfold: arising separately from the individual humors (doṣas), from combinations of two, from the combination of all three, and from external causes. Indeed, through improper diet and conduct, the humors take refuge in the stomach (āmāśaya).
When the digestive fire is cast outward and the humors follow it, they become the givers of fever.
That disease in which there is an obstruction of perspiration, a general heat, and a seizing of all the limbs simultaneously is designated as *jvara*.
Fatigue, restlessness, discoloration of the skin, a bad taste in the mouth, watering of the eyes,

frequent desire and aversion toward cold, wind, heat, and so forth, yawning, aching of the limbs, heaviness, horripilation, loss of appetite, and darkness before the eyes [are the premonitory symptoms].
Lack of exhilaration and coldness occur when fever is about to arise. Generally, however, from a predominance of wind (vāta) there is excessive yawning;
from bile (pitta) there is a burning sensation in the eyes; and from phlegm (kapha) there is a loss of appetite for food.
They know that fever born from a combination of two [doṣas] arises when two of the symptoms are combined;
when all the doṣas are provoked, there is a convergence of all their signs. Trembling, an irregular onset, and dryness of the throat and lips [occur].
Loss of sleep, suppression of sneezing, dryness of the limbs, pain in the head, heart, and body, a bad taste in the mouth, hardness of stool, colic, flatulence,
and yawning occur in fever born of Vāta.
Violent impulse, diarrhea, diminished sleep, as well as vomiting,
inflammation of the throat, lips, mouth, and nose, and a natural state [of the body] arise.
Delirium, bitterness in the mouth, fainting, burning sensation, intoxication, and thirst [occur].

In the Pitta-type [fever], there is yellowness of the feces, urine, and eyes, as well as giddiness (11). There is also a sense of numbness, sluggishness of the bodily urges, laziness, a sweet taste in the mouth,
whiteness of the urine and feces, stiffness, and a feeling of satiety (12).
Heaviness, coldness, excessive moisture, horripilation, excessive sleep,
obstruction of the channels, mild pain, salivation, a salty taste in the mouth,
lack of body heat, vomiting, drooling, and indigestion [are the symptoms].
In the case of fever born of kapha, there is coryza, loss of appetite, cough, and whiteness of the eyes;
13 thirst, fainting, giddiness, burning sensation, loss of sleep, headache, dryness of the throat and mouth, vomiting, horripilation, anorexia, and darkness before the eyes. 14
The premonitory symptoms are yawning, a form of fever characterized by wind and bile,
stiffness, breaking pain in the joints, drowsiness, heaviness, stiffness of the head, catarrh, cough, and the non-emergence of perspiration. (15)
Fever caused by vāta and śleṣman has the form of burning heat and moderate intensity (16).
A coated and bitter mouth, drowsiness, delusion, cough, anorexia, thirst, alternating burning heat and alternating cold— these are the characteristics of fever caused by śleṣman and pitta (17).
There is burning at one moment and coldness at another; there is pain in the bones, joints, and head;
the eyes are watery, turbid, red, and sunken;
the ears are painful and ringing; and the throat feels as if it were covered with bristles.
Drowsiness, delusion, delirium, cough, dyspnea, anorexia, and vertigo;
a parched tongue with a rough touch, extreme flaccidity of the limbs, and expectoration of blood and bile mixed with phlegm—these are the signs. (19–20)
Rolling of the head, thirst, loss of sleep, pain in the heart,
and the delayed or scanty appearance of sweat, urine, and feces; emaciation of the limbs that is not excessive, and constant moaning from the throat— 21.
The appearance of dark-red pustules and circular patches, muteness, suppuration of the orifices, heaviness of the abdomen,
and the delayed maturation of the humors constitute the clinical form of *sannipāta* fever. (22–23)
When the doshas are obstructed and the digestive fire (agni) is destroyed, Sannipata fever exhibits all symptoms in their entirety; it is incurable, whereas otherwise it is difficult to cure.
This occurs when the seventh, tenth, or even the twelfth day has arrived.
Becoming even more terrible, it either subsides or destroys;
the seventh, the twelfth, the ninth, and likewise the eleventh— these,
consisting of the three humors, lead both to liberation and to death.

At the end of a fever caused by the combination of all three humors (sannipāta), a most severe swelling arises at the root of the ear; because of this, only some few are liberated from it. When the three humors are provoked, they follow the channels of the chest.
When the *āmāśaya* increases, the intellect, the senses, and the mind become constricted;
they produce a most terrible and persistent fever characterized by paralysis.
There is numbness in the ears and eyes, and one does not desire any activity whatsoever.
His vision would no longer be capable of seeing forms; he would not perceive odors, nor touch, nor indeed sound.
He would constantly toss his head about and take no pleasure in food.
He moans and suffers pain, and strives for a change of position;
he speaks but little—this is called *abhinyāsa*.
When rejected, he mostly fails, though perhaps someone here may succeed.

Exogenous disease arises from physical injury, malevolent spells, curses, or contagion; one should identify it according to its specific cause. In cases caused by poison, there is a darkening of the face as well as diarrhea.

Loss of appetite for food, thirst, piercing pain, and fainting (occur) in [fainting] born from the smell of medicinal herbs. In that born of desire (kāmaja), there is fainting, headache, nausea, and sneezing;
in that born of mental affliction (cittavibhraṃśa), there is drowsiness, laziness, and lack of appetite.
In his heart there is pain and his body withers;
from fear there is delirium, from grief there is trembling, and from anger there is shivering;
through malevolent magic and curses, delusion and thirst arise. 29
Agitation, laughing, weeping, and trembling result from possession by spirits (bhūtābhiṣaṅga).
Vāyu [is provoked] by lust, grief, and fear; pitta by anger; these are the three impurities (malas).
Due to possession by spirits, those [humors] which share the characteristics of the spirits become aggravated.

A small amount of morbid humor (doṣa), arising from unwholesome causes or occurring again in one who has recently recovered from a fever, reaches another tissue element (dhātu) and produces irregular fever (viṣamajvara). That [fever] is continuous (santata) when located in the plasma (rasa) and blood; it occurs on alternate days (anyedyuḥ) when residing in the flesh (piśita).
If it has entered the flesh on the third day, but has entered the bones and marrow again,
one should know it will produce a terrible quartan fever— a mixture of diseases that brings about death—
lasting for seven days, ten days, or even twelve days.
That which continues without interruption is called "continuous" (santata). The "constant" (satataka) fever persists for two periods throughout a day and night;
the "daily" (anyedyuṣka) fever, however, occurs at one period during a day and night.

The tertian fever occurs on the third day, and the quartan fever on the fourth day; some authorities state that this irregular fever (viṣamajvara) arises from possession by malevolent spirits (bhūta-abhiṣaṅga).
The fever arising from kapha and pitta seizes the sacrum (trika), while that consisting of vāta and kapha affects the back.
The tertian fever (tṛtīyaka), which seizes the head due to wind and bile, is of three types.
The quartan fever (caturthaka) manifests its power in two ways:
the phlegmatic type first [affects] the calves, while that arising from wind first [affects] the head.
There is another type of irregular fever, a variation of the quartan (caturthaka),
which causes fever in the middle of the day and leaves one free from it at the beginning and the end;
by this, the patient suffers from constant mild fever, becomes parched, and develops swelling.

A person with stiff limbs and a predominance of phlegm suffers from vātabalāsaka. In pralepaka fever, the patient feels as if his limbs are being smeared with a paste due to heat and heaviness; he experiences mild fever and a coating sensation accompanied by pain.
When the essence of food has been digested and the phlegm (śleṣman) and bile (pitta) are situated within the body,

by that [disturbance], half of the body becomes cold and half becomes hot. When the bile is corrupted in the upper part of the body and the phlegm is situated at the end [in the lower part], [the same occurs].
Therefore, there is heat in the body and coldness in the hands and feet.
When phlegm (śleṣmā) is corrupted within the body and bile (pitta) is situated at the extremities,
because of that, there is coldness in the limbs and heat in the hands and feet.
When kapha and vāta are located in the skin during fever, they first produce cold;
once these two have subsided, pitta causes a burning sensation at the end.
Likewise, when pitta is located in the skin, it produces excessive burning at the very beginning.
When that [fever] has subsided, however, the other two produce cold at the end.
These two types of fever, characterized by burning and cold respectively, are known as those born of combined causes (saṃsargaja).
Of these two, the one preceded by burning is more difficult and is considered the most challenging to treat.
Heaviness, agitation of the heart, prostration, vomiting, and loss of appetite—these are the symptoms when fever resides in the rasa (plasma); moreover, a sense of wretchedness arises in the patient.
When it resides in the blood, there is spitting of blood, burning sensation, delusion, fainting, and vertigo.
In fever that has reached the blood (rakta-prāpta), men experience incoherent speech (pralāpa), pustules (piḍakā), and thirst (tṛṣṇā).

In fever located in the muscle tissue (māṃsa-ga), there is cramping of the calves (piṇḍikodveṣṭana), thirst, discharge of urine and feces, internal heat (ūṣmā), a burning sensation within the body (antardāha), restlessness (vikṣepa), and exhaustion (glāni). 49–50.
Excessive perspiration, thirst, fainting, delirium, and vomiting;
foul odor, anorexia, exhaustion, and intolerance—these occur when [the poison] resides in the fat (medas).
Furthermore, there is fracture of the bones, creaking sounds, labored breathing, purging, and vomiting. (51)
Tossing of the limbs occurs when the fever has reached the bones (52).
Entering into darkness, hiccup, cough, coldness, vomiting,
internal burning, labored breathing, and the cutting pain of the vital organs (marmas) occur when the fever has reached the marrow (53).

If the fever has reached the seat of the semen, one may meet death there; specifically, there is stiffness of the penis and the discharge of semen. That fever which resides in the blood and flesh is curable, as is that which has entered the muscle and fat.
When it has reached the marrow, it is difficult to cure; when it resides in the semen, it is incurable.
The natural (prākṛta) type arises from Vāta and the other doshas respectively during the rainy season, autumn, and spring;
the unnatural (vaikṛta) type occurs at other times. That unnatural type is hard to treat, as is the natural type arising from Vāta.
In the rainy season, the vitiated wind (vāta), combined with bile (pitta) and phlegm (kapha), produces fever;
and in autumn, it is bile that causes it, with phlegm acting as its secondary force.
Due to the nature of these seasons and the natural elimination [of humors], there is no danger from fasting during those times.
In spring, kapha increases, followed by vāta and pitta;
at their respective times, there is either the onset or the increase of all [doshas] according to their own nature.
Non-relief from the causes as described constitutes the etiology, while relief through the opposite [of those causes] constitutes the therapeutic pacification.
Internal burning, excessive thirst, delirium, labored breathing, giddiness, pain in the joints and bones, absence of perspiration, and the suppression of the humors and feces—
these one should recognize as the signs of fever with internalized force (antarvega). 59.
Excessive external heat, softness of the tongue and other parts,
salivation, nausea, impurity of the heart, and loss of appetite are the signs of the external stage (bahirvega), as well as its being easily curable. (60-61)
Drowsiness, lassitude, indigestion, a bad taste in the mouth, heaviness of the limbs, loss of appetite, excessive urination, stiffness, and a violent fever—
these are the symptoms of *āmaja-jvara* (fever caused by undigested matter); one should not administer medicine in such a case.
For medicine administered during the stage of undigested morbid humors (āmadoṣa) further inflames the fever;
it causes irregular fever (viṣamajvara) through both purificatory (śodhana) and palliative (śamanīya) actions.
There is an excessive force of the fever, thirst, delirium, labored breathing, and vertigo.
The onset of impurity (mucus) and internal agitation are the signs of the fever being ripened.

Hunger, emaciation, lightness of the limbs, and the mildness of the fever are the signs of the departure of the humors; the eight-day period is the characteristic of a fever free from *āmaja* (undigested morbid matter).
Fever that arises from strong but few causes, which is without complications, and which is produced by many potent factors with many symptoms, is curable; however,
that fever which brings about the end of life and quickly destroys the sense organs is incurable.

Fever in one who is emaciated or swollen, which is deep-seated and chronic, is incurable; likewise, a fever that is powerful and causes the parting of the hair is incurable. A fever should be known as deep-seated when it is accompanied by internal burning and thirst.

That which is irregular from the very onset due to extreme constriction and the emergence of labored breathing and coughing, as well as that which persists for many nights, and that which is deep-seated in one who is emaciated and excessively parched— these kill the patient. (69)
The man who is unconscious and gasping, or who lies down even while falling,
who is afflicted by cold externally yet has internal heat, dies from fever; likewise, he whose hair stands on end, whose eyes are bloodshot, and who suffers from piercing pain in the heart [dies].
Fever kills that man who breathes through the mouth alone,
who is afflicted by hiccup, dyspnea, and thirst, and whose mind is deluded and eyes are wandering;
it destroys the man who breathes incessantly and is emaciated.
One should avoid treating a fever patient whose radiance and senses are destroyed, who is emaciated and afflicted by anorexia (arocaka), who suffers from deep-seated and sharp-onset intensity,
and who is burning with heat, sweating, experiencing vertigo, thirst, tremors, diarrhea, and loss of consciousness.
Cooing, a foul odor, and the physical appearance [of the patient] during the release from fever;
perspiration, lightness of the head, itching, and suppuration of the mouth; sneezing and a desire for food—these are the signs of one released from fever. (74–75)
Now, the etiology of diarrhea: [diarrhea arises] from heavy, excessively unctuous, dry, hot, liquid, bulky, or excessively cold substances.
Due to incompatible or excessive eating, indigestion, and irregular meals; from the overuse of oleation and other therapies, or their improper application; from poisons, fears, and grief;
from drinking contaminated water or excessive alcohol; and from changes in habitual diet and seasonal transitions.
Due to sporting in water, the obstruction of natural urges, or the presence of parasites, diarrhea occurs in men; its symptoms will now be described.
When the bodily element of water is suppressed, the digestive fire becomes aggravated and, mixed with feces, is driven downward by the wind.
One who suffers excessively from diarrhea is said to have that terrible disease; they describe it as being of six types:
by each of the *doṣas* individually, by all of them combined, by grief as another, and the sixth is said to be caused by undigested matter (*āma*).
[Its symptoms include: pain in the heart, navel, anus, abdomen, and flanks; a piercing pain; exhaustion of the limbs; and the obstruction of the vital air (*vāyu*).
Attachment to unwholesome food, flatulence, and indigestion will be the precursors of that [disease].
When it is provoked by Vāta, one suffers from diarrhea characterized by reddish, frothy, dry, scanty, and frequent stools that are undigested and accompanied by pain and sound. (5–6)
From *pitta*, [the discharge] is yellow, blue, or reddish, accompanied by thirst, fainting, burning, and suppuration;

from *śleṣman*, it is white, thick, associated with phlegm, with a cadaverous odor, cold, and the person has bristling body hair. When it resembles the fat, flesh, or water of a boar, it possesses all these characteristics.
One should know that diarrhea arising from the three *doṣas* is difficult to cure (verse 8).

When a person who is grieving over various circumstances and eating little has the heat of his tears enter the fire [of digestion], it goes into the digestive tract (*koṣṭha*) and agitates his blood; that blood, appearing like the *kākaṇantī* plant, flows downwards (verse 9).

Whether mixed with feces, or without feces, odorless or even fragrant, this diarrhea arising from grief is difficult to treat; it is declared by physicians to be an exceedingly severe and painful disease.
(10) Due to indigestion of food, the aggravated *doṣas* rush forth, agitating the abdominal cavity, the tissues (*dhātus*), and the waste products (*malas*).
They repeatedly discharge various colors of matter accompanied by a piercing pain; this they call the sixth [type of diarrhea].
When mixed with these defects, it sinks when placed in water—extremely foul-smelling, slimy, and designated as *āma*.
If these very symptoms are indeed reversed,
and especially if there is lightness, one should declare that [the fever] is ripe (cured). It resembles a ripe jambu fruit or a piece of liver, and is thin.
Resembling clarified butter, oil, fat, marrow, minced meat, milk, curd, or the water used for washing meat; black, blue, or reddish in luster,
dark, glossy, variegated like a *karbura* deer, or dense like the moon's reflection in water— [such clouds portend calamity].
The corpse-like body resembles brain-matter, is foul-smelling, putrid, and copious;

it is afflicted by thirst, burning sensations, darkness, labored breathing, hiccups, and pain in the flanks and bones; it is possessed of fainting, aversion, and delusion, with its anus resembling a ripened fig. 16.
The best of physicians should avoid a patient suffering from diarrhea who is accompanied by incoherent speech (17).

One should abandon a patient with diarrhea who has an unrestrained anus, is emaciated, suffers from severe distension, is afflicted by complications, has a ripened anus, whose body heat has departed, and who bears the marks of chronic diarrhea (18).
Diarrhea especially destroys a man who is emaciated, afflicted by dyspnea, colic, and thirst, and oppressed by fever— particularly if he is an elderly person.
[It also brings] swelling, colic, fever, thirst, cough, dyspnea, and loss of appetite.
One should abandon a patient suffering from diarrhea upon observing vomiting, fainting, and hiccupping.
When a person with a Pitta-type condition eats substances that excessively aggravate Pitta, then a severe and persistent bloody diarrhea arises. 20.
In one who consumes unwholesome food, the aggravated Vāyu pushes the accumulated phlegm (balāsa) downward;
experts call that condition *pravāhikā*, characterized by frequent and scanty discharges mixed with waste matter.
*Pravāhikā* caused by Vāta is accompanied by pain, by Pitta it is accompanied by burning, and by Kapha it is accompanied by phlegm.

Those [disorders] arising from blood and originating in the blood are considered to be produced by unctuousness (sneha) and dryness (rūkṣa); one should indicate their symptoms and the sequence of their ripening (āmavipakvatā) as being like those of diarrhea (atīsāra). When urine and flatus pass properly even without the discharge of feces, [the condition is known as pravāhikā].
For one who has a stimulated digestive fire and a light gastrointestinal tract, the abdominal disease may persist.
Whatever etiology was stated separately for fever and diarrhea, that same etiology applies here to fever-dysentery (jvarātisāra), and thus it is not stated again. 1–23.
The Etiology of Grahani Disease:
Now, regarding the etiology of grahani disease,
even when diarrhea has ceased, if one with weak digestive fire continues to consume unwholesome food, [the disease arises].
Furthermore, the vitiated fire (digestive heat) may afflict the *grahaṇī*.
When corrupted by each of the *doṣas* individually or by all of them combined, being excessively overwhelmed, that [fire] frequently discharges undigested food as it is consumed. 1–2.

Those learned in Ayurveda call that disease *grahaṇī* when the stool is either cooked (digested), painful, putrid, or alternately bound and alternately liquid. Its premonitory symptoms, however, are thirst, lassitude, and loss of strength.

There is a burning sensation during digestion and a delayed digestion of food, as well as heaviness of the body (4), caused by meals that are excessively pungent, bitter, astringent, or dry; by eating in insufficient quantities or fasting;
and by excessive travel, suppression of natural urges, and sexual intercourse (5).
When the wind (māruta) is aggravated, it obscures the fire and produces diseases;
his food is digested with difficulty, becoming sour during digestion, and there is roughness of the limbs (6),
dryness of the throat and mouth, hunger, thirst, darkness of vision, and ringing in the ears.
Pain in the sides, thighs, groins, and neck; frequent indigestion (visūcikā);
oppression of the heart, emaciation, weakness, a bad taste in the mouth, cutting pain in the rectum, a craving for all kinds of flavors, and likewise depression of the mind.
When it has been digested, the patient suffers from flatulence; after eating, he attains a sense of well-being;
yet that person remains suspicious of having vātagulma, heart disease, or splenic enlargement.
After a long time, he voids stool that is painful, liquid, dry, thin, scanty, accompanied by sound, and frothy.
Afflicted by cough and dyspnea due to vāta, one may repeatedly pass feces.
When pitta is aggravated by pungent, undigested, burning, sour, alkaline, and similar substances, it drenches the digestive fire, just as hot water extinguishes a flame.

Afflicted by indigestion, he passes liquid stools that appear blue or yellow; being himself of a yellowish complexion, he suffers from foul and sour eructations, burning sensations in the heart and throat, loss of appetite, and thirst.
This occurs due to the consumption of heavy, excessively unctuous, or cold foods, as well as overeating. (12)
Furthermore, in one who has just eaten, aggravated *kapha* destroys the digestive fire due to bathing;
his food is digested with difficulty, and there occur nausea, vomiting, anorexia, coating of the mouth,
sweetness in the mouth, cough, spitting, and chronic rhinitis.
One perceives heaviness in the heart, a distended and heavy abdomen, a foul and sweet eructation, lassitude, a lack of desire for women,
and the passage of stool that is broken up, mixed with phlegm, and heavy. (15)
In the kapha-type [hemorrhoid], there is weakness and laziness even in one who is not emaciated (16).

When there is a combination of causes and symptoms individually specified for vāta and the other doshas, one should diagnose it as being caused by all three doshas (tridoṣaja); I shall now describe their treatment (17).
Gurgling in the intestines, laziness, weakness, and a sense of exhaustion;
stool that is liquid, cold, thick, and unctuous, accompanied by pain in the waist (17-1); undigested matter (āma) in great quantity, slimy, with sound, and mild pain.
Whether it releases [the patient] after a fortnight, a month, ten days, or even constantly;
whether its provocation occurs by day and it finds peace at night—that which is difficult to recognize, difficult to treat, and persists for a long time—[is known as *sannipāta*]. (17-2, 17-3)
That condition caused by āmavāta is considered saṃgrahagrahaṇī;
when there is pain in both flanks and a sound like that of a water-pot dripping, they call that incurable grahaṇī disease "ghaṭīyantra. 17-4

One should recognize the presence of *doṣas* as being either with or without *āma*, just as in the case of diarrhea (*atisāra*). That disorder of the *grahaṇī* which is incurable by those same symptoms by which the disease of diarrhea is not cured, and which certainly occurs in the elderly, does not cease even after destroying the body. 18–19.
Grahani is curable in a child, declared difficult to treat in a youth, and incurable in an elderly person; this is the opinion of Dhanvantari. (19-1) Diagnosis of Arsha (Hemorrhoids).
Now, regarding the etiology of hemorrhoids:

one should know that there are six types of hemorrhoids— those caused by the individual doṣas, by all the doṣas combined, those arising from blood, and the congenital ones— located within the three folds of the rectum.
The doshas, having vitiated the skin, flesh, and fat, produce various types of fleshy sprouts in the anal region and other areas; these they call hemorrhoids (arśas).
Astringent, pungent, and bitter tastes, as well as dry, cold, and light qualities [exacerbate them].
Eating measured or small amounts of food, sharp liquor, indulgence in sexual intercourse, fasting, cold regions and seasons,
physical exercise, grief, and exposure to wind and sun are considered the causes of vāta-type hemorrhoids.
Bitter, sour, salty, and hot [tastes]; physical exercise, fire, sunlight, and glare; unsuitable place and time, lack of coldness, anger, wine, and envy;
and all drinks, foods, and medicines that are burning, sharp, and hot—[these increase pitta].
The causes for the provocation of hemorrhoids (arśas) characterized by a predominance of pitta should be known as follows:
sweet, unctuous, and cold substances; salty, sour, and heavy foods; lack of physical exercise; sleeping during the day; and an attachment to the comfort of beds and seats. (Verses 6–7)
The consumption of eastern winds and exposure to cold, along with disregard for place and time,
are declared to be the causes of hemorrhoids caused by phlegm (ślaiṣmika).
One should recognize those hemorrhoids characterized by a predominance of two humors through the combination of their respective causes and symptoms.
The etiology of all three doshas is identical to that of the congenital types.
The anal polyps caused by vata are numerous, dry, accompanied by a tingling sensation (cimicimā), flaccid, dusky-red or reddish-brown, stiff, clear, rough, and harsh. 9–10.
Mutually dissimilar, crooked, sharp, and with gaping mouths,
they resembled the fruits of the *bimbī*, the date palm, the *karkandhū*, and the *kārpāsī* plant;
some had the appearance of *kadamba* flowers, while others were like mustard seeds.

They cause excessive pain in the head, sides, shoulders, waist, thighs, groins, and other areas; they produce sneezing, eructation, constipation, cardiac oppression, and loss of appetite; and they bring about cough, dyspnea, irregularity of the digestive fire, tinnitus, and vertigo. (12–13)

Afflicted by these, one passes stool that is knotted, scanty, noisy, and accompanied by mucus and dysentery (pravāhikā); it is mixed with froth and slimy secretions, and is passed with great effort. Furthermore, the skin, nails, feces, urine, eyes, and face become darkened.
From that very same [cause], there arises gulma, splenic enlargement (plīhodara), and aśṭhīlā.
Those [tumors] in which pitta is predominant have blue openings and exhibit red, yellow, or black luster;
they secrete thin blood, have a fleshy odor, and are small, soft, and flaccid.
Resembling the tongue of a parrot, pieces of liver, or the mouth of a leech, they produce burning sensations, suppuration, fever, perspiration, thirst, fainting, loss of appetite, and delusion;
they are hot to the touch and discharge liquid, blue, black, yellow, red, or pale-colored stools. (17)
Those dominated by phlegm (kapha) have barley-shaped centers, green, yellow, or turmeric-colored skin and nails;
they have large roots, are dense, slightly painful, white, elevated, thick, oily, stiff, round, heavy, and firm. (18–19)
They are slimy, motionless, smooth, abundant with itching, pleasant to the touch,
resembling the seeds of the *karīra* or the kernel of the *panasa* fruit, and similar to cow's teats; they cause distension of the groin and pull upon the anus, bladder, and navel.
They cause dyspnea, cough, nausea, excessive salivation, loss of appetite, and rhinitis;
they produce urinary disorders, dysuria, heaviness of the head, and cold-fever;
and they bring about impotence, weak digestion, vomiting, and various disorders characterized by undigested matter (āmadoṣa).

Those whose feces consist mostly of fat, blood, phlegm, and excrement, accompanied by tenesmus, who do not pass stool nor experience its breaking away, and whose skin and other features are pale and oily— these, along with those possessing all the symptoms together, are said to have congenital hemorrhoids. (23)
In the anal region, the polyps (kīla) are dominated by blood and possess the characteristics of pitta;
they resemble the shoots of the *vaṭa* tree, and are like the *guñjā* berry or coral.
Afflicted by excessively foul and hot, hard feces, they [bleed]. 24–25.
Blood flows suddenly from him due to excessive discharge, and he suffers the pains arising from the loss of blood;
his complexion, strength, and vitality are diminished, his energy is destroyed, and his senses become clouded. (26)
In that condition, there are two types of residual secretion (anubandha), one from phlegm (śleṣman) and one from wind (māruta).
The stool is dark-brown, hard, and dry, and the downward wind does not flow;
the blood of the hemorrhoids is thin, reddish in color, and frothy.
If there is pain in the hips, thighs, and anus, along with excessive weakness; if the underlying cause is a Vata complication or a drying factor;
and if the stool is loose, white or yellow, yet unctuous, heavy, and cold—[these are the signs]. 28–29.

If the blood from hemorrhoids is thick, stringy, pale, and slimy; and if the anus is slimy, numb, heavy, and unctuous; and if the cause is associated with phlegm (kapha), the wise should recognize this as the involvement of kapha in cases of blood-born hemorrhoids. 30

Stagnation of food, weakness, distension of the abdomen, emaciation, excessive belching, lassitude of the thighs, and scanty stools— these are the signs, as well as the apprehension of *grahaṇī* disorder, anemia, and abdominal enlargement. (31)
The premonitory symptoms for the aggravation of hemorrhoids have been described.
The fivefold wind (vāyu), bile (pitta), phlegm (kapha), and the three folds of the rectum—
all these indeed become provoked at the onset of hemorrhoids.
Therefore, arśas (hemorrhoids) cause many sufferings, give rise to numerous diseases,
afflict the entire body, and are generally most difficult to endure; however,
those arising in the outer fold of the anus are caused by the aggravation of only a single doṣa.
Hemorrhoids that have not been present for long are easily curable;

those born from the combination of two doshas (dvandvaja) and those located in the second layer of the anal folds (balī) are said to be difficult to cure, as are those that have persisted for more than a year.
Those congenital disorders of the three *doṣas* and those that arise from internal parasites (*balis*) by depending on the teeth should be designated as incurable; however,
these may be treated if the patient still possesses a remainder of life and is endowed with the four pillars of therapy.
Otherwise, they must be rejected as incurable for one whose bodily fire is blazing.
(38) He in whom there is swelling in the hands, feet, mouth, navel, anus, or testicles, as well as pain in the heart and the sides, is indeed incurable. (39)
Pain in the heart and flanks, delusion, vomiting, body ache, fever, thirst,
and inflammation of the anus destroy one afflicted by hemorrhoids (gudaja). One who suffers from thirst, anorexia, and pain, and from whom blood flows excessively, [is likewise lost].
Indeed, these destroy hemorrhoids accompanied by swelling and diarrhea.
Furthermore, those arising from the umbilicus will be described according to their respective types; they resemble the mouth of an earthworm, are slimy, and soft. 41–42.
The Vyāna wind, having seized the phlegm (śleṣman), produces a growth on the exterior of the skin that resembles a wedge, being firm and rough; this they know as Carmakīla.
Due to Vāta, there is pricking pain and roughness; due to Pitta, there is blackness at the tip.
Due to *śleṣman* (phlegm), there is oiliness (*snigdhatā*), a state of being knotted (*grathitatva*), and a similarity in color (*savarṇatā*). 44.
Now, the etiology of weak digestion (*agnimāndya*), indigestion (*ajīrṇa*), choleraic disorder (*visūcikā*), intestinal torpor (*ālasaka*), and chronic dyspepsia (*vilambikā*).
Here follows the etiology of weak digestion, indigestion, choleraic disorder, intestinal torpor, and chronic dyspepsia.
The digestive fire (*jāṭharo 'nalaḥ*) is of four types—dull, sharp, irregular, and even—arising from a predominance of phlegm (*kapha*), bile (*pitta*), and wind (*anila*), or from their equilibrium.
The irregular fire produces diseases born of wind; the sharp fire produces those caused by bile.
Likewise, a weak digestive fire produces disorders arising from phlegm (kapha).

A moderate amount of food eaten by one with a balanced digestive fire is properly digested, whereas even a very small amount is not so for one with a weak fire; however, for a person with an irregular digestive fire, digestion is inconsistent.
Sometimes food is digested properly, and sometimes it is not digested;

he for whom even food eaten in excessive measure is digested comfortably should be known as having a sharp digestive fire (tīkṣṇāgni). One with an even digestive fire (samāgni) is said to be the best. 4.

Some authorities maintain that there are four types of indigestion (ajīrṇa): the undigested (āma), the burnt (vidagdha), the obstructed (viṣṭabdha), caused respectively by the three humors—kapha, pitta, and vāta—and a fourth type arising from the residue of undigested food (rasaśeṣa). Others, however, recognize a fifth type of indigestion which is free from the involvement of the humors and is digested within a single day.
They say that there is also a sixth type of indigestion, which is natural and occurs every day (6).

Due to excessive drinking of water, irregular eating, suppression of natural urges, and the reversal of sleep patterns, even food that is timely, wholesome, and light does not undergo digestion for a person (7).
Food consumed by one overwhelmed by envy, fear, and anger; by one who is greedy; by one afflicted by disease and dejection; or by one possessed by intense hatred, does not undergo proper digestion.
Even wholesome food, when eaten in the correct quantity, does not digest [properly] in such a person.
Due to anxiety, grief, fear, anger, and the sleeplessness caused by painful beds,
there occurs in the stomach a heaviness and excessive moisture, as well as swelling in the cheeks and the regions of the eyes;
furthermore, undigested eructations arise exactly like what was eaten.
In the state of *vidagdha* (acidic digestion), there occurs delusion, thirst, fainting, and various pains due to *pitta*;
moreover, eructations accompanied by smoke and acidity arise, along with perspiration and a burning sensation.
In the state of *viṣṭabdha* (obstructed digestion), there is colic, flatulence, and various types of Vata-related pain.
The non-movement of feces and flatus, stiffness, delusion, and pain in the limbs; when there is a residue of rasa (nutrient fluid), there is aversion to food, impurity and heaviness of the heart,
fainting, delirium, vomiting, excessive salivation, lassitude, and giddiness.
These complications arise, and death itself results from indigestion (ajīrṇa). Those who lack self-control eat like animals without moderation;
they indeed reach the root of the host of diseases, which is indigestion.
The types of indigestion described as *āma*, *viṣṭabdha*, and *vidagdha* give rise to *visūci*,
*alasaka*, and also *vilambikā*.
In *visūci*, the wind (*anila*) remains, piercing the limbs as if with needles.
When that [indigestion] occurs due to undigested food, it is designated by physicians as *visūcī*.

Those who observe moderation in diet and are learned in the scriptures do not suffer from it; rather, it is the deluded ones—those who have not conquered their selves and are greedy for food—who contract it.

In that [condition], fainting, diarrhea, vomiting, thirst, colic, vertigo, convulsions, yawning, burning sensations, discoloration, tremors, pains in the heart, and a splitting sensation in the head occur;
the abdomen becomes excessively distended, the patient faints, and makes moaning sounds.
When the suppressed wind rushes upward within the abdomen,
and when there is excessive suppression of flatus and feces,
it indicates ālasyaka (intestinal torpor); likewise for one who experiences thirst and eructations.
When undigested food (āma), corrupted by kapha and vāta, neither moves upward nor downward,
the ancient experts in the scriptures call that condition *vilambikā*, which is extremely difficult to treat.
Wherever the āma is located, it causes pain specifically in that very region through various types of morbidities.
By whichever humor the body is pervaded, it manifests the symptoms arising from that specific *āmaya*.

A man whose teeth, lips, and nails are discolored, who has diminished consciousness, who suffers from vomiting, whose eyes are sunken inward, whose voice is weak, and whose joints are all loosened— he shall depart for non-return.
Cleanliness of eructation, enthusiasm, timely evacuation of the urges, lightness of the body, and hunger and thirst are the signs of digested food.
(24) Loss of sleep, restlessness, trembling, suppression of urine, and loss of consciousness [are signs of undigested food].
For these five terrible and dreadful complications occur in *visūcī*.
Generally, indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) arises in humans from an imbalance of food;
it is the root of the multitude of diseases, and by its destruction, that multitude perishes.
Malaise, heaviness, constipation, vertigo, numbness from wind (māruta), obstruction, or the onset of [undigested matter]—these are the general symptoms of indigestion (ajīrṇa). 27.
[Now follows] the etiology of worms (krimi).
Now, the etiology of worms:
worms are said to be of two kinds, distinguished by being external or internal; they are further divided into four types based on their origin from external filth, phlegm, blood, or feces. (1)
By name, there are twenty kinds of external [parasites] that arise from impurities;
they are the size, shape, and color of sesame seeds, and they reside in the hair and clothing.
Furthermore, by name, there are those with many legs, the minute ones, the *yūka*, and the *likṣā*.
These two types produce boils, pustules, itching, and swellings.

One who eats while suffering from indigestion, who constantly consumes sweet and sour foods, who is fond of meat, who consumes flour-based foods and molasses, who avoids physical exercise, who sleeps during the day, and who eats incompatible foods, contracts intestinal worms.
Those born from feces arise from black gram flour, sour substances, salt, jaggery, and vegetables;
those originating from phlegm arise from meat, fish, jaggery, milk, curd, and fermented gruel;
and indeed, those arising from blood arise from incompatible foods, indigestion, and leafy greens.
Fever, discoloration, colic, heartburn, lassitude, giddiness,
aversion to food, and diarrhea are the symptoms of worms that have arisen.
Born from phlegm (kapha) in the stomach (āmāśaya), they increase and spread everywhere.
Some resemble broad plows, some are like earthworms,
some have the shape of sprouted grain shoots, and others are thin, long, or minute;
they are white or copper-colored, and thus they are of seven kinds by name.
The *antrādā*, *udarāveṣ� Darbha-flower-like worms, and *mahāguda* worms— these are fragrant and cause nausea,
salivation, indigestion, and loss of appetite. 9–10.
Minute creatures born from blood, residing in the blood-carrying vessels, cause fainting, vomiting, fever, constipation, emaciation, sneezing, and catarrh;
they are footless, circular, and copper-colored, and some are invisible due to their extreme minuteness.
Keśāda, Romavidhvaṃsa, Romadvīpa, Udumbara—these six, along with Kuṣṭha and Saurasamātṛ, share the same function;
When these [doshas] become greatly increased and tend toward the stomach (āmāśaya),
then his eructations and breaths will follow the odor of feces;
they will be large, circular, thin, or thick, and dark-brown, yellow, white, or black.
These five types of worms, known by the names Kakeruka, Makeruka, Sausurada, Shula, and Lelihana, indeed produce diarrhea,
colic, constipation, emaciation, roughness, and pallor.
Horripilation, burning sensation, and a sense of heaviness, along with itching in the anus and discharge through abnormal channels (16).
Now begins the diagnosis of *pāṇḍuroga* (anemia), *kāmalā* (jaundice), *kumbhakāmalā*, and *halīmaka*.
[The diagnosis of] *pāṇḍuroga*, *kāmalā*, *kumbhakāmalā*, and *halīmaka*.
Five types of anemia (pāṇḍuroga) are recognized: three caused by vāta, pitta, and kapha;
the fourth by the combination of all three (sannipāta); and the fifth from the ingestion of earth (mṛdbhakṣaṇa).
[One should avoid] physical exercise, sour things, salts, wine, earth, sleeping during the day, and excessively sharp substances.

In one who indulges [in these], the humors (doṣas), having vitiated the blood, lead the skin to a pale-yellow state (pāṇḍuratā). Cracking of the skin, spitting, lassitude of the limbs, a craving for eating earth, a yellowish swelling of the eyes, and yellowness of the feces and urine— these, along with indigestion, are the precursors of that which is about to arise.

In Vāta-pāṇḍu, there is dryness and a dark, reddish-brown discoloration of the skin, urine, eyes, and other parts, along with pricking pain, trembling, constipation, vertigo, and so forth. In [Pitta-pāṇḍu], the urine, feces, and eyes are yellow, accompanied by burning sensations, thirst, and fever.
A person suffering from pitta-type anemia (pittapāṇḍvāmaya) has loose stools and an excessively yellow complexion.
One with kapha-type anemia has excessive salivation, swelling, drowsiness, lassitude, and extreme heaviness;
due to the kapha, the skin, urine, eyes, and face are white.
A patient suffering from jaundice who is afflicted by fever, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, thirst, and exhaustion,
and who has all three doṣas aggravated, as well as one who is emaciated and has impaired senses, should be abandoned. In one habituated to eating clay, any one of the humors (mala) becomes provoked.
Astringent (kaṣāya) water aggravates wind (vāta), alkaline (ūṣara) water aggravates bile (pitta), and sweet (madhura) water aggravates phlegm (kapha).
Soft water causes diarrhea due to its moisture, and because of its dryness, it dries up the food consumed; moreover, being undigested, it fills and even obstructs the channels (srotas).
Having destroyed the strength of the sense organs, as well as their brilliance, vigor, and vitality,

it quickly causes anemia (pāṇḍuroga), which destroys strength, complexion, and digestive fire. The patient has swelling of the eye-sockets, cheeks, and eyebrows, as well as swelling of the feet, navel, and penis.

One with *krimikoṣṭha* (intestinal worms) suffers from diarrhea accompanied by feces mixed with blood and phlegm. Chronic jaundice (*pāṇḍuroga*) that has become hardened does not succeed [in treatment]; nor does it succeed in those who are swollen for a long duration, or who see yellow objects.

He who suffers from diarrhea characterized by scanty, greenish, and phlegmy stools, being dejected, with his body smeared with white excretions, and afflicted by vomiting, fainting, and thirst; and he who, due to the loss of blood and other factors, becomes pale and attains a whitish complexion—[these are incurable]. (13)
He whose teeth and nails are pale, he whose eyes are pale,
and he who perceives everything as a pale mass— such a person afflicted by jaundice perishes.
One whose extremities are swollen while the middle is wasted away, or likewise whose extremities are withered while the middle is swollen;

One who desires fame should avoid a patient with *pāṇḍu* (anemia/jaundice) who has swelling in the anus, penis, and scrotum, who is fainting and nearly unconscious, as well as one afflicted by diarrhea and fever. Furthermore, a patient suffering from *pāṇḍu* disease who excessively consumes *pittala* (pitta-aggravating) substances [will perish].
Having burnt his bile, blood, and flesh, it leads to disease. His eyes become intensely turmeric-yellow, as do his skin, nails, and face;
his feces and urine are red and yellow, he takes on the color of a frog, and his sensory faculties are destroyed.

Kāmalā, characterized by a burning sensation, lack of digestion, weakness, exhaustion, lassitude, and loss of appetite, is considered to be caused by an excessive flow of pitta affecting both the visceral tract (koṣṭha) and the peripheral tissues (śākhā). When it becomes chronic over time and hardened, it is known as Kumbhakāmalā, which is difficult to cure.

A person whose feces and urine are blackish-yellow, who is excessively swollen, whose eyes, face, vomit, feces, and urine are tinged with blood, and who suffers from fainting, accompanied by burning sensations, loss of appetite, thirst, abdominal distension, drowsiness, and delusion; 19–20.
One whose digestive fire has lost its function quickly perishes from jaundice,
being afflicted by vomiting, loss of appetite, nausea, fever, and exhaustion;
one suffering from dyspnea and cough, and having loose stools, dies of "pot-jaundice" (kumbhakāmala).
When, however, the complexion of the patient becomes greenish, dark-yellow, or pale-yellow;

when there is a loss of strength and enthusiasm, drowsiness, weak digestion, mild fever, lack of sexual desire, body ache, burning sensation, thirst, anorexia, and giddiness— [then it is a sign of imminent death].
Then one should recognize that as *halīmaka*, arising from wind and bile (23).
There is a burning sensation, diarrhea, and yellowness both externally and internally;
furthermore, the patient's eyes exhibit a pale yellow tint, which are the characteristics of *pānaka*.
Now, the etiology of *raktapitta*: through excessive indulgence in heat, physical exercise, grief, travel, and sexual intercourse, [the blood and pitta become provoked].
Pitta, being aggravated by pungent, hot, alkaline, salty, sour,
and bitter substances, quickly burns the blood through its own qualities;
consequently, the blood flows upwards, downwards, or in both directions.
When it is aggravated, it flows upward through the nose, eyes, ears, and mouth; downward through the penis, vagina, and anus; and through all the pores of the skin.
It causes lassitude, a desire for cold things, a sensation of smoke rising in the throat, and vomiting.
In this [condition], the breath will have the smell of iron;
it will be thick, pale, unctuous, and slimy, associated with *kapha*.
That which is dusky-red, frothy, thin, and dry is due to *vāta*.
Raktapitta caused by pitta is reddish-brown, black, resembling cow's urine,
or like the smoke from a dark house and like collyrium;
that which arises from the combination [of two doshas] has combined symptoms, while that which arises from the combination of all three has the symptoms of all three.
That which moves upward is associated with *kapha*, while that which moves downward follows *vāta*;
that which follows both paths is governed by both *kapha* and *vāta*.
That which moves upward is curable, that which moves downward is palliable, and that which moves simultaneously in both directions is incurable.

Raktapitta that follows a single path, is strong yet not excessively rapid, has recently arisen, occurs at a favorable time, is free from complications, and is associated with only one doṣa, is curable. That which involves two doṣas is said to be palliable. (8–9)
That which arises from all three doṣas is incurable, as is that which occurs in one with weak digestion,
excessive force of the disease, a body emaciated by other ailments, or in the elderly who does not eat;
likewise, weakness, dyspnea, cough, fever, vomiting, intoxication, pallor, burning sensations, and fainting [are signs of incurability].

After eating, there is a terrible burning sensation, as well as constant instability and incomparable pain in the heart; thirst, a splitting sensation in the abdomen, and a burning in the head; spitting of foul matter, aversion to food, indigestion, and even morbid changes—these are the complications of *rakta-pitta*. 11.
That which resembles the wash-water of meat, or is like putrid mud-water, or resembles fat, pus, or blood; that which is like liver, or has the luster of a ripe jambū fruit;

that which is black or blue, extremely foul-smelling like a corpse, or where the aforementioned morbid changes occur—that rakta-pitta is to be rejected, as is that which shines like a rainbow in the sky.
Furthermore, the person afflicted by *raktapitta* (blood-bile) who sees the visible world and even the sky as red— this condition is undoubtedly incurable.
Likewise, one who vomits blood profusely and has bloodshot eyes [is incurable].
One who sees blood in vomit dies from a bile-based hemorrhage (raktapaittika). Now begins the etiology of pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman) and wasting due to injury (kṣatakṣīṇa).
From the suppression of natural urges, from depletion, from rashness, and from irregular eating— through these four causes, the disease of consumption (yakṣmā) arises due to the three doṣas.
When the channels of rasa are obstructed by the doṣas, with kapha being predominant...

Or even for one who indulges excessively in sexual intercourse, when the semen is depleted, all the other bodily constituents (dhātus) are subsequently diminished; thereafter, the person withers away.
[The symptoms include: dyspnea, body aches, excessive phlegm, dryness of the palate, vomiting, loss of digestive fire, intoxication, catarrh, cough, and sleepiness.
In the case of consumption (*śoṣa*), these [dreams] occur; that person also becomes pale-eyed, desiring flesh, and longing for the body.
In dreams, crows, parrots, cranes, peacocks, vultures, monkeys, and lizards carry him away; he sees rivers devoid of water, and trees withered, afflicted by wind, smoke, and forest fires.
Burning pain in the shoulders and sides, heat in the hands and feet,
and fever affecting the entire body— these are the symptoms of *rājayakṣman*. Loss of appetite, fever, dyspnea, cough, and the appearance of blood [in the sputum] are also present.
Hoarseness of voice arises; in rājayakṣman there are six symptoms:
from vāta, hoarseness and pain in the shoulders and sides;
from pitta, fever, burning sensation, diarrhea, and the discharge of blood. (6)
Fullness of the head, aversion to food, cough, and hoarseness of the throat should be known as resulting from the provocation of *kapha*.
This [fever] may be accompanied by either all eleven of these symptoms or even by six.

One who desires a perfectly stainless reputation should abandon a person afflicted by consumption (śoṣa) when suffering from cough, diarrhea, pain in the flanks, hoarseness of voice, loss of appetite, and fever— either individually or from three of these symptoms— or from cough, dyspnea, and blood disorders.

One who possesses all three types of signs, or even two, when there is a loss of flesh and strength, should be rejected; however, if the condition is otherwise, even one with all symptoms may be treated.
One who eats excessively while wasting away and is afflicted by diarrhea [is incurable].

One should avoid a person with swollen testicles and a distended abdomen who suffers from consumption (yakṣman). Consumption destroys a man in this world who has white eyes, who loathes food, who is oppressed by upward-breathing (orthopnea), and who voids urine excessively with great difficulty.

One should treat a man who is free from lingering fever, strong, capable of enduring treatment, self-controlled, possessing a keen digestive fire, and not emaciated; as well as those who have been withered by sexual indulgence, grief, old age, physical exercise, or travel on foot. 13.
Now hear the characteristics of those suffering from wasting due to wounds and chest injuries (14).
One who suffers from wasting due to sexual excess is afflicted by the signs of seminal depletion;
his body becomes pale, and his bodily tissues waste away as before (15).
Constantly lost in thought, with drooping limbs, he is likewise withered by grief;
emaciated by old age, he is lean, with his vigor, intellect, strength, and senses all diminished.
He trembles, has no appetite, and his voice is broken like that of a cracked bell-metal vessel.
Afflicted by heaviness and aversion, he spits out phlegm that is deficient [in quantity]; his mouth, nose, and eyes are constantly running; his complexion is parched, dry, and scaly;
he is withered by travel, his limbs are drooping, and his skin is scorched and harsh. (17–18)

With the limbs and members of the body sluggish, with the *kloma*, throat, and mouth parched, excessively emaciated by physical exertion, and endowed with most of the symptoms produced by chest-wounds— even in the absence of an actual wound— [one is afflicted by this disease]. (19)
From the loss of blood, from painful sensations, and likewise from the restriction of food, consumption may arise in one who is wounded; and that is considered most incurable.
(20) [This occurs] in one who exerts himself excessively with a bow or who carries a heavy load.
While fighting with the powerful, or falling from a high and uneven place;
while running after a bull or a horse, or restraining a wild animal;
while hurling blows with stones, wood, or rocks, or striking down enemies—(in these situations, one may speak). 21–22.
Or for one who is reciting very loudly, or walking a great distance quickly, or crossing large rivers, or running along with horses;
or for one who suddenly rises up and goes far away, or who dances rapidly. (23)
Likewise, in one who is severely afflicted by other cruel karmas,
or when the chest is wounded, a powerful disease is provoked;
this also occurs in one who is excessively attached to women and who eats food that is dry, scanty, or measured.
The chest becomes excessively divided, split, and aching; then both sides are oppressed, the limbs wither, and one trembles.
Gradually, vitality, strength, complexion, appetite, and digestive fire decline. (26)
Fever, pain, mental depression, diarrhea, and loss of digestive fire also occur.
Furthermore, when coughing repeatedly, there flows forth a large amount of phlegm that is vitiated, dark-brown, extremely foul-smelling, yellow, clotted, and mixed with blood. (27–28)
In one with chest injury (kṣata), there is excessive wasting due to the depletion of semen and ojas;
its unmanifest signs are known as the premonitory symptoms (pūrvarūpa).
Chest pain, vomiting of blood, and a specific type of cough occur in the case of chest injury.

When [the doshas] are diminished, there is blood-stained urine and stiffness in the sides, back, and waist. A case with few symptoms, occurring in a person with a strong digestive fire and great strength, is curable if it is recent; one that has persisted for a year is palliable; however, one exhibiting all the symptoms should be rejected as incurable.
Now, the causes of cough are as follows: from injury by smoke, from the consumption of unwholesome food, and likewise from physical exertion and the intake of dry foods.
Indeed, due to eating while on a wrong path, or from the suppression of natural urges such as sneezing, the *prāṇa* wind, following the *udāna*, becomes vitiated;
it suddenly issues forth from the mouth with a sound resembling that of a cracked bell-metal vessel, accompanied by morbid humors (*doṣa*). This is designated as "cough" (*kāsa*) by the wise.
Five types of cough are recognized: those caused by vāta, pitta, śleṣman, chest injury (kṣata), and wasting (kṣaya).
If all of these are neglected, they lead to emaciation; furthermore, each subsequent one is more severe than the preceding.
Their premonitory symptom is a sensation as if the throat and mouth were filled with bristles.
Itching in the throat and obstruction to food occur;
afflicted by pain in the heart, temples, head, abdomen, and flanks, with a withered face and diminished strength,
voice, and vitality, the patient suffers from constant urges and, due to the wind (vāta), coughs up only dry matter with a broken voice.

Afflicted by burning pain in the chest, fever, and dryness of the mouth, with a bitter taste in the mouth and tormented by thirst, one vomits yellow and pungent matter due to pitta; he coughs, is pale, and suffers from a burning sensation.
With a mouth as if smeared [with phlegm], sinking down, afflicted by headache, and with his body filled with kapha— 6. [Thus is the patient described.]
One afflicted by lack of appetite, indigestion, heaviness, and itching, with thick phlegm, should cough excessively due to the accumulation of *kapha*.

(7) In one who is dry due to excessive sexual indulgence, carrying heavy loads, walking long distances, fighting, or struggling with horses and elephants, the *vāyu* seizes the chest and causes a cough. (8)
First he coughs dryly, and then he spits out blood;
with his throat excessively pained and his chest as if shattered,
he suffers as if being pierced by sharp needles and is tormented by piercing pains.
Afflicted by the painful touch of a piercing agony that causes splitting and tormenting pain,
and oppressed by the breaking of joints, fever, labored breathing, thirst,
and loss of voice, he utters cries like a pigeon due to the force of coughing born from internal injury.

In men who consume unwholesome food, engage in excessive sexual intercourse, suppress natural urges, or are characterized by loathing and grief, the three humors become aggravated when the digestive fire is impaired;
they then cause cough born of wasting (kṣayaja-kāsa), which brings about the destruction of the body.

He may experience body aches, fever, burning sensations, and delusion, as well as the loss of vital strength; coughing and becoming emaciated, the weak patient with wasted flesh spits out blood mixed with pus.
Those who know medical treatment call this "kṣayaja" (wasting-type) when it exhibits all these symptoms and is extremely difficult to cure. 13

Thus, this cough born of wasting (kṣayaja-kāsa) destroys the bodies of those who are already emaciated; it may be curable for the strong, but in such cases, that which arises from injury (kṣata-ja) is only palliable.
However, if both types are newly arisen and endowed with one-quarter of their natural strength, they may sometimes be cured.

In the elderly, all coughs caused by old age are declared to be palliative; one should treat the three curable types with curative measures, while one should manage the palliative types with supportive care. (15) This concludes the etiology of hiccup and dyspnea.
Now, the etiology of hiccup and dyspnea: [it arises] from foods that cause burning, heaviness, constipation, dryness, or excessive secretions;
and from cold drinks, food, and dwellings, as well as dust, smoke, sunlight, and wind. 1.
Hiccups, dyspnea, and cough arise in men due to physical exertion, labor, carrying heavy loads, travel, suppression of natural urges, and fasting.
The vāyu repeatedly rises with a sound, as if throwing the liver, spleen, and intestines out through the mouth.

Because it makes a loud sound and swiftly destroys the vital breaths (asus), it is therefore called *hikkā* by the wise. Indeed, the wind (*vāyu*), accompanied by phlegm (*kapha*), produces five types of hiccups: those born of food (*annajā*), the twin (*yamalā*), the small (*kṣudrā*), the deep-seated (*gambhīrā*), and the great (*mahatī*).
Heaviness in the throat and chest, astringency of the mouth, hiccups,
and distension of the abdomen are the premonitory symptoms [of hiccups]. Furthermore,
when the bodily wind (vāyu) is suddenly provoked by excessive consumption of food and drink, it causes these afflictions.
The physician should recognize that as *annajā* (food-born) which, having moved upward, causes hiccuping;
that hiccup which proceeds with slow and double (yamala) paroxysms,
shaking the head and neck, one should designate as *yamalā*.
That hiccup which occurs with long intervals and slow force,
having surged up from the base of the collarbones, is called *kṣudrikā*. That hiccup which originates from the navel is terrible and makes a deep sound.
That [fever] which is accompanied by many complications is known as Gambhīrā;
that which proceeds constantly as if piercing the vital points (marmans) and causing all the limbs to tremble should be recognized as Mahāhikkā.

One whose body is stretched out while hiccuping, whose gaze is constantly turned upward, who is emaciated, who loathes food, and who sneezes excessively— these two types of persons suffering from hiccups should be abandoned as they approach their end. This applies especially to one whose humors (doṣas) are excessively accumulated and who has been weakened by the cessation of food intake.
In one whose body is emaciated by diseases, who is aged, or who has overindulged in sexual intercourse,
the hiccup that arises from these [causes] quickly destroys life— especially when it is double (yamikā) and accompanied by delirium, distress, confusion, and thirst.
This [attainment] can be accomplished by one who is undiminished, not dejected, and possesses stable elements and faculties; otherwise, it cannot be achieved.
(14) It is fivefold through the distinctions of great, high, severed, dark, and small.

That great disease is divided [into types], specifically into one called *śvāsa* (dyspnea). *Kṣudra-śvāsa* (minor dyspnea) arises from an excess of *vāta*, while *stamaka* (asthma) is born from *kapha*.
Furthermore, that which is characterized by a combination of both *kapha* and *vāta* is known as *saṃsṛṣṭa* (combined) or *chinna-saṃjñaka* (the interrupted type).
Breath mixed with wind (māruta) is considered the great upward-moving [breath] (mahā-ūrdhva).
Its premonitory symptoms are pain in the heart, colic, flatulence, constipation, a bad taste in the mouth, and piercing pain in the temples. 12–16.
When the wind (māruta), preceded by phlegm (kapha), obstructs the channels and moves in all directions while being constricted, it then produces various types of dyspnea (śvāsa).
That man whose wind is agitated and who breathes with a sound experiences great suffering.
Obstructed, he pants loudly and incessantly like a rutting bull;
his knowledge and discernment are lost, his eyes are wandering, his mouth and eyes are agape, his urine and excrement are suppressed, and his speech is broken.
The sighing of one who is dejected is clearly perceived from afar;
however, one afflicted by labored breathing (mahāśvāsa) perishes very quickly.
He who breathes out long and upward, but cannot draw the breath back down, [is likewise lost].
With the channels of his mouth obstructed by phlegm and afflicted by the provoked wind (vāyu),
he gazes upward and looks about with eyes wandering here and there; he becomes deluded, tormented by pain, has a pale face, and is oppressed by restlessness.
When the upward breath (ūrdhvaśvāsa) is provoked, the downward breath (adhaḥśvāsa) is obstructed;
as the patient faints and gasps for air, that very upward breath destroys his life-breaths. He who breathes with broken intervals, oppressed by all his vital energy, [is likewise lost].
Afflicted by suffering and tormented by the pain of the severing of his vital organs, he does not even breathe (24).
Distressed by abdominal distension, sweating, and fainting, with his bladder burning,
his eyes rolling, emaciated, gasping for breath, and with one eye turned blood-red (25).
Confused in mind, with parched mouth and discolored complexion, the man who speaks incoherently and is cut off by labored breathing quickly abandons his life-breaths (26).
This occurs when the vital wind moves in a contrary direction, entering the channels in reverse order.
Seizing the neck and head and provoking the phlegm,
it causes chronic catarrh (pīnasa), as well as a wheezing sound (ghurghuraka) when obstructed,
and an extremely violent breathlessness (śvāsa) that afflicts life itself.

He faints from the force [of the breath], becomes thirsty, and is constricted; coughing, he repeatedly falls into a state of delusion (29). When the phlegm is not released, he becomes intensely distressed.
And at the end of that very liberation, he obtains happiness for a moment;
likewise, his throat becomes parched, and with great difficulty he is able to speak,
nor does he find sleep while lying down, being oppressed by labored breathing.
The wind seizes his side as he lies down;
when sitting, he finds no comfort and longs for warmth.
With eyes staring upward and a forehead profusely perspiring, he is in great agony. (32)
With a parched mouth, frequent labored breathing, and repeatedly making a blowing sound,
this condition increases due to clouds, rainwater, cold, eastern winds, and phlegm-inducing factors;
such Tamaka-śvāsa is palliable, though it may be curable if it has recently arisen.

One should recognize that Pratamaka occurs in one who is overwhelmed by fever and fainting; it arises from upward-moving wind (udāvarta), dust, indigestion, or the obstruction of a body saturated with fluids.
It increases excessively during darkness and is quickly pacified by cold measures.
One should recognize *saṃtamaka* as being like fainting in darkness.
*Kṣudra-śvāsa* (minor dyspnea) arises from dryness and exertion when the minor *vāta* is provoked in the digestive tract; it is not excessively painful nor does it greatly afflict the limbs.
It does not injure his limbs, nor is there suffering as with others;
it does not obstruct the proper passage of food and drink, nor does it cause any affliction or pain to the sense organs. 38.
It is said that all [types of] *śvāsa* when occurring in a strong person are curable, yet they possess unmanifest symptoms.
O Kṣudra! Among them, *tamaka* is considered curable, while *kṛcchra* is said to be difficult to treat.
Three types of *śvāsa* are not cured, as is *tamaka* occurring in a weak person.
Granted that there are many diseases that take away life, yet they are not like dyspnea and hiccough, which snatch away life so swiftly. (41) The etiology of hoarseness.
Now, regarding the etiology of hoarseness (*svarabheda*): the wind and other [doshas], provoked by excessive speaking, the study of toxic texts, physical trauma, or corrupting factors,
enter the channels that carry the voice and establish themselves there.
The voice may indeed be destroyed, for it is of six types:
caused by vāta and the others individually, by all of them combined, by medas (fat), and by wasting (kṣaya).
Due to vāta, the eyes, face, urine, and feces become black; one speaks slowly with a broken voice that is harsh like that of a donkey.
One should say that when bile (pitta) is involved, the eyes, face, urine, and feces become yellow, and there is a burning sensation in the throat.

When phlegm (kapha) is involved, the throat is constantly obstructed by phlegm; one speaks very little and slowly, especially during the day. The sages declare that when all three [humors] are involved, all the symptoms appear together, and such a case of hoarseness of voice (svarabheda) is incurable.
Speech may become smoky when caused by wasting (kṣaya), and it reaches a state of exhaustion; such a person, whose speech is impaired, should be avoided.
One with a coated throat speaks after a long time, with a voice that has lost its internal resonance and with indistinct words, due to the accumulation of fat and being afflicted by thirst.
[This applies] to one who is emaciated, aged, or thin, whether the disease arose long ago or was born together with him.
One who is obese, from whom everything arises, and whose voice is diseased—such a person does not attain success. 5.
Now, the etiology of anorexia (arocaka).
Here follows the etiology of anorexia.

Loss of appetite may arise from wind (vāta) and other humors, as well as from grief, fear, excessive greed, anger, mental distress, improper food, or foul sights and smells. When the teeth are excessively sensitive and the mouth has an astringent taste, it is considered to be caused by wind (anila). One should recognize a bitter, sour, hot, tasteless, or putrid mouth, as well as a salty mouth, as being caused by bile (pitta).
Anorexia (arocaka) arises from grief, fear, excessive greed, anger, and other such factors, as well as from unwholesome sights and foul odors.
In the natural state, the mouth may be unpleasant; however, when caused by the three *doṣas*, the taste is not uniform.
It is accompanied by pain and pressure in the heart due to *vāta*, while from *pitta* it is characterized by great thirst, burning sensations, parching, and excessive salivation with *kapha*.

One should know that the [vomit] caused by phlegm is characterized by many pains and by various defects such as delusion and dullness; this is another [type]. 4. Now begins the diagnosis of vomiting (chardi-nidāna). Now, the diagnosis of vomiting.

The five types of vomiting (chardi) are to be understood as being caused by individual or all the humors (doṣas) combined with loathsome sights and other factors; their characteristics are now described. [Vomiting] from excessively dry, excessively unctuous, unpalatable, or excessively salty substances...
By eating at improper times, in excessive quantities, or foods that are unwholesome;
by fatigue, fear, agitation, indigestion, or the presence of parasitic worms; in women who are pregnant, or by eating too quickly—(these cause the tongue to become stiff). 2–3.

When the humors (doṣas) are forcibly provoked by disgusting causes or other factors, they rush toward the mouth with great speed, covering the face and causing pain through convulsions that break the limbs; this condition is designated as vomiting (chardi). 4.
Nausea, suppression of eructation, salivation, a salty taste, emaciation, and a strong aversion to food and drink are the premonitory symptoms of vomiting.
[5] [These are further accompanied by] pain in the heart and flanks, dryness of the mouth, distress in the head and navel, cough, hoarseness of voice, and piercing pains.
Afflicted by wind (vāta), the patient here vomits with great difficulty and force, producing a sound like belching, accompanied by foam, broken into fragments, blackish, thin, and astringent;
he suffers greatly from fainting, thirst, dryness of the mouth, and a burning sensation in the head, palate, and eyes, as well as from darkness and vertigo.
One afflicted by pitta vomits what is yellow, intensely hot, green, bitter, and smoky, accompanied by a burning sensation (7).

One suffering from drowsiness, sweetness in the mouth, salivation, a sense of satiety, sleepiness, loss of appetite, and heaviness vomits what is unctuous, thick, sweet, and frothy due to kapha; this is accompanied by horripilation and little pain (8).

For those men who vomit saltish, sour, blue, thick, hot, and bloody matter due to the three *doṣas*, there will be constant pain, indigestion, burning, thirst, labored breathing, and great delusion. When the wind, having obstructed the channels that carry feces, sweat, urine, and water, moves upwards; 9.
When the humors have been suppressed, that accumulated humor is violently expelled from the person's abdomen;
it is equal in smell and color to feces and urine, and accompanied by persistent thirst, dyspnea, hiccups, and pain.
Due to this excessive forceful vomiting, the corrupted humor is discharged, and the patient quickly meets with destruction.

That [nausea] which arises from loathing, from pregnancy-longing, from fasting, from unwholesome food, and that fifth type which arises from worms— one should understand that as being caused by the very aggravation of the *doṣas*, as previously described. In particular, the type arising from worms is characterized by an abundance of colic and nausea.
That vomiting which is characterized by symptoms identical to those of *krimihṛd* (heart-disease caused by worms) should be recognized as such.

One should declare that vomiting which occurs in a weakened person, is excessively persistent, accompanied by complications, and mixed with blood and pus—resembling the *candrakā* (moon-stain)—to be incurable; however, one should treat that which is curable and free from complications.
Cough, dyspnea, absence of fever, hiccup, thirst, mental confusion, heart disease, and asthma should be known as the complications (upadrava) of vomiting (chardi). 15.
The Etiology of Thirst (tṛṣṇā-nidāna).
Now, thirst arises when pitta, aggravated by its own causes, by fear, fatigue, or loss of strength, and increased by factors that augment pitta,
becomes provoked along with vāta and reaches the palate in human beings.

When the channels carrying water are vitiated by the *doṣas*, thirst arises here in a living being. At the time of its onset, the following specific premonitory symptoms indeed appear: a burning sensation and heat in the palate, lips, throat, and mouth, along with delusion, giddiness, and incoherent speech.
These three are traditionally recognized; the fourth arises from wasting (kṣaya), and likewise that produced from undigested matter (āma).
Know that the seventh arises from food (bhakta); now learn their symptoms in due order:
in the one born of wind (māruta), there is emaciation of the face as well as a pricking pain in the temples and the head.
Cessation of the flow [of saliva], a distasteful mouth, and swelling with cold water;

fainting, aversion to food, lamentation, burning sensations, redness of the eyes, constant emaciation, longing for cold things, bitterness in the mouth, and a general sense of distress—these occur in the Pitta-type [fever]. 3–4.
