When the digestive fire is obstructed by phlegm due to the suppression of tears, thirst arises from that *balāsa* (phlegm), as well as sleepiness, heaviness, and a sweet taste in the mouth; one afflicted by this dries up excessively. Thirst caused by injury (*kṣataja*) is considered the fourth type, resulting from the pain of a wound and the loss of blood.

That [fever] which arises from the depletion of the *rasa* (plasma) is known as *kṣaya-sambhavā*; one overcome by it drinks water with great longing during the nights and days, yet finds no relief. Some authorities call this *sannipāta*.
The physician should diagnose it completely by observing all the symptoms mentioned for the depletion of *rasa*.
Arising from the three doṣas and from undigested matter (āma), it causes heart pain, spitting, and exhaustion;
likewise, the consumption of unctuous, sour, salty, or heavy food quickly produces thirst.
The patient has a weak voice, is fainting, is dejected, and has a parched mouth, throat, and palate.
Indeed, that thirst which arises from such afflictions is emaciating and painful;
it occurs in those whose bodies are afflicted by fever, delusion, wasting, cough, dyspnea, and the like,
and it is present in all those who are excessively attached to worldly things, who are emaciated by disease, or who are afflicted by vomiting.
Thirst associated with terrible afflictions should be understood as leading to death.
Now, the etiology of fainting, vertigo, sleep, lethargy, and syncope.
Now, the etiology of fainting, vertigo, sleep, lethargy, and syncope.
In one who is emaciated, whose humors are greatly aggravated, who consumes incompatible food, or who, being of weak constitution, suppresses natural urges or suffers a physical injury,
intense pains arise in the external and internal sense organs.
When the humors (doṣas) settle [in the channels], then human beings lose consciousness.
When the channels carrying perception are obstructed by wind and the other humors,
darkness suddenly overcomes them, causing the cessation of pleasure and pain.
When a person falls like a log due to the removal of pleasure and pain,
that state is called fainting (moha); it is proclaimed to be of six kinds,
caused by wind and the other humors, by blood, by alcohol, and by poison.
In all six of these [diseases], however, bile (pitta) predominates.
Heartache, yawning, lassitude, and weakness of consciousness are the premonitory symptoms of them all; one should recognize them according to their respective natures.
Seeing the sky as blue, or black, or even reddish, he enters into darkness and awakens quickly;
there is trembling, aching of the limbs, and pain in the heart.
In fainting caused by Vāta, there is emaciation and a dusky-red complexion;
seeing the sky as red, green, or yellow, the patient enters into darkness and awakens perspiring.
Thirsty and afflicted with heat, with eyes clouded by red and yellow,
one who faints immediately upon birth and quickly regains consciousness, and whose stool is broken and yellowish— such a child has fainted due to the arising of *pitta*. 10.
Seeing the sky covered with dense masses of darkness like clouds, he enters into darkness and awakens only after a long time,
just as one whose limbs are covered by heavy hides feels as if they were covered by the skin of a mountain.

Accompanied by salivation and nausea, when fainting arises from phlegm (kapha), it possesses all the symptoms; having arrived like epilepsy (apasmāra) due to the derangement of all three humors (sannipāta),
it quickly casts the person down, even without loathsome movements.
Earth and water are of the nature of *tamas*, and red fragrance is their derivative;
therefore, on this earth, human beings faint from the scent of blood.
Some say that this is the inherent nature of substances, seeing that one becomes deluded upon perceiving it.
The qualities [of poison and alcohol] exist in a more intense state in both poison and liquor;
therefore, from those two, the two types of delusion arise as previously described.
One who is fainted by blood has stiffened limbs and eyes, and shallow breathing. (15–16)
Lamenting through intoxication, he lies with his mind ruined and bewildered,
tossing his limbs upon the ground until he reaches old age;
trembling, sleep, thirst, and darkness also occur when one is unconscious from poison.

It should be understood that [the poison] is more intense according to its own specific characteristics: fainting (mūrchā) arises primarily from bile and darkness (tamas); dizziness (bhrama) from passion (rajas), bile, and wind (vāta);
lethargy (tandrā) from darkness, wind, and phlegm (kapha); and sleep (nidrā) arises from phlegm and darkness. 18–19.
When the body constantly falls to the ground as if spinning like a wheel,
it should be known as *bhrama-rogah* (the disease of vertigo), which consists of *rajas*, *pitta*, and *anila*.
There is also lack of perception regarding the objects of the senses, heaviness, yawning, and exhaustion.
One should diagnose sleepiness as being like that of one who has violated the cosmic order (*ṛta*); likewise, one should point out lethargy (*tandrā*) in such a person.

When the force of the humors (*doṣas*) causing intoxication and fainting has spent itself in embodied beings, these conditions subside by themselves; however, a state of total unconsciousness (*saṃnyāsa*) does not subside without medicines.
The exceedingly powerful impurities, having seized the activity of speech, body, and mind, abandon the weak creature while residing within the seat of the vital breaths.
Thus, he is one who has been "renounced" by renunciation; become like a piece of wood, he is as if dead.
One is quickly released from life after performing an act that yields immediate results.
Now begins the diagnosis of alcoholism (*pānātyaya*), intoxication (*paramada*), indigestion from drinking (*pānājīrṇa*), and the confusion caused by drinking (*pānavibhrama*).
Now begins the diagnosis of alcoholism (*pānātyaya*), intoxication (*paramada*), indigestion from drinking (*pānājīrṇa*), and the confusion caused by drinking (*pānavibhrama*).

Whatever qualities are declared for poison are also established in wine; therefore, when consumed improperly, it causes severe intoxication. However, by its very nature, wine is considered to be just like food.

That which is improperly administered leads to disease, while that which is properly administered is like nectar. Food is the life-force for living beings; when taken improperly, it destroys the vital breaths, yet even poison that takes away life becomes an elixir (rasāyana) when properly administered.

For one who drinks wine joyfully according to the prescribed method, in proper measure, at the right time, with wholesome food, and in accordance with their strength— when consumed together with unctuous foods, meats, and edibles— it becomes like nectar. (4)

When liquor is consumed according to the prescribed rules, it leads to the prolongation of life, as well as strength and physical growth; moreover, the qualities of desirability, mental satisfaction, brilliance, and even valor are present therein. (5–6)

The first stage of intoxication is said to be exceedingly delightful; it brings joy through the recollection of the Buddha, is pleasant, increases the enjoyment of food, drink, and sleep, and enhances the quality of chanting and singing.
(7) In the second stage, one's intellect, memory, speech, and movements become indistinct; one behaves like a madman and is not tranquil.

Stricken repeatedly by sloth and sleep, and intoxicated in his middle stage by passion, a man may approach those who should not be approached and fail to respect his elders; he eats what should not be eaten, loses his sense of propriety, and in the third stage of intoxication, lacking self-control, he speaks the secrets hidden in his heart. 8–9.
But in the fourth stage of intoxication, one is deluded and motionless like a broken log; no longer discerning between what should and should not be done, he is dead even more than a corpse.
Who would indulge in such intoxication, which is like another form of madness? 10.10
Like a wise and self-controlled person traversing a wilderness full of many dangers,
a man who constantly consumes liquor that is utterly devoid of any wholesome qualities will bring about most grievous disorders and even cause the dissolution of the body.
By one who is angry, afraid, thirsty, tormented by grief, hungry,
exhausted by physical exertion, heavy loads, or travel, or even afflicted by the suppression of natural urges;
likewise by one whose stomach is distended from excessive drinking or eating, or who has eaten during indigestion, or who is weak.
When consumed by one afflicted by heat, liquor produces various disorders:
alcoholism (pānātyaya), extreme intoxication (paramada), indigestion from drinking (pānājīrṇa), and severe alcohol-induced delirium (pānavibhrama); I shall now describe the symptoms of these.
One should recognize a case of alcoholism (madātyaya) dominated by Vāta by the presence of hiccups, dyspnea, trembling of the head, pain in the flanks, insomnia, and much delirious talk.
[16] [A case dominated by Pitta is characterized by] thirst, burning sensation, fever, perspiration, delusion, diarrhea, and confusion.
One should recognize that a greenish discoloration indicates a pitta-predominant alcoholism (madātyaya).

One should recognize that when the patient is overcome by coldness accompanied by vomiting, anorexia, nausea, drowsiness, a sense of being wrapped in a wet cloth, and heaviness, it is a kapha-predominant alcoholism.
Madātyaya arising from all three doṣas should also be recognized by all their symptoms:
an increase of phlegm (śleṣman), heaviness of the limbs, a bad taste in the mouth,
retention of feces and urine, as well as drowsiness and anorexia.
Those who know the truth say that the symptoms of this supreme intoxication are thirst,
pain in the head and the joints, burning sensations, splitting pains, severe flatulence, vomiting, and a burning acidity. 19.
When one consumes [the poison] in water, the following symptoms arise:
piercing pain in the heart and limbs, discharge of phlegm, a sensation of smoke in the throat, fainting, vomiting, fever, headache, and a burning sensation. 20.
The wise declare that aversion even toward various preparations of wine and food constitutes the entirety of that delusion of drinking;
it is characterized by a parched upper lip, extreme coldness, and intense burning.
One should also abandon a horse that has the luster of oil, or one struck by a drink [of poison],
or one whose tongue, lips, and teeth are black or blue,
or whose eyes are yellow or have the luster of blood.
Hiccups, fever, vomiting, tremors, pain in the flanks, cough, and vertigo—these afflict one who has consumed [alcohol] improperly; this is the origin of burning sensations.
22. The Etiology of Dāha.
When that heat of the drink reaches the skin, it becomes intensified by pitta and blood and produces a terrible burning sensation; the remedy for this is the same as for pitta disorders.
Blood that has become aggravated and spreads throughout the entire body certainly causes a burning sensation.
He feels feverish and thirsty; his complexion becomes coppery and his eyes likewise.
His body and face emit the smell of iron, as if he were being scorched by fire.
This condition is known as pitta-jvara (bilious fever), and its treatment is prescribed according to the methods for pitta.
Due to the cessation of craving, when the water element has been exhausted, the fire element becomes intensely agitated;
it may burn the body—both internal and external—of one with dull intellect.
With his throat, palate, and lips parched, he draws out his tongue and trembles.
For one whose internal cavities are filled with blood, there occurs another burning sensation that is extremely difficult to endure.

That burning sensation arising from the depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātu-kṣaya) causes fainting and thirst; afflicted by it, the patient becomes weak-voiced, deprived of the power of action, and sinks down, being intensely tormented.
Blood-born fever occurs in one who abstains from food, or in one who grieves in many ways;
by this, the patient is consumed internally, characterized by thirst, fainting, and delirium.
There is also that born from injury to a vital organ (marman); this is considered the seventh type and is incurable.
Indeed, all [these factors] should be avoided by an embodied being whose limbs have become cold. 7. Now begins the diagnosis of insanity (unmāda-nidāna).
Because the defects (doṣas), having become excessively aggravated and having deviated from their proper course, cause intoxication,
this mental disorder is therefore proclaimed as "unmāda" (insanity).
It arises both individually and collectively from the defects that have reached a state of extreme intensification.
And mental suffering is considered to be of five kinds;
the sixth arises from poison, and for each there is its own appropriate remedy.
Furthermore, when it is not fully developed and is still young, it bears the name "mada" (intoxication).
Incompatible, harmful, or impure foods; the assault of gods, gurus, or the twice-born;

mental trauma preceded by fear or joy; and irregular physical activities—these are the causes of insanity. By these, the vitiated humors (malas) of a person of weak constitution corrupt the heart, which is the abode of the intellect.
Occupying the channels that carry the mind, they quickly delude the consciousness of a person.
Confusion of intellect, agitation of the mind, a turbid vision, lack of fortitude,
incoherent speech, and a vacant heart are the general symptoms of the disease of insanity.
When vāyu is excessively aggravated by dry, scanty, or cold food, purgation, depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātus), or fasting,
it vitiates the heart corrupted by anxiety and other factors, and swiftly destroys both intellect and memory.
[The patient exhibits] inappropriate laughter, smiling, dancing, singing, speech, flailing of limbs, and weeping.

Harshness, emaciation, a reddish complexion, and weakness when the food is digested are the symptoms of [unmada] born of vāta. (8) Pitta, accumulated by undigested food and by pungent, sour, burning, and cold edibles, having its force intensified, quickly produces an extremely fierce unmadā that affects the mindless person, as described previously, once it is situated in the heart. (9)

Impatience, agitation, a state of nakedness, threats, excessive running, heat, and anger; a desire for shade, cold food, and water, and a yellowish complexion—these are the signs of that which is produced by *pitta*.
When *kapha* is severely vitiated in a vital organ (*marman*) due to over-satiation and lack of physical exertion, it becomes hot. 10.
It impairs growth and memory, deludes the mind, and produces morbid changes.

In the case of the kapha-type, there is sluggishness of speech and movement, loss of appetite, a fondness for women and solitude, excessive sleep, vomiting, salivation, consumption of strength, whiteness of the nails and other parts, and so forth. (11–12)

That which arises from a combination [of humors] and is extremely terrible occurs through all the causes combined; it assumes all symptoms and must be avoided as its treatment involves mutually contradictory remedies.
[This applies to one] who is terrified by thieves, royal officers, enemies, or others, or due to the loss of wealth and kinsmen.
When the mind is deeply wounded by a beloved woman who desires to sport, an exceedingly intense transformation of the mind arises;
bewildered and deprived of his senses, he speaks strangely according to the dictates of his mind, and he sings, laughs, and even weeps.
With bloodshot eyes, his strength and senses destroyed, extremely dejected, and with a dark-complexioned face, he becomes unconscious when afflicted by poison;
moreover, such a man may fall prone or stand upright, his flesh and strength utterly wasted.
For one who is vigilant, there is no doubt that he will not perish through insanity.

One whose speech, prowess, valor, and actions are immortal, and who possesses knowledge, specialized understanding, strength, and other such qualities, yet for whom the onset of insanity is unpredictable—that one should be declared as having insanity arising from the influence of spirits (bhūta). (16–17)

Contented, pure, possessing the scent of most divine garlands, free from drowsiness, speaking with unerring and refined speech, radiant, steady-eyed, a bestower of boons, devoted to Brahmanas— such a man becomes beloved by the gods.
(18) One who perspires excessively, speaks of the faults of the twice-born, gurus, and gods, has downcast eyes, is devoid of fear, and looks toward the wrong path [is one who does not attain this].
That evil-minded person, who is not satisfied with various kinds of food and drink, is possessed by a *deva-śatru* (demon).

(19) A man afflicted by the *gandharva-graha* dances and laughs beautifully with soft sounds; his mind is joyful, he frequents riverbanks and forest interiors, his conduct is refined, and he delights in music, perfumes, and garlands. (20)

One with copper-colored eyes, wearing pleasant red garments, deep-voiced, moving swiftly, speaking little, patient, and radiant—such a person asks, "What shall I give, and to whom? This is the man afflicted by the *yakṣa* spirit.
He, being peaceful in soul and dressed in garments turned to the left, offers rice-balls upon the sacrificial grass for the *pretas*. (21)
One who desires meat, who longs for sesame, molasses, and milk-rice pudding, and who is devoted to them, is possessed by a paternal spirit (pitṛ-graha).
But he who at times glides along the ground like a serpent and likewise licks the corners of his mouth with his tongue,
being full of anger and desiring molasses, honey, milk, and milk-rice pudding, should be known as one possessed by a serpent (bhujaṅgama).

Desirous of meat, blood, and various kinds of liquor, shameless, exceedingly cruel, and over-bold, prone to anger, possessed of great strength, wandering at night, and hating purity— one seized by the *rākṣasas* becomes thus.
(24) With upraised arms, emaciated and harsh, speaking incoherently for a short time, foul-smelling, extremely impure, and likewise very fickle;
One who eats excessively, dwells in secluded forest interiors, makes frantic gestures, wanders about weeping, and is possessed by a *piśāca* [25];
one with swollen eyes, who runs swiftly, licks foam, is drowsy, falls down, and trembles;
and one who has fallen from a mountain, an elephant, or a tree—if such a person exists, he becomes incurable, as does one in the thirteenth year [of the disease]. [26]
The planetary spirits (devagrahas) afflict on the full moon day; the asuras also on the two twilights;
the gandharvas mostly on the eighth day; and the yakṣas on the first day of the lunar fortnight.
The ancestors (pitṛs) afflict on the new moon day, and the serpents (uragas) on the fifth day.
For indeed, Rākṣasas enter at night and Piśācas on the fourteenth day;
just as a reflection enters a mirror and the like, just as cold and heat enter living beings,
and just as the sun’s rays enter its own jewel and the embodied soul enters the body.
Just as planets enter [a body] yet are not seen, so too do embodied beings;
having quickly entered the body, they indeed inflict unbearable pain.
Likewise, there are severe austerities, as well as charity, vows, righteousness, self-restraint, and truth.
Likewise, those eight qualities are eternal within them, both individually and collectively, according to their respective power.
They do not dwell together with human beings, nor do they ever enter into human beings;
those who say that they enter [human beings] out of delusion are to be excluded from the domain of the science of spirits (bhūtavidyā).
The attendants of those planets, numbering in the thousands of millions of billions,
who consume blood, fat, and flesh, who are most terrifying, and who roam at night— these likewise enter [the body] as the cause of epilepsy.
Now, regarding the etiology of epilepsy (apasmāra):
the humors (doṣas), provoked by anxiety, grief, and other such factors, reside in the channels of the heart;
having caused the destruction of memory, they produce epilepsy. (1)

The entry into darkness, agitation, and the loss of memory due to the excess of the humors (doṣas) should be known as epilepsy (apasmāra), a terrible disease of four types. [Its prodromal symptoms are:
trembling of the heart, a sense of emptiness, perspiration, brooding, fainting, and confusion.
In that condition, there will be loss of sleep for both the patient and the physician;
moreover, he trembles, bites his teeth, froths at the mouth, and pants.
Due to the wind (vāta), he sees harsh, reddish, and black forms.

One with yellow foam, limbs, face, and eyes, appearing as yellow blood, and seeing the world pervaded by thirsty, hot fire, is of the bile (paittika) type. One with white foam, limbs, face, and eyes, with cold, horripilant, and heavy limbs, [is of the phlegm type].
One with a predominance of phlegm (ślaiṣmika) sees white forms and is released [from the seizure] after a long time.
Apasmāra arising from all three doshas together is to be recognized by all these symptoms combined; it is incurable when it occurs in one who is emaciated and when it is chronic.
Apasmāra (epilepsy) destroys one who is frequently convulsing, emaciated, with trembling eyebrows, and whose eyes are distorted;
the humors (malas), when provoked, may do so after a fortnight, twelve days, or a month.
They manifest the impulse toward epilepsy with some slight interval;
just as certain seeds, even when it rains,
sprout in the autumn, so too do the outbreaks of diseases.
Now, the etiology of wind disorders (vātavyādhi): through dry, cold, scanty, and light food, as well as excessive sexual indulgence and staying awake too long.
From improper medical treatment, from the discharge of morbid humors (doṣas) and blood,
from excessive activities such as fasting, jumping, long journeys, and physical exercise,
from the depletion of the bodily tissues (dhātus), and from emaciation caused by anxiety, grief, and disease.
Due to the suppression of natural urges, from intoxication, injury, fasting,
affliction of the vital spots (marmans), or from the rapid running, leaping, and galloping of elephants, camels, and horses,
the powerful wind (anila) fills the empty channels within the body.
It produces various diseases affecting either the whole body or specific parts.
Their unmanifest characteristic is known as the premonitory stage (*pūrvarūpa*);
however, that which is manifest as its own form consists of malaise and lightness.
Contraction of the joints, stiffness, and fracture of the bones and joints; horripilation, delirium, and seizing of the hands, back, and head;
lameness, deformity of the fingers, and hunchback; swelling of the limbs, and loss of sleep—[these are the symptoms].
The destruction of the embryo, semen, and menses; throbbing; numbness of the limbs;
and the distortion of the head, nose, eyes, collarbones, and neck; as well as piercing pain, tearing, excessive convulsions, and constant exhaustion. (7–8)
The provoked Vāyu produces such symptoms;
moreover, due to the specific nature of its cause and location, it becomes the producer of specific diseases.
Among these, when the vitiated [Vāyu] is situated in the visceral cavity (koṣṭha), there is suppression of urine and feces.
Heart disease, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, and pain in the flanks occur when Vāta is provoked;
when Vāta is aggravated throughout the entire body, there is twitching and breaking sensations in the limbs, and his joints feel as if they are bursting from the pains that pervade them.

When [the vāyu] is located in the rectum (guda), it causes retention of feces, urine, and flatus; colic, flatulence, urinary stones, and gravel; diseases of the thighs, sacrum, feet, and back; emaciation;
pain in the sides, abdomen, heart, and navel; thirst, eructation, and visūcikā. (12)
When located in the stomach (āmāśaya), it causes cough, dryness of the throat and mouth, and dyspnea;

when located in the large intestine (pakvāśaya), it produces rumbling in the intestines, colic, flatulence, difficulty in passing urine and feces, abdominal distension, and pain in the sacrum (trika).

When the vitiated wind (vāyu) affects the sense organs such as the ears, it causes injury to the senses; when the wind is located in the skin, the skin becomes rough, cracked, numb, thin, and black, and is characterized by pricking pain, stretching, redness, and pain in the joints. 15
When Vāyu has entered the blood, there are sharp pains accompanied by a burning sensation, discoloration, emaciation, loss of appetite, eruptions on the body, and a sense of stiffness after eating.
The limbs feel heavy and are excessively pricked, as if struck by a staff or a fist. (16)
When Vāyu has entered the flesh and fat, there is pain, excessive exhaustion,
splitting sensations in the bones and joints, pain in the articulations, and loss of muscle strength (17).
When Vāyu is provoked in the marrow and bones, there is insomnia, constant pain, and continuous distress (18).

Vāta, when aggravated and located in the semen (śukra), quickly causes its discharge or retention, or even the conception of an embryo, or it may produce deformity. When located in the vessels (sirā), it causes pain, as well as the contraction and distension of the vessels.
Vāyu located in the tendons (snāyu) causes emaciation of the limbs, internal and external contraction, as well as kyphosis; it may also produce diseases of all the limbs or of a single limb.
When located in the joints (sandhi), it destroys the joints and causes pain and distension.
The five vital airs— prāṇa, udāna, samāna, vyāna, and apāna— residing in their respective locations, sustain the embodied being.
When prāṇa is enveloped by pitta, vomiting and a burning sensation arise.
When [the *udāna*] is enveloped by *kapha*, there is weakness, exhaustion, drowsiness, and a bad taste in the mouth.
When the *udāna* is associated with *pitta*, however, there is burning sensation, fainting, vertigo, and fatigue;
when it is enveloped by *kapha*, there is absence of perspiration, horripilation, weak digestion, and coldness.
When the Samāna Vāyu is obstructed by Pitta, there occurs perspiration, a burning sensation, heat, and fainting;
when it is obstructed by Kapha, stiffness of the limbs arises along with retention of feces and urine.
When the Apāna Vāyu is joined with Pitta, however, there is a burning sensation, heat, and the passing of blood in the urine.

When Kapha obstructs Vyāna, there is heaviness and coldness in the lower body (25). When Pitta obstructs Vyāna, there is burning, tossing of the limbs, exhaustion, stiffness, "staff-like" rigidity, as well as pain and swelling (26).
But when the provoked wind (māruta) enters all the vessels (dhamanī), then that ever-moving [wind] quickly causes the body to convulse again and again;
because it convulses repeatedly, it is known as ākṣepaka (the convulsor). 27.27–28ab.
When provoked by its own irritants, the wind rises upward from its seat;
having reached the heart, it causes pain there, and afflicting the head and the temples, it bends the limbs like a bow, convulses them, and then causes delusion. (28–29)
He breathes with great difficulty, his eyes either fixed or closed;
he coos like a pigeon and becomes unconscious—this is apatantraka.
Having paralyzed the vision and destroyed consciousness, he makes a cooing sound from the throat.

When the heart is released [from the affliction], the person attains composure; when it is enveloped by delusion again, they say it is severe. Some call that *apatanaka*, if the wind, joined with phlegm, remains intensely in those very [channels]. (31–32)
When one stiffens the body like a staff, that is known as *daṇḍāpatānaka*;
when one bends like a bow, it is designated as *dhanuḥstambha*.
[These states] reside in the fingers, the ankles, the abdomen, the heart, the chest, and the throat.
When the forceful wind (vāyu) violently agitates the network of tendons,
the person’s eyes become fixed, the jaw becomes stiff, the sides of the body feel broken, and while vomiting phlegm,
he bends inward like a bow. (34–35)
Then the powerful wind, residing within the external network of tendons, effects internal extension, and it also effects external extension;
the wise declare that condition incurable, involving the breaking of the chest, hips, and thighs. (36)
Vata associated with Kapha and Pitta, or Vata alone, causes Akṣepaka;
furthermore, there is a fourth type born of injury, as well as those caused by miscarriage and excessive hemorrhage. (37–38)
Furthermore, apatānaka does not arise from external trauma;
rather, the vāyu, having seized the channels and sinews below the body and dried them up, destroys one side of the body by loosening the bonds of the joints. (39)
His entire lower body becomes useless and devoid of sensation;
some call this "disease of a single limb," while others know it as "hemiplegia" (pakṣavadha).
Similarly, when the Vāyu resides throughout the whole body, it causes a disease of all the limbs.
When Vāyu is associated with Pitta, there occur burning sensations, feverish heat, and fainting;
when that same [Vāyu] is associated with Kapha, there is coldness, swelling, and heaviness.
A hemiplegia (pakṣaghāta) caused by pure Vāyu is known to be the most difficult to cure.
A condition associated with another [disease] is difficult to cure, as is one caused by wasting;
one should avoid treating hemiplegia in pregnant women, those who have recently given birth, children, the elderly, the emaciated, or those suffering from hemorrhage, provided it is devoid of pain.
When one speaks too loudly, eats hard foods, laughs, yawns, or sleeps on uneven ground due to fatigue,
[the wind] enters the joints of the head, nose, lips, chin, forehead, and eyes. 44.
The wind (vāyu) afflicts the mouth and thereby produces ardita;
consequently, one half of the face becomes distorted, the neck also turns aside, the head shakes, there is a loss of speech, and deformities of the eyes and other organs occur. 45.
In that [condition], there is pain in the neck, chin, and teeth, as well as on that side.

When there is horripilation at the beginning, trembling, turbid vision, upward movement of the wind (vāyu), numbness of the skin, pricking pain, and stiffness of the neck and jaw— these are the symptoms.
Those expert in diseases call that condition *ardita* (facial paralysis).

It is incurable when it occurs in one who is emaciated, whose eyes do not blink, who speaks incessantly and indistinctly, and especially in one who has tremors; likewise, facial paralysis that is severe or has persisted for three years is not cured.
When the force has subsided, recovery occurs in all cases of *ākṣepaka* and similar disorders.
(48) Due to scraping the tongue, eating dry food, or from injury, the aggravated *vāyu*, located at the root of the jaw, causes the jaw to dislocate. (49)
It causes either the mouth to remain open or to become closed;
that condition is called *hanugraha* (lockjaw), by which chewing and speaking occur only with great difficulty.
[This is caused] by sleeping during the day, improper postures, and gazing upward with the mouth wide open.
That same wind, when obstructed by phlegm, causes stiffness of the neck (manyāstambha). When located in the channels that carry speech, the wind paralyzes the tongue;
this is called jihvāstambha, by which there is an inability to consume food, drink, or speak.
When the wind (vāyu), having taken hold of the blood, causes the vessels of the head to become rough,
painful, and black, that condition known as *sirāgraha* (vascular constriction) is incurable.
[In *sāṃnipātika-śiraḥśūla*,] it begins in the buttocks and spreads sequentially through the waist, back, thighs, knees, calves, and feet.
Gṛdhrasī seizes [the limb] with stiffness, pain, and throbbing, and it twitches repeatedly (54).
From Vāta alone, or from Vāta-Kapha, it is accompanied by drowsiness, heaviness, and anorexia;
in the Vāta-born type, there is piercing pain and a curvature of the body.
In the condition arising from vāta and śleṣman, there is a throbbing and extreme stiffness of the joints of the knees, hips, and thighs (55); the causes are a weak digestive fire,
drowsiness, salivation, and likewise an aversion to food (56).
The tendons (kaṇḍarā) of the fingers that extend from the back of the arms to the palms,
when they cause the loss of function in the arms, are called Viśvācī; likewise,
a swelling with great pain in the middle of the knee caused by vāta and blood is also so designated.
When the thick *jñeya-kroṣṭuka-śīrṣa* wind, which is like the head of a jackal (*koṣṭuka*), located in the waist, seizes the tendons (*kaṇḍarā*) of the thigh, then the person becomes lame (*khañja*);
if both thighs are affected, he becomes a cripple (*paṅgu*). (59)

One who trembles while walking and moves as if limping should be known as suffering from *kalāyakhañja*, characterized by the loosening of the ligaments of the joints. Furthermore, when pain arises in the foot due to uneven placement or from exhaustion... (60–61)

When the wind (vāta), localized at the ankle, is accompanied by pitta and blood, it causes a burning sensation in the feet; this condition is called vātakaṇṭaka. One should specifically designate it as pādadāha when it occurs especially while walking.
When both feet become numb and experience a tingling sensation,
that condition is to be known as *pādaharṣa* (numbness of the feet), caused by the provocation of *kapha* and *vāta*.
When the *vāyu* located in the region of the shoulders dries up the shoulder-joint ligaments, [it causes *aṃsavabhañja*].

The Vāyu, constricting the vessels located there and becoming enveloped by Kapha, obstructs the sound-carrying *dhamanīs* and produces Avabāhuka; it renders men incapacitated, making them mute, nasal-voiced, or stammering. (65)
The pain that descends downward, arising from the receptacles of feces and urine (66),
as if tearing through the anus and the perineum, is known by the name *tūnī*.
That which arises from the anus and the perineum and rushes upward against the natural direction (67) [is also called *tūnī*].

When it moves with force into the colon (pakvāśaya), it is called Pratitūnī; in this condition, the abdomen becomes greatly distended with flatulence (āṭopa), accompanied by extremely severe pain. One should recognize that as Ādhmāna, a terrible disease born from the obstruction of Vāta.
One should recognize that very condition arising from the stomach (āmāśaya), with the sides and heart released, as *pratyādhmāna*, where the wind is agitated by phlegm;
it is produced below the navel and may be either mobile or stationary. (69–70)
One should recognize *vātāṣṭhīlā* as a stone-like, knotted mass that is elongated upward and elevated, obstructing the external passage;
this very same condition, when accompanied by pain and obstructing flatus, feces, and urine, [is known as *vātāṣṭhīlā*]. 71.
One should say "pratyaṣṭhīlā" regarding a stone-like mass that has arisen transversely in the abdomen (verse 72).
When the wind (vāyu) is favorable in the bladder (vasti), urine flows properly; however, when it is contrary, various disorders arise for him (verse 73).
Trembling of all the limbs or of the head is known as *vāyurvepathu*;
*khallī*, however, is the crushing pain in the feet, calves, thighs, and the roots of the arms.
When the *vāyu* is obstructed below by *śleṣman* or *māruta*, [it causes this condition].
It causes excessive belching; this is called ūrdhvavāta (upward wind).
One should diagnose the remaining types by their symptoms corresponding to their locations and names.
In all these cases, one should observe for the association with pitta and the other humors.
Trismus (hanustambha), facial paralysis (ardita), convulsions (kṣepa), hemiplegia (pakṣāghāta), and tetanus (apatānaka)—
these wind disorders may, after a long time, be cured with effort or they may not; however,
one should successfully treat these conditions in strong men who are free from complications.

Due to erysipelas, burning sensations, pain, fainting, anorexia, and weak digestion, the Vātas destroy the strength and muscle tissue of one who is emaciated; such a person suffers from facial paralysis and other disorders, being swollen, with numb skin, broken limbs, and afflicted by tremors and flatulence.

Vāta-disease destroys a man who is afflicted with pain. However, he whose vāyu remains in its natural state, staying in its proper place with unimpeded movement, shall live for more than a hundred years free from disease.
The Etiology of Vātarakta: Now,
regarding the etiology of vātarakta,
[it arises] from salty, sour, pungent, alkaline, unctuous, hot, and undigested foods, as well as from [unsuitable] vessels.
With moist and dry water-born plants, marshy meat, oil-cakes, and radishes;
with horse-gram, black gram, flat beans, leafy vegetables, and the flesh of animals; with sugarcane, curd, fermented rice-gruel, *sauvīra*, *śukta*, buttermilk, wine, and spirits.

Vāta-śoṇita (blood vitiated by Vāta) generally becomes provoked in those who are delicate, those who indulge in improper diet and lifestyle, the obese, and even those who live in comfort, due to incompatible or excessive eating, anger, sleeping during the day, and staying awake at night. (3)

For one who travels by means of elephants, horses, or camels, or while eating, the food becomes inflamed; that inflammation of the food quickly inflames the entire blood. That blood, being displaced and vitiated, accumulates in the feet.
Because it is corrupted by the aggravated Vāyu (wind), it is called *vātarakta*. 4.
Excessive sweating, or conversely, its absence; blackness of the skin; loss of tactile sensation; intense pain in wounds;
looseness of the joints; lassitude; malaise;
and the eruption of pustules in the knees, calves, thighs, hips, shoulders, hands, feet, and the joints of the limbs.
Pricking pain, throbbing, a splitting sensation, heaviness, numbness, and itching;
pain occurring repeatedly in the joints and then subsiding, discoloration, and the appearance of circular patches— these are the premonitory symptoms of vātāsṛj (vātarakta).
When Vata is predominant, there is excessive pain, throbbing, and breaking sensations;
the swelling becomes dry, blackish, or dark-brown, and it fluctuates in size. There is contraction of the vessels, fingers, and joints, as well as stiffness of the limbs and intense pain.
In blood [diseases], there is swelling, excessive pain, and pricking;
it is copper-colored and experiences a tingling sensation.
It is not relieved by either unctuous or dry treatments, and is accompanied by itching and moisture. (9–10)
In the case of pitta, there is a burning sensation, confusion, perspiration, fainting, intoxication, thirst,
intolerance to touch, pain, redness, swelling, suppuration, and intense heat. In the case of kapha, there is stiffness, heaviness, numbness, oiliness, and coldness.
Itching, mild pain, and the symptoms of all [three] types of fever arise from their combination (12).
Taking its seat at the base of the feet, or sometimes even in the hands, it creeps up that body like the enraged venom of a rat (13).
That which is cracked down to the knees, that which is split open and exuding,
and that which is afflicted by complications such as the wasting of vital breath (*prāṇa*) and flesh— such *vātarakta* is incurable; however, that which has persisted for one year may be palliable.
Insomnia, anorexia, dyspnea, putrefaction of the flesh, stiffness of the head (15), fainting, intoxication, pain, thirst, fever, delusion,
trembling, hiccup, convulsions, erysipelas, suppuration, pricking pain, vertigo, and exhaustion (16).
Curvature of the fingers, cracking, burning, affliction of the vital points (*marmas*), and tumors—these complications, or even just delusion alone, render [the condition] incurable.
That which lacks these complications is palliable; that which is free from complications is curable.
That which is associated with a single doṣa is curable; that born from two doṣas is palliable;
that born from three doṣas is incurable, as is that which possesses complications. (18) [The diagnosis of ūrustambha.]
Now, the etiology of thigh-stiffness (ūrustambha) is as follows:
it arises from the consumption of cold, hot, liquid, dry, heavy, or unctuous foods;
likewise, from indigestion or digestion, as well as from physical exertion, agitation, sleep, and wakefulness.
When the wind (vāyu), combined with phlegm (kapha) and fat (medas), becomes excessively accumulated along with undigested matter (āma),
it overcomes the other doshas and enters the thighs; it then fills the interior of the bones of the legs with stagnant phlegm.
Then it stiffens the thighs; thus stiffened, they become cold and insensible, as if belonging to another person, heavy, and extremely painful.
There is body ache resulting from meditation, numbness, drowsiness, vomiting, loss of appetite, and fever.

Accompanied by stiffness of the feet, difficulty in lifting the legs, and numbness, this condition is called ūrustambha; others, however, call it āḍhyavāta. Its premonitory symptoms are excessive sleep, excessive brooding, torpor, and fever.
Horripilation, loss of appetite, vomiting, as well as a sense of weakness in the calves and thighs may occur;
furthermore, due to ignorance, those who suspect it to be caused by Vāta may apply oleation,
which results in weakness and numbness of the feet, as well as difficulty in lifting them.
There is extreme and constant exhaustion of the calves and thighs, along with burning sensations and piercing pains;
the foot, when placed down, suffers and one no longer perceives the sensation of cold touch. Furthermore, one is powerless regarding posture, pressure, movement, and locomotion. (8)
For when a person afflicted by the pain of burning and piercing sensations becomes trembling, as if his thighs and feet were on fire like those of another,
then *ūrustambha* (thigh-stiffness) shall kill him; otherwise, if it is of recent onset, it may be cured.
Now, the etiology of āmavāta:
for one who consumes incompatible food and engages in improper activities, whose digestive fire is weak, and who remains sedentary;
For when one who has eaten unctuous food likewise engages in physical exercise, the undigested matter (āma),
impelled by the vital air (vāyu), rushes toward the seat of phlegm (śleṣman).
Consequently, becoming excessively aggravated, it enters the channels (dhamanīs).
Furthermore, that food-derived rasa (nutrient fluid), vitiated by vāta, pitta, and kapha, causes the channels to become congested; becoming multicolored and excessively slimy,
it quickly produces weakness and heaviness of the heart.
This extremely dreadful condition known as *āma* is indeed the seat of all diseases.
When the two [vātas] become simultaneously aggravated within and enter the trika-joint, they cause the body to become stiff; that is called *āmavāta*.

Aching in the limbs, loss of appetite, thirst, lethargy, heaviness, fever, indigestion, and swelling of the limbs are the symptoms of āmavāta (rheumatic condition). It is a distressing disease when it becomes aggravated among all ailments.
In the hands, feet, head, ankles, sacrum, knees, and thighs,
it produces painful swelling wherever the humors (doṣas) reach;
that region becomes excessively painful, as if pierced by scorpions.
It produces weakness of the digestive fire, excessive salivation, loss of appetite, heaviness, loss of energy, a bad taste in the mouth, burning sensations, excessive urination,
hardness in the abdomen, colic, as well as insomnia.
Thirst, vomiting, vertigo, fainting, cardiac oppression, constipation, numbness, intestinal gurgling, flatulence, and other painful complications arise;
due to pitta, there is burning sensation, redness, and pain following the course of vāta.

One should designate that swelling as vitiated by *kapha* which is stiff and characterized by heavy itching. A swelling following from a single *doṣa* is curable; one following from two *doṣas* is said to be palliable;
and a swelling that moves throughout the entire body due to all three *doṣas* combined (*sānnipātika*) is difficult to treat.
Now,
regarding the etiology of *śūla* resulting from the transformation of food (*pariṇāma-śūla*) and liquid *śūla*:
due to the *doṣas* acting individually, collectively, or in pairs, *śūla* becomes eightfold.
In all these types of colic, wind (vāta) is generally the predominant factor [1].

It arises from physical exertion, fasting, excessive sexual intercourse, staying awake at night, drinking cold water in excess, eating peas, mung beans, *āḍhakī*, and *koda* grains, as well as from excessively dry food, overeating, and injury [2].
Due to astringent and bitter foods, excessively sprouted grains, incompatible foods, dried meat, and dried vegetables;

due to the suppression of the urges of feces, semen, urine, and flatus; and due to grief, fasting, and excessive laughing or talking—the Vāyu (wind), thus aggravated, indeed produces colic (śūla) in the regions of the heart, sides, back, sacrum (trika), and bladder.
In old age, during the evening, at the onset of the rainy season, and in cold weather, it becomes intensely aggravated.
It repeatedly undergoes subsidence and aggravation through constipation, suppression of flatus, stiffness, piercing pain, and splitting sensations;
however, it finds relief through fomentation, oil massage, rubbing, and the consumption of unctuous and warm foods.

Pitta, quickly provoked by alkaline, extremely sharp, hot, and burning oils; by *niṣpāva* beans, oil-cakes, and *kulattha* soup; by pungent, sour, fermented grain-liquor (*sauvīra*), and varieties of wine; by the fire of anger, physical exertion, and the heat of distress; and by indigestible foods consumed in excessive quantities through rural habits, produces colic (*śūla*).
Indeed, it causes thirst, delusion, and excessive burning; it is accompanied by perspiration at the navel, fainting, vertigo, and a parched sensation.
It flares up at midday, at midnight, during the time of digestion, and at the end of the rainy season. It finds relief through cold measures and even with very sweet and cool foods. (7–8)

Through marshy water-products, *kilāṭa*, milk-preparations, meat, sugarcane, flour-cakes, *kṛśarā*, sesame-cakes, and other causes that generate *balāsa*, the *śleṣman* (phlegm) reaches a state of provocation and produces pain (9), accompanied by nausea,
cough, lassitude, loss of appetite, excessive salivation, a sense of fullness in the stomach, and heaviness of the abdomen and head.
Indeed, it always causes excessive pain after eating, at sunrise, during the cold season, and at the arrival of spring (the season of flowers).

A physician should recognize that when all the *doṣas* are involved, the colic exhibits all symptoms; for this "all-originated" (*sarvaja*) colic is extremely difficult to endure, resembling poison or a thunderbolt, and those who know the truth declare it to be avoidable.
Distension, nausea, vomiting, heaviness, a sense of numbness, and flatulence— along with the symptoms of phlegm such as excessive salivation—
they describe this as colic arising from phlegm (āmaja), which possesses symptoms identical to those of phlegm.
That colic occurring in the bladder, heart, flanks, and back is of the phlegm-wind (kaphavātika) type.
That piercing pain (śūla) located in the abdomen, the heart, and the middle of the navel is caused by phlegm and bile (kapha-paittika).
It is terrible and produces burning sensations and fever; it should be recognized as being caused by wind and bile (vāta-paittika).
That which arises from a single doṣa is curable, while that born from two doṣas is difficult to cure.
Then, the formidable Vāyu, arising from all the [three] doṣas, incurable, and accompanied by many complications, having become aggravated by its own causes and being present nearby,
envelops both Kapha and Pitta and becomes powerful, causing piercing pain (śūla). 15.
The pain that occurs when food is being digested is precisely that which arises from the process of digestion (pariṇāmaja).
Its symptoms are also stated here in brief: flatulence, abdominal distension, obstruction of feces and urine, aversion to food, and trembling. 16–17.
The physician should declare that a Vātika [dysentery] is characterized by unctuousness and heat, and is generally pacified by cooling measures;

one should observe that a Paittika [dysentery] involves thirst, burning sensations, restlessness, and perspiration, is dominated by pungent, sour, and salty tastes, and is generally pacified by cold applications. A wise man should recognize it by these signs. 18.18–19a.

Vomiting accompanied by nausea and delusion, with mild pain that persists for a long duration, and which is relieved by pungent and bitter substances— this should be known as being of the nature of phlegm (kapha).
Having recognized the combined symptoms, one should determine it to be caused by two doṣas.

That which arises from the three doṣas is incurable, as is that which occurs when the flesh, strength, and digestive fire are depleted; and that colic which arises whether the food is digested or undigested, through the use of wholesome or unwholesome things, or by eating or fasting. (21)
It does not subside through restrictive measures; this is described as *annadrava* (liquid-like food).
In cases of colic known as *annadrava*, one does not attain health until the vomited old bile has been expelled; once vomited, it quickly removes the colic. (22–22.1)

Now, the etiology of upward-moving wind (udāvarta) and abdominal distension (ānāha): [these arise] from the suppression of flatus, feces, urine, yawning, tears, sneezing, eructation, vomiting, and the sensory organs.

Through the suppression of hunger, thirst, respiration, and sleep, there arises the upward movement of gases (udāvarta). From the suppression of wind, urine, and feces, there occur retention of these, distension, exhaustion, pain, and other diseases in the abdomen born of Vāta.
Distension, colic, cutting pain, obstruction of feces, and upward movement of wind occur when a man's urge to defecate is suppressed; furthermore, feces may even emerge from the mouth.
There is pain in the bladder and penis, difficulty in urination, and headache.
Vināma (contraction) and vaṅkṣaṇānāha (distension of the groin) are the signs of the suppression of urine.
From the impairment of yawning, disorders of the wind (vāta) arise, such as stiffness of the neck and throat, afflictions of the head,
and likewise severe diseases of the eyes, nose, and mouth, along with diseases of the ears.
Indeed, for one who does not release tears that have arisen from joy or sorrow once they have reached the eyes,
heaviness of the head and severe eye diseases occur, along with coryza (pīnasa), stiffness of the neck (manyāstambha), headache, facial paralysis (ardita), and hemicrania (ardhāvabhedaka).

There may be weakness of the sense organs due to the suppression of sneezing (7). Furthermore, when the urge to belch is suppressed, there occurs excessive fullness of the throat and mouth, piercing pain, rumbling, or the non-movement of wind;
terrible disorders born of the wind (pavana) arise when the force of belching is obstructed (8).
Itching, urticaria, anorexia, freckles, edema,
jaundice, fever, skin diseases, erysipelas, and nausea— these are the ailments arising from the suppression of vomiting.
Furthermore, there is swelling and pain in the bladder, anus, and scrotum, as well as the suppression of urine.
From the obstruction of semen (śukra) arise seminal calculi (śukrāśmarī), its discharge, and various other disorders;
from the suppression of hunger (kṣudhā) come lethargy, body ache, loss of appetite, fatigue, and emaciation;
from the suppression of thirst (tṛṣṇā) come dryness of the throat and mouth, deafness, and pain in the heart. 10–11.
From the suppression of breath when one is fatigued, there may arise heart disease, delusion, or even abdominal tumors (gulma);
or from the suppression of yawning, there may be body ache, extreme heaviness of the eyes and head, sleeplessness, or even drowsiness.
Furthermore, the Vāyu moving within the digestive tract becomes dry due to astringent, pungent, and bitter [foods]. 12.
Indeed, provoked by foods, [the wind] immediately causes udāvarta;
it indeed turns back the channels that carry flatus, urine, feces, blood, kapha, and fat, and causes the feces to move upward. 13–14.
Then, afflicted by pain in the heart and bladder, and oppressed by nausea, fainting, and distress, the person passes wind, urine, and feces with great difficulty; [he suffers from] dyspnea,
cough, catarrh, burning sensations, delusion, thirst, and fever.
One suffers from vomiting, hiccups, diseases of the head, tinnitus,
and many other disorders born of the provocation of Vata (16),
as well as undigested feces that have accumulated gradually and become further obstructed by the deranged wind.

When this [undigested matter] proceeds according to its own nature, they describe it as a "transformation" (vikāra). However, when its emergence is obstructed, there arise thirst, catarrh, and a burning sensation in the head;
furthermore, pain and heaviness in the stomach, rigidity of the heart, and suppression of eructations occur. 17–18.
Stiffness in the waist, back, feces, and urine; colic, fainting, vomiting of stool, dyspnea, and the symptoms described for alasaka occur when [the vāyu] is born in the colon (pakvāśaya).
One who is afflicted by thirst, exhausted, emaciated, and overwhelmed by colic [is incurable].
The wise physician should abandon a patient suffering from upward-moving wind (udāvarta) who vomits feces. 20.
Now begins the diagnosis of abdominal tumors (gulma).
The vitiated *vāta* and other doshas, due to improper diet and lifestyle, produce five types of *gulma*, appearing as a knot within the abdominal cavity;
its five locations are the sides, the heart, the navel, and the bladder. (1)

A knot-like mass located between the heart and the navel, whether mobile or immobile, circular and subject to increase and decrease, is known as *gulma*. It arises from the humors (*doṣas*) individually or from all of them when they are aggravated.
Likewise for men and women, another [type] should be known by the blood.
Excessive belching, constipation, lack of satiety, gurgling in the intestines,
flatulence, distension, and lack of digestive power are said to be the signs of an impending gulma.

One should observe loss of appetite, difficulty in the passage of feces, urine, and flatus, rumbling in the intestines, abdominal distension, and upward movement of wind as symptoms present in all types of gulma.
Dry food and drink, irregular or excessive exertion, and the suppression of natural urges [are the causes].
Grief, injury, excessive depletion of the *mala*s (waste products), and fasting are the causes of *anila-gulma* (wind-type abdominal tumor).
It manifests as a variation in location, shape, and pain; obstruction of feces and flatus; dryness of the throat and mouth;
a dusky-red complexion; cold-fever; and pain in the heart, abdomen, flanks, shoulders, and head.

That gulma which increases its provocation when [the food] is digested, becomes mild after eating, and arises from vāta, does not respond well to dry, astringent, bitter, or pungent substances. [Likewise, it is aggravated by] pungent,
sour, sharp, hot, and burning substances, as well as dryness, anger, excessive wine, and exposure to the sun and fire.
Undigested matter (āmā), trauma, and vitiated blood are said to be the causes of Pittaja gulma.

Fever, thirst, redness of the face and limbs, severe pain during digestion, perspiration, a burning sensation, and a gulma that is tender like a wound and intolerant to touch— these are the characteristics of Pittaja gulma.

Cold, heavy, unctuous, and sedentary habits, as well as over-nutrition and sleeping during the day, are the causes of a *gulma* arising from *kapha*; however, when all [the *doṣas*] are vitiated, it is of a combined nature (*nicaya-ātmaka*). [The symptoms include:
a sense of stiffness, cold fever, exhaustion of the limbs, nausea, cough, loss of appetite, and heaviness.
Coldness, mild pain, and hardness or elevation are the characteristics of a gulma caused by kapha.

Having observed these etiological factors and symptoms, as well as the relative strength and weakness of the doshas in a gulma born of two doshas, one should designate the other three types of gulmas with mixed signs for the purpose of formulating the appropriate treatment.

One should designate as incurable a gulma born from the three doṣas that is characterized by great pain, enveloped in burning heat, hard and elevated like a stone, rapidly suppurating, and dreadful; it robs the strength of the mind, the body, and the digestive fire.
(14) A woman who has recently given birth, one who eats unwholesome food, or one who miscarries an embryo during her menstrual period [is also at risk].
For the Vāyu, having seized her blood, produces a Gulma that is painful and accompanied by a burning sensation;
it possesses symptoms identical to those of the Pittaja type, so learn now another distinguishing characteristic:
that which remains as a single mass, does not spread through the limbs, is painful for a long time, and exhibits signs similar to pregnancy.
That blood-born gulma, occurring specifically in women, is to be treated after the tenth month has passed.
When the gulma has gradually accumulated, occupying a vast space, become firmly rooted, bound by veins, and protruded like a tortoise shell; 17.
Accompanied by weakness, anorexia, nausea, cough, vomiting, restlessness, fever, thirst, drowsiness, and coryza, that [fever] does not succeed [is incurable].
Having seized [the patient] with fever, it afflicts him with dyspnea, vomiting, and diarrhea.
Swelling in the heart, navel, hands, and feet draws away the life of the one afflicted with gulma; moreover, dyspnea, colic, thirst, aversion to food, numbness of the glands,
and weakness arise as signs of death for the patient with gulma.
Now, the etiology of heart disease (hṛdroga):
[it arises] from excessive heat, heavy food, astringent and bitter tastes, physical exertion, trauma, overeating, and indulgence.

Heart disease is declared to be of five types caused by excessive reflection and the suppression of natural urges. When the humors (doṣas), having become vitiated, corrupt the rasa and reach the heart, they produce affliction in the heart; that is designated as hṛdroga (heart disease).
In the vātika type of heart disease, the heart is stretched, pierced, churned, torn, split open, and even rent asunder;
in the paittika type, there is thirst, heat, burning, parching, and exhaustion of the heart.
Fuming, fainting, perspiration, and dryness of the mouth; heaviness, discharge of phlegm, loss of appetite, rigidity, weakness of the digestive fire,
and sweetness in the mouth— these occur when the heart is pervaded by *balāsa*.
One should recognize that the worm-born (krimija) type possesses all the symptoms of the three doṣas, along with intense pain and piercing sensations, and itching;
furthermore, in the worm-born type, there occurs excessive salivation, spitting, pricking, colic, nausea, fainting, anorexia, darkening of the eyes, and swelling. (6)
Fatigue, prostration, vertigo, and emaciation are to be known as their complications; these are considered the [symptoms] of those born from worms and those arising from kapha. 7.
The etiology of dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra).
Now, the etiology of dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra):

from excessive physical exercise, sharp medicinal substances, dry food, habitual consumption of wine, constant riding on fast-moving vehicles, eating the meat of marshy animals, indigestion, and likewise [other factors], eight types of dysuria arise in men. (1)
When the various doshas, provoked by their respective etiological factors, or all of them together,

reach the bladder and afflict the urinary passage, then one voids urine with difficulty here. Due to Vata, one experiences intense pain in the groin, bladder, and penis, and voids urine in small quantities repeatedly.

Due to Pitta, one voids urine that is yellowish or reddish, painful, and accompanied by a burning sensation, passing it with difficulty and frequently; in Kaphaja Mūtrakṛcchra, there is heaviness and swelling of the penis along with the bladder, and the urine is slimy. In the Sānnipātika type, all these symptoms occur together, and this indeed is the most difficult form of Mūtrakṛcchra.
When the urine-carrying channels are injured by a foreign body, or are wounded or struck,
a most severe dysuria arises from that trauma;
one should recognize its symptoms as being identical to those of Vata-type dysuria.
Due to the obstruction of feces, however, the Vāyu becomes disordered;
it causes flatulence, colic pain from wind, and retention of urine.
One should declare that this is the precursor to urinary calculi (aśmarī) and is characterized by painful urination (mūtrakṛcchra).
When the semen is afflicted by the doshas and flows into the urinary tract,
one voids urine with semen with difficulty, suffering from pain in the bladder and the penis;
both urinary calculi (ashmarī) and gravel (śarkarā) have identical origins and symptoms.
Listen as I describe the specific characteristics of *śarkarā* (gravel):

when a urinary stone (*aśmarī*) is being cooked by bile (*pitta*) and dried up by wind (*vāyu*), and its connection with phlegm (*kapha*) is broken apart, it is considered to be *śarkarā* as it falls away. 9–10.
There is pain in the heart, trembling, colic in the abdomen, and weak digestion;
likewise, fainting occurs and there is severe difficulty in urinating (mūtrakṛcchra). When the flow of urine is released, the pain subsides.
As long as this pill does not return to the opening of the urinary passage— this is the diagnosis of urinary obstruction (mūtrāghāta).
Now follows the diagnosis of urinary obstruction.
Thirteen types of urinary obstruction (mūtrāghāta) arise from the aggravated doshas;
these include conditions such as vātakuṇḍalika, which generally result from the suppression of the urge to urinate and other factors.
Due to dryness or the suppression of the urge, the vāyu becomes painful within the bladder.
Entering the urine, it moves about in a distorted state, coiled like a ring;
then the urine is discharged in very small quantities or with pain—one should know that this disease is indeed Vātakuṇḍalikā, which is extremely severe. (2–3)
The wind, having obstructed the bladder and rectum and causing them to distend, produces a painful, mobile, and elevated mass known as *aṣṭhīlā*, which blocks the passages for urine and feces.
This occurs in a man who, being unskilled, suppresses the urge to urinate. (4)
The Vayu located in the bladder obstructs the opening of that organ;
consequently, there occurs a retention of urine accompanied by pain in the bladder and the abdomen.
This disease is known as Vata-vasti, and it is difficult to treat.

When one suppresses the urge to urinate for a long time, it does not flow quickly even when one attempts to urinate with haste; this condition is called *mūtrātīta*. Furthermore, when the flow of urine is forcibly checked, it arises from the cause of upward-moving wind (*udāvarta*).
When the apāna vāyu becomes aggravated, it fills the abdomen excessively;
it produces distension below the navel accompanied by intense pain.
One should recognize this as mūtrajaṭhara (urinary abdominal enlargement), which causes obstruction of the lower urinary tract.

In the bladder, or in the urethral canal, or in the glans penis, if the urine of a person begins to flow but becomes obstructed, or flows with blood, or dribbles slowly in small quantities, whether accompanied by pain or free from it; 10. [This is the condition known as Mutrakṣaya.]
A disease arising from vitiated wind is known as *mūtrotsaṅga*.

When pitta and vāyu are located in the bladder of a person who is dry and whose body is exhausted, they produce a deficiency of urine accompanied by pain and burning; that condition is called by that same name (*mūtrakṣaya*).
A round, firm, small nodule that appears suddenly at the opening of the bladder,
causing pain similar to that of a urinary stone, is called *mūtragranthi* (urinary glandular tumor).
[13] When a man who has urinated engages in sexual intercourse with a woman, his semen is agitated by the *vāyu*.
In one who urinates while displaced from the proper position, the urine flows either before or after [the act].
When pitta, accompanied by vāyu, reaches the bladder due to physical exertion, walking, or exposure to the sun,
it causes a burning sensation in the bladder, the penis, and the anus, and discharges [urine] downwards.
When urine is yellowish, or mixed with blood, or even purely red,
and is voided with great difficulty again and again by a person, they call that *uṣṇavāta*.
If both pitta and kapha are congealed by vāyu, [the same condition occurs].
Then, with difficulty, one voids urine that is yellow, white, or red, thick, and accompanied by a burning sensation; it may have the color of the powder of *rocanā* or conch shell.
When dried, it may be of all these colors; this condition is called *mūtrasāda*.
When the feces of a person who is dry or weak are turned upward by Vata and enter the urinary passage,
the man then voids urine mixed with stool, accompanied by the odor of feces and with difficulty; this should be diagnosed as Viḍvighāta (obstruction of stool).
Due to the exertion of traversing a long path quickly, or from injury and pressure,
the bladder is displaced from its natural position; it remains enlarged like a pregnancy and,
afflicted by pain, throbbing, and burning, it discharges drop by drop.
When pressed, it emits a stream [of urine]; accompanied by stiffness and the pain of twisting, they call this *vastikuṇḍala*. It is terrible, like a weapon or poison;
generally driven by wind, it is difficult for those lacking wisdom to subdue.
In that condition associated with pitta, there is burning, colic, and discoloration of the urine (24).
With kapha, there is heaviness, swelling, and the urine is unctuous, thick, and white.
When the opening of the bladder is obstructed by kapha and aggravated by pitta, it is not curable.
The condition is curable when the opening is not distorted, but it is not so when it has become coiled.
When [the bladder] becomes coiled, there occurs thirst, delusion, and dyspnea. This is the etiology of urinary calculi (*aśmarī*).
Now begins the diagnosis of urinary calculi (aśmarī).
There are three types caused by vāta, pitta, and kapha, and a fourth type born of semen;
all these calculi generally reside in the phlegm (śleṣman) and are like Yama, the god of death.

When the wind (vāyu), along with bile (pitta) or phlegm (kapha), dries up the urine located in the bladder together with semen, then a stone (aśmarī) is gradually produced, just as a gallstone (rocanā) forms within the bile of a cow.
Not all stones are dependent on a single doṣa; now follows their premonitory symptoms.
Distension of the bladder, intense pain all around its vicinity,
urine smelling like a goat's urine, dysuria, fever, and anorexia are the general symptoms; the pain is located in the navel, the *sevanī*, the bladder, and the head of the bladder.
When the passage is obstructed by that [stone], the urine may be discharged in broken streams;
upon its removal, one may urinate comfortably, with clear urine resembling a *gomedaka* gem.
From the agitation of that [stone] causing injury, blood may appear, and excessive pain arises from the exertion.
Therein, one severely afflicted by Vāta gnashes his teeth, trembles, seizes the penis and the navel, suffers from constant moaning,
passes feces with wind, and voids urine drop by drop repeatedly.
His urinary stone (aśmarī) is dark-brown and reddish, as if covered with thorns;
due to pitta, the bladder is burned, feeling as if it were being cooked and emitting heat.
The stone is shaped like the kernel of a bhallātaka fruit and is red, yellow, or black.
The bladder feels as if it is being pricked by phlegm; it is cold and heavy.
Large, smooth stones, honey-colored or white, occur in children, and especially in them.

Because the substrate (the seminal vesicle) is small and its accumulation is slight, the processes of grasping and drawing forth [semen] are easy; however, seminal calculi (*śukrāśmarī*) arise from the retention of semen by those who possess large quantities. Indeed, when the semen has moved from its place but is not discharged, the *vāyu* (wind-humor) within the scrotum— 11. ...[causes it to become obstructed]. When the semen is displaced from its location but not released, the wind (anila) within the scrotum... [obstructs it]. (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a verse describing the pathophysiology of seminal calculi. The translation reflects the medical context of *Suśruta Saṃhitā* or similar Ayurvedic texts.)
Having seized the semen, it dries it up; that semen becomes a stone (aśmarī).
It causes pain in the bladder and thighs, difficulty in urination, and swelling of the scrotum.
As soon as it has arisen, the semen dissolves within it. 12–13.
When this space is constricted, the stone or gravel is broken into minute particles by the Vayu; if that [Vayu] moves in its natural downward direction,
it passes out along with the urine, but if it moves in the reverse direction, it becomes obstructed.
If it enters the urinary tract and becomes obstructed, it produces complications:
weakness, lassitude, emaciation, abdominal pain,
anorexia, pallor, hot wind (uṣṇavāta), thirst, cardiac distress, and vomiting.

The urinary stone (aśmarī), accompanied by gravel (sikatā) and pebbles (śarkarā), quickly destroys one who has suppressed the urge to urinate, whose testicles are swollen, whose urine is obstructed, and who is afflicted with pain. 17.
Thus ends the chapter on the diagnosis of urinary stones (aśmarī-nidāna) in the Mādhavanidāna composed by the illustrious Mādhavakara. 33.
Thus ends the diagnosis of urinary calculi (aśmarī-nidāna). Now begins the diagnosis of urinary disorders (prameha-nidāna).
In the latter half [of the treatise],

it is stated that the pleasure of sitting, the pleasure of sleep, curdled milk, the tastes of domestic, aquatic, and marshy animals, milk, food and drink, and preparations of molasses— all these are causes of *prameha* and all produce *kapha*.
Kapha, having reached the bladder and become vitiated, produces urinary disorders (mehas) by corrupting the fat, muscle, and the moisture born of the body;
likewise, Pitta, when aggravated by hot things, vitiates those very same substances and produces them.
And Vāyu, when the [other] doshas are diminished, draws in the tissues (dhātus), vitiates them, and produces urinary disorders.
Ten types arising from *kapha* are curable; six born of *pitta* are palliable; and four caused by *vāta* are incurable.
This is respectively because they possess similar treatments, dissimilar treatments, or because of their extreme severity.
*Kapha*, along with *pitta* and *vāta*, are the *doṣas*; while fat (*medas*), blood (*asṛj*), semen (*śukra*), water (*ambu*), muscle-fat (*vasā*), and lymph (*lasīkā*) [are the *dūṣyas*].
Marrow, semen, and flesh are the corrupted elements (dūṣyas). There are exactly twenty types of urinary disorders (pramehas).

An abundance of impurities on the teeth and other parts, burning sensations and stickiness in the hands and feet, bodily heat, thirst, and a sweet taste in the mouth arise as the premonitory symptoms (pūrvarūpa).
The general characteristic of these [mehas] is the production of copious, turbid urine;

even though there is no distinction in the involvement of the *doṣas* and *dūṣyas*, the differentiation among the various mehas is determined by their specific combinations, resulting in differences in the color and other qualities of the urine.
One who passes urine that is clear, abundant, white, cold, odorless, and like water does so with *udakameha*.
One who passes urine that is slightly turbid and slimy,
and extremely sweet like the juice of sugarcane, is one suffering from *ikṣumeha*.
In *sāndrameha*, one voids urine that has become thick after standing overnight;
in *surāmeha*, one voids urine resembling liquor—clear on top and dense at the bottom.
In *piṣṭameha*, with hair standing on end, one voids copious, white urine resembling flour paste.
One who suffers from *śukrameha* passes urine that has the appearance of semen or is mixed with semen; one who suffers from *sikatāmeha* passes fine, solid particles of impurity in the form of sand;
and one who suffers from *śītameha* passes urine that is very copious, sweet, and extremely cold.
In śanairmeha, the patient voids urine very slowly;
in lālāmeha, the urine is slimy and mixed with threads of saliva;
and in kṣārameha, it is like alkaline water in its smell, color, taste, and touch. (12)
In *nīlameha*, the urine has a blue luster; in *kālameha*, it resembles ink.
In *hāridrameha*, one voids pungent urine resembling turmeric, which is burning and foul-smelling;
in *māñjiṣṭhameha*, it is like the water of madder.
One who suffers from *raktameha* passes urine that is foul-smelling, warm, salty, and blood-colored;
one with *vasāmeha* frequently urinates urine mixed with fat (*vasā*), resembling fat in appearance;
and one with *majjameha* frequently passes urine resembling marrow (*majjā*) or mixed with marrow.
The wise physician should declare *kṣaudrameha* to be astringent, sweet, and dry.
The patient suffering from *hastimeha* passes urine that is like that of an elephant in rut—constantly discharged without force, accompanied by a slimy discharge, and obstructed. (16–17)
Lack of digestion, loss of appetite, vomiting, drowsiness, cough accompanied by nasal catarrh— these complications arise from urinary disorders born of kapha (18).
Pricking pain in the bladder and penis, tearing sensation in the scrotum, and fever [are also present].
Burning sensation, thirst, acidity, fainting, and diarrhea arise from disorders born of pitta (19).
From those born of vāta, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), trembling, cardiac oppression, restlessness, colic, insomnia, emaciation, cough, and dyspnea occur (20).
When afflicted by the aforementioned complications, excessively emaciated, and tormented by carbuncles, severe prameha kills the man.
One who has developed prameha, or one who is a case of madhumeha, is declared incurable, for it arises from a defect in the seed.
Furthermore, whatever complications arise from the [patient's] family lineage, they declare those to be incurable.
Indeed, all types of prameha, if left untreated over time, turn into madhumeha; at that stage, they truly become incurable.
Madhumeha arises as something resembling honey; it is indeed of two types:
when vāyu is provoked by the depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātu), or when its path is obstructed by the doṣas.
Being thus obstructed, it manifests symptoms of the doṣas without any apparent cause.
In one moment it is diminished, in another moment it is full; it becomes difficult to cure.
(25) That which is sweet in urinary disorders, generally passing like honey, is called by the name Madhumeha (diabetes mellitus), because of the sweetness of the body [in that state]. (26)
Śarāvikā, kacchapikā, jālinī, vinatā, alajī, masūrikā, sarṣapikā, putriṇī,
savidārikā, and vidradhi— these are the ten types of pustules that arise from the neglect of urinary disorders (prameha).
They arise at the joints, vital points (*marmas*), and in fleshy parts. A *śarāvikā* is characterized by being elevated in the center and depressed in the middle;
a *sarṣapī* has the appearance and size of a white mustard seed. (28–29)
Kūrmasaṃsthānā, characterized by constant burning, should be known by the wise as Kacchapikā; Jālinī, however, is marked by intense burning and is covered with a network of flesh.
It possesses deep-seated pain and discharge, occurring either on the back or even on the abdomen. (30)
A large, blue swelling is known by the name Vinatā;
it should be understood as a large swelling that is small at its base. Furthermore, a swelling shaped like a lentil is to be recognized as Masūrikā. 31–32.
Red or white, covered with pustules, and characterized by severe inflammation, it becomes an *atālajī*.
When it is round and hard like the tuber of a *vidārī* plant, it is called *vidārikā*. It should be known as *vidradhikā* when it possesses the symptoms of a *vidradhi* (abscess).
Those which are traditionally known as the types of *prameha* are composed of these [doshas], yet even without *prameha*, these [complications] arise in one whose fat (*medas*) is corrupted;
and they are not perceived as such until they have occupied their respective sites. (34–35)

One should avoid treating carbuncles (piḍakā) that have arisen in the anus, heart, head, shoulders, back, or vital organs (marmas), especially when accompanied by complications and occurring in those with weak digestive fire. 36.
[This concludes] the diagnosis of diseases of fat (medoroga).
Now, the etiology of disorders of fat (medas):
In one who indulges in lack of exercise, sleeping during the day, and foods that increase kapha, the predominantly sweet taste of food generally increases fat through its unctuousness. 1.
Because their channels are obstructed by fat, the other tissues do not nourish [the body]; instead, fat itself accumulates,
and consequently, one becomes incapable of all activities due to labored breathing,
thirst, delusion, sleep, snoring, and exhaustion.
One who is afflicted by hunger, perspiration, and foul odors has little vitality and little sexual desire.
Fat (medas), however, resides in the bellies and bones of all living beings; for this very reason, an increase in the belly generally occurs in those who possess much fat.
Because its pathways are covered by fat, the vāyu moving particularly within the digestive tract (koṣṭha) kindles the digestive fire and even dries up the food;
therefore, it digests food quickly and craves more.
And due to the lapse of time, he may undergo certain terrible transformations;
these two, fire and wind, are especially causative of complications,
for they burn the gross body just as a forest fire consumes a forest.

When fat has increased excessively, the wind and other humors suddenly produce terrible disorders and swiftly destroy life. Due to the excessive growth of fat and flesh, his buttocks, abdomen, and breasts become unstable.
A person who exerts effort in improper accumulation is said to be excessively obese. 9.
Now begins the diagnosis of abdominal diseases (udararoga).
10. Now begins the diagnosis of abdominal diseases (udararoga).
All diseases, and especially abdominal disorders,
arise from weak digestion due to the accumulation of impurities caused by indigestion and unwholesome food. The accumulated doshas obstruct the channels that carry sweat and water.
By vitiating the prāṇa, agni, and apāna [vāyus], they produce abdominal enlargement (udara) in men. There is flatulence, inability to move, debility, weak digestion,
swelling, lassitude of the limbs, and the obstruction of flatus and feces.
