Indeed, burning sensations and lassitude occur in all types of abdominal enlargements caused by the individual doṣas, as well as by their combination, and by splenic enlargement, intestinal obstruction, perforation, and ascites.
Thus, eight types of udara arise; hear now their specific symptoms individually.

In that condition, vātodara (wind-bellied abdomen), there is swelling in the hands, feet, navel, and abdomen; pain in the sides of the abdomen, the belly, the waist, and the back; splitting pain in the joints;
dry cough; aching of the limbs; heaviness in the lower body; and retention of waste products.

The abdomen becomes dark-brownish or reddish in complexion, with sudden swelling and subsiding, accompanied by piercing pain and a tearing sensation; it is covered with thin, black veins, makes a sound like a blown leather bag when struck, and produces a rumbling noise.
In this condition, the wind (vāyu) moves everywhere with a painful sound.
In Pitta-type abdominal enlargement (pittodara), there is fever, fainting, burning sensation, thirst, a bitter taste in the mouth, giddiness, diarrhea,
yellowness of the skin and other parts, and the abdomen appears greenish-yellow.
In *śleṣmodara* (abdominal enlargement due to phlegm), the abdomen is bound with yellowish-red veins,
is perspiring, warm, burning, and smoky; it is soft to the touch, ripens quickly, and is intensely painful, accompanied by lassitude of the limbs, numbness, swelling, and heaviness.
Drowsiness, distress, loss of appetite, labored breathing, coughing, and whitening of the skin and other parts;
the abdomen becomes distended, unctuous, marked by white streaks, large, slowly increasing in size, hard, cold to the touch, heavy, and stable.
Women of immoral conduct may administer food and drink mixed with their own nails, hair, urine, feces, or menstrual blood;
or enemies may give poison (gara), or [the patient] may consume contaminated water or artificial poisons.
By this means, the blood becomes quickly vitiated and the provoked humors (doṣas) produce a most terrible abdominal enlargement (jaṭhara) characterized by the three symptoms.
In cold winds and especially during very cloudy weather, it becomes aggravated and causes a burning sensation.
That patient indeed faints repeatedly; his face becomes pale and withers from thirst.
This is described as *dūṣyodara*; now listen as I describe *plīhodara*. 14–15.
In a person who has consumed burning and obstructing substances, the blood and phlegm become excessively vitiated;
when these two increase, they cause an enlargement of the spleen. This, arising from the spleen, is called *plīhodara* (splenic abdominal enlargement).
It increases specifically on the left side of the body, and in this condition, the patient suffers from exhaustion.

When the liver is enlarged on the left side, accompanied by mild fever, weak digestion, symptoms of *kapha* and *pitta*, diminished strength, and extreme paleness, that condition is to be known as *yakṛddālyudara*. It is further characterized by upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*), pain, flatulence, fainting, thirst, burning sensations, and fever. (17)
One should recognize the impurities therein by heaviness, aversion to food, and hardness, respectively.
When his intestines are properly obstructed by foods that cause coating, or by hair and stones, his morbid waste gradually accumulates within the channel like a mixture of refuse. (18–19)
When feces are obstructed in the rectum and emerge only with great difficulty and in very small quantities,

and the abdomen becomes distended in the region between the heart and the navel, they call that *baddhaguda* (intestinal obstruction). Likewise, when a foreign body (*śalya*) or food lodged in the intestines pierces the bowel, whether it has entered normally or otherwise, [it causes this condition].
Therefore, a watery discharge flows from the intestines like water, and there is even more exudation from the rectum;
the abdomen below the navel increases in size, and it is excessively pierced and split open—this is declared to be *parisrāvyudara*; now listen as I describe *dakodara*. 21–22.
If one who has drunk oil, or undergone an excessive unctuous enema (anuvāsana), or has vomited, or been purged, or even experienced the growth of new hair (virūḍha),

should drink cold water immediately, his channels that carry those substances will indeed become vitiated. Or, when those channels are smeared with oil, ascites (dakodara) arises as previously described.
That which is glossy, large, with a prominent navel, and feels as if full of water like a leather bag,

and which becomes agitated, trembles, and makes a sound— that is *dakodara* (ascites). Generally, all types of abdominal enlargement (*udara*) are considered most difficult to cure from the very moment of their birth.
That which has not yet produced fluid is curable with effort even in a strong person if it has recently arisen; however,
after a fortnight, all cases where the rectum is obstructed or where fluid has already formed lead generally to the death of men, as does abdominal enlargement caused by perforated intestines.
One should avoid a patient who has swollen eyes, a deformed perineum, and moist, thin skin; one whose strength, blood, flesh, and digestive fire are exhausted;
and one afflicted by pain in the sides, aversion to food, swelling, and diarrhea. 27.1–27.2b.
Furthermore, one should avoid a patient with abdominal dropsy who has been purged but whose abdomen continues to swell.
Now follows the diagnosis of swelling (śopha).
Vāyu, when vitiated, leads the vitiated blood, pitta, and kapha into the external vessels; its movement being obstructed by these, it produces a swelling localized in the skin and flesh.
Because it arises from a collection [of humors], they call it *utsedha* (elevation) or *śotha* (swelling). 1.
Due to specific causes, it manifests in nine forms according to the variations in its physical appearance (rūpa).
It arises from the individual humors (doṣas), from two combined, from all three together, from injury, or even from poison.
Its premonitory symptoms (pūrvarūpa) are a burning sensation, stiffness of the vessels, and heaviness of the limbs.

The consumption of alkaline, sour, sharp, hot, and heavy foods by those who are emaciated and weak from purification therapies or disease; the ingestion of curd, raw food, clay, vegetables, incompatible foods, or food contaminated by poison;
lack of physical activity; failure to purify the body; injury to the vital organs (marmans); and difficult labor—these lead to hemorrhoids.
Improper medical treatment and the primary causes of the swelling itself have been declared.
A sense of heaviness, instability, elevation, heat, thinness of the veins,
horripilation, and discoloration are declared to be the general symptoms of swelling.

Swelling caused by wind (samīraṇa) is characterized by a mobile body, rough and reddish or dark skin; it is accompanied by excessive deep sleep and exhilaration, subsides without apparent cause, rises when pressed, is strong during the day,
and is soft, malodorous, and possesses black or yellow discoloration, along with vertigo, fever, perspiration, thirst, and intoxication.

That which is characterized by clear pain and redness of the eye is a swelling caused by *pitta*, accompanied by intense burning and suppuration. That which is heavy, firm, pale, and associated with anorexia, salivation, drowsiness, vomiting, and diminished digestive fire, which arises and subsides with difficulty, and does not suppurate even when pressed—provided it has three folds—is of the nature of *kapha*. (8–9)
Due to the combination of two causes, two types of humors may produce swelling that exhibits the characteristics of both;
from the combination of all three humors (sannipāta), swelling arises with mixed symptoms.
[This swelling] may also result from trauma caused by cutting, piercing, wounding, and so forth with weapons and other instruments.
From contact with the vapors of snow, wind, or the ocean, or with the juices and bristles of the *bhallātaka* and *pikacchu* plants, a swelling accompanied by spreading (visarpa) occurs;
it is intensely hot, reddish in appearance, and generally characterized by the symptoms of pitta.
Poisoning arises from the crawling over or urination by venomous creatures, or from the bites, teeth, and claws of even non-venomous animals;
it also arises from being defiled by feces, urine, semen, or contact with soiled garments. (13)

Due to contact with the wind from a poison tree, or by the application of a poisonous powder (gārayoga), the humors (doṣas) located in the stomach (āmāśaya) produce swelling that is soft, mobile, pendulous, rapid, and causes burning pain; indeed, they cause the swelling to move upward. 14–15.
When located in the colon, they cause swelling in the middle part of the body; when situated in the receptacle of feces, they cause it below;

and when they have reached the entire body, they likewise produce a generalized swelling (sarvasara). Furthermore, swelling in the middle region is difficult to treat, as is that which is generalized throughout the body.
One whose disease spreads upward to occupy half the body should be considered doomed;
likewise, one who suffers from labored breathing, thirst, vomiting, weakness, and fever, and who has no appetite for food— one should avoid such a person, as he is afflicted with swelling (śvayathu).
Swelling caused by no other affliction arising from the feet kills a man;
that arising from the mouth kills a woman; and that arising from the private parts kills both.
A swelling that is recent and without complications is curable, while that which has been described previously is incurable.
One should avoid [excising] a growth located in the flanks or the abdomen, as well as one situated in the throat or at a vital point (*marman*).
Furthermore, those that are thick or rough should be avoided, as should those occurring in children, the elderly, or the weak.
This concludes the diagnosis of *vṛddhi*.
Now, regarding the etiology of scrotal enlargement (*vṛddhi*):
the aggravated *vāyu*, moving upward and causing swelling and pain,
reaches the scrotum from the groin and enters the channels that carry to the testicles.
By compressing [the scrotum], it causes an enlargement of the vessels in the testicles;
that disease, Vṛddhi, is sevenfold, consisting of [enlargements caused by] the Doṣas, blood, fat, urine, and the intestines.
Even those two types caused by urine and the intestines arise from Vāta, though there is a distinction solely in their causes.
The swelling caused by Vāta feels like the touch of a wind-filled leather bag, is rough, and is painful without an apparent cause (3).
That caused by Pitta resembles a ripe Udumbara fruit and is characterized by burning, heat, and suppuration.
That caused by Kapha is cold, heavy, unctuous, itchy, hard, and slightly painful (4).
Covered with black vesicles, it is characterized by an increase in pitta and arises from blood;
an increase caused by phlegm and fat is soft and resembles the fruit of the palmyra palm.
That which arises from urine occurs in one who habitually suppresses the urge to urinate while walking.
Like a leather bag filled with water, the soft [prostate] undergoes agitation;
there is dysuria and a downward movement that shakes the scrotum,
caused by foods that provoke Vāta and by immersion in cold water.

When the wind (vāyu), agitated by carrying burdens, traveling on roads, uneven terrain, or the consumption of food, and by other such disturbances, becomes disordered and drives the small intestines downward from its own location; 8.
Then, situated at the groin joint, it produces a swelling resembling a glandular tumor (granthi).

If neglected, that Vāyu causes enlargement of the scrotum (muṣkavṛddhi) accompanied by distension, pain, and stiffness; being compressed within, it moves with a sound, and having inflated [the area], it departs and returns once again when released.
Intestinal hernia (antravṛddhi) is incurable; it has a clinical appearance identical to that of Vata-type scrotal enlargement (vātavṛddhi).
Now begins the diagnosis of goiter (galagaṇḍa), cervical lymphadenitis (mālā), scrofula (apacī), nodules (granthi), and tumors (arbuda).
Now begins the diagnosis of goiter, cervical lymphadenitis, scrofula, nodules, and tumors.
One for whom a fixed swelling hangs from the neck like a scrotum—

whether large or small— should be diagnosed as having *galagaṇḍa*. Furthermore, when Vāta and Kapha are vitiated in the throat and likewise take refuge in the *manya* muscles and the fat (*medas*), [the same condition arises].

They gradually produce a swelling endowed with its own specific symptoms; that is called *galagaṇḍa*. That which is caused by Vāta is accompanied by pricking pain, covered with black vessels, dark-brown or reddish, characterized by roughness, grows slowly, and does not suppurate; it may occasionally reach suppuration by chance.
The mouth of that person becomes tasteless, and there is constant dryness of the palate and throat.
This [swelling] is of the nature of kapha; it is stable, the same color as the skin, heavy, intensely itchy, cold, and large.
It undergoes growth slowly or takes a long time to suppurate, and is sometimes accompanied by mild pain.
The mouth of that person becomes sweet, and there is a coating on the palate and throat (5).
Arising from fat (*medas*), it is unctuous, heavy, pale, foul-smelling, accompanied by itching, and slightly painful;
it hangs down like a gourd, has a small base, and undergoes decrease and increase in accordance with the body (6).
If a person has a glossy face and constantly makes a gurgling sound in the throat;
if he breathes with difficulty, has soft limbs, has been ill for over a year, suffers from loss of appetite,
is emaciated, and has a hoarse voice— the physician should avoid treating such a patient afflicted with *galagaṇḍa*.
In the armpits, shoulders, neck, and groins, there appear many swellings the size of *karkandhu*, *kola*, or *āmalaka* fruits;
due to fat and phlegm, they undergo slow and chronic suppuration. This condition is called *gaṇḍamālā*.
Some of these nodules (*granthi*) reach suppuration and discharge, while others disappear and yet others reappear.
Those experts declare that very same condition to be *apacī* when it persists for a long time due to the duration of the morbid humors;
those accompanied by chronic catarrh (*pīnasa*), pain in the flanks, cough, fever, and vomiting are considered curable, whereas those [associated with] incurability are otherwise.
Vāta and the other humors, being vitiated, corrupt the flesh and blood, as well as the fat and the vessels.
Because it produces a swelling that is round, elevated, and knotted, it is therefore designated as a *granthi* (knot).
[In the Vataja type,] it is stretched, cut, pricked, pressed, churned, and split;
it is blackish, soft, and distended like a bladder, and when burst, it discharges clear blood.
It burns, fumes, is excoriated, suppurates, and seems as if it were on fire;
being red or even yellowish due to *pitta*, it discharges extremely hot blood when burst.
Cold, discolored, with little pain and excessive itching, it is characterized by a hardness like that of stone.

When long-standing, due to the provocation of *kapha*, it bursts open and discharges thick, white pus. A tumor caused by fat (*medas*) increases or decreases according to the growth or wasting of the body; it is unctuous, large, itchy, and painless, and when incised, the fat flows out resembling crushed oil-cake mixed with ghee. 14–15.

In a person who is weak, the Vāyu, provoked by various forms of physical exertion, seizes the network of vessels (sirā-pratāna), contracts, compresses, and dries it up, thereby quickly forming a raised, circular knot (granthi).
This is a vessel-born knot (sirāja-granthi); it is difficult to cure if it is painful and mobile.
Even when it is painless, immobile, large, and arising from a vital spot (marman), it should be avoided for removal.

(17) In a certain part of the body, the humors (doṣas), having become concentrated and vitiated the flesh and blood, produce a growth that is round, firm, with mild pain, large, deep-rooted, slow to increase, and non-suppurating. (18)
Those learned in the scriptures declare that when they form an excessively deep mass of flesh, it is called arbuda;
it arises through vāta, pitta, kapha, blood, muscle, or fat,
and its symptoms are always identical to those of a granthi (cyst).

The vitiated *doṣas*, having constricted and thickened the blood and the vessels, then cause a non-suppurating swelling that exudes discharge; it is a mass of flesh covered with fleshy sprouts, growing rapidly, and constantly discharging blood—this blood-natured condition is indeed incurable. 20–21.

Due to being afflicted by complications from the depletion of blood, one becomes pale; however, one afflicted by an arbuda (tumorous growth) suffers from pain in the limbs caused by blows with the fist and the like, for the vitiated flesh produces a swelling that is painless,
unctuous, non-distinct in color, non-suppurating, stone-like, and immovable.
This [condition] occurs severely in a man whose flesh is corrupted and who is excessively devoted to meat.

This fleshy tumor (māṃsārbuda), however, is said to be incurable; even among those that are curable, one should avoid treating these: that which has exuded, that which is born upon a vital organ (marman), that which is located in the channels (srotas), or that which is immovable. 23–24.
Indeed, that which arises subsequently upon a previously formed growth should be known as an *adhyarbuda* by those who know arbudas;
and that which arises as a pair, either simultaneously or sequentially, is a *dvirarbuda*, and that is incurable.
(25) Due to the predominance of phlegm (*kapha*) and especially due to the abundance of fat (*medas*), these do not undergo suppuration.

Because of the stability of the humors (*doṣas*) and their binding together, all tumors (*arbudas*) are indeed [classified] by their very nature. 26. Now begins the diagnosis of elephantiasis (*ślīpada*). [The diagnosis of elephantiasis follows.]
That swelling which arises in the groin accompanied by fever, or which occurs gradually in the feet of men, is known as *ślīpada*;
some say it may also occur in the hands, ears, eyes, penis, lips, and nose.
That caused by Vāta is blackish, dry, cracked, and characterized by intense pain.
Its pain is without a distinct cause and is accompanied by frequent fever.
That caused by pitta resembles yellow and is associated with burning sensations and fever; it is mild.
That caused by kapha is glossy in appearance, white, pale, heavy, and stable.

Like an anthill that has grown, it increases with thorns; being one year old and large, it must especially be avoided. One should know that all three of these types of elephantiasis arise from an excess of phlegm (kapha).
Since heaviness and largeness do not exist without phlegm (kapha),
elephantiasis (ślīpada) occurs especially in those regions where there is an abundance of old water and which remain cold throughout all seasons.

That which arises from phlegm-inducing diet and lifestyle, even in a man who is naturally of a phlegmatic constitution— characterized by discharge, with all symptoms highly elevated, accompanied by itching and associated with phlegm— should be rejected [as incurable].
This concludes the diagnosis of abscess (vidradhi).
Now, the diagnosis of abscess (vidradhi): The doshas, having vitiated the skin, blood, flesh, and fat, and having taken refuge in the bone,
gradually produce a severe swelling that is highly elevated.
A swelling with deep roots, accompanied by pain, whether circular or elongated, is known as Vidradhi; it should be understood to be of six types:
caused by each of the doṣas individually, by all three combined, by injury, and likewise by blood.

Now, the characteristics of all six of these will be fully described: A *vidradhi* (abscess) arising from *vāta* is black or reddish-brown, uneven, extremely painful, and characterized by various stages of onset and suppuration. (3-4)
A Pitta-born abscess resembles a ripe udumbara fruit, or is dark-brown, accompanied by fever and a burning sensation,
and characterized by rapid onset and suppuration. A Kapha-born abscess resembles a shallow bowl (śarāva), is pale, cold, unctuous, and mildly painful.
The Vidradhi (abscess) originating from Kapha is characterized by slow onset and delayed suppuration.
Their discharges are respectively known to be thin, yellow, and white.
The Ghata type is large, uneven, and possesses various colors, pains, and discharges.
Furthermore, a *vidradhi* (abscess) caused by the simultaneous derangement of all three humors (*sānnipātika*) may also cook in an irregular manner.
When an unwholesome person is afflicted by various factors or suffers an injury,
the heat of the wound spreads through the *vāyu*, which then impels the *pitta* along with blood.
Fever, thirst, and a burning sensation arise in that embodied being.
This is indeed an exogenous abscess (āgantuvīdradhi), possessing the characteristics of a pitta-type abscess;
it is covered with black vesicles, is dark-brown in color, and causes intense burning and pain.

A blood abscess (raktavidradhi) is said to have the symptoms of a bile abscess (pittavidradhi). When the doshas— either individually or combined— are aggravated, they produce an abscess within the body that resembles a tumor (gulma), rising up like an anthill.
In the rectum, at the opening of the bladder, in the umbilicus, in the abdomen, as well as in the groins,
in the kidneys, the spleen, the liver, the heart, or the kloman—
the symptoms of these [internal abscesses] have been described by means of the characteristics of external abscesses.
Listen specifically to the symptoms according to the particular location of the obstruction: in the anus, there is suppression of flatus; in the bladder, painful and scanty urination (14);
in the umbilical region, hiccups as well as flatulence; and in the abdomen, the provocation of wind.
When the abscess (vidradhi) arises in the groin, there is severe pain in the waist and back;
when it occurs in the kidneys, there is contraction of the sides; in the spleen, there is obstruction of the breath;
and in the heart, there is severe stiffness of all the limbs and the onset of cough.
When [the bile] is in the liver, there is labored breathing; when in the *kloman*, one repeatedly drinks water.
(16) Those [bile-disorders] arising above the navel, when matured, go upward; others, however, go downward. One may live if they flow downward, but one does not live if they flow upward. (17)

If those abscesses (vidradhi) located outside the heart, navel, and bladder are ruptured, a person might perhaps survive; but never in the case of the others. Of the five types of abscesses, those caused by the combination of all three humors (sānnipātika) are to be rejected as incurable.
One should diagnose their stages of being unripe, ripening, or suppurated as one does for swellings (śotha).
A vidradhi (abscess) accompanied by distension, obstructed discharge, vomiting, hiccup, thirst, pain,
and dyspnea destroys the man.
The Diagnosis of Ulcerative Swelling (Vraṇaśothanidāna).
Now, regarding the diagnosis of ulcerative swelling:
a swelling arising in a specific location is the primary symptom of ulcers.

There are six types of swelling (śotha), arising individually from all [three doshas], blood, or exogenous causes. These six swellings are to be understood through the previously mentioned characteristics of swelling;
however, their specific distinctions regarding the determination of whether they are suppurated or unsuppurated, and so forth, shall now be stated.
A swelling arising from Vāta ripens irregularly; one born of Pitta ripens quickly, while that born of Kapha takes a long time.
A swelling originating from blood or an exogenous cause (āgantu) ripens like that of Pitta.
It is characterized by mild heat, slight swelling, hardness, and a color identical to that of the surrounding skin.
Mildness of sensation is a secondary characteristic of these swellings.
(4) It burns as if by fire, it suppurates as if by lye, it is stung as if by a swarm of ants, and likewise it feels as if it were being cut. (5)
He is indeed pierced by weapons and beaten as if with a staff;
he is tormented within as if by hands, and pricked as if by needles.
He becomes parched with thirst, discolored, and is crushed as if by his own fingers.
Whether sitting, lying down, or standing, one does not find peace, as if pierced by a scorpion (verse 7). When the swelling extends, it becomes like an overdistended bladder;
fever, thirst, and loss of appetite are the symptoms of the ulcer being suppurated (verse 8).

The subsiding of pain, the absence of redness, the swelling being slight and not elevated, the appearance of wrinkles, and the frequent occurrence of pricking and itching; the alleviation of complications, and the depression and cracking of the skin—[these are the signs]. 9.
If the swelling is pressed with the fingers, there is a sensation like the movement of water in a vast expanse;
when one end is pressed, it causes pain at the other end, and a desire for food arises— these are the characteristics of a matured swelling.
There is no swelling without wind, nor is there suppuration without bile, and even pus does not exist without phlegm;
therefore, at the time of suppuration, all three doshas indeed cook the swellings. Just as fire, driven by the wind, violently consumes dry wood once it has reached it, so too do these doshas act.
In the same way, pus that has not yet issued forth indeed devours the flesh, the veins, and the sinews here;
the physician who can recognize a wound as being raw, inflamed, or properly healed, he alone is a true doctor— others are merely thieves in the guise of practitioners.

He who cuts raw flesh through ignorance, or he who neglects what is already ripe, both should be considered like dog-cookers— those who act without certainty. (15) This is the diagnosis of physical wounds.
Now, regarding the diagnosis of bodily ulcers: an ulcer is to be known as twofold, distinguished by being either endogenous (śārīra) or exogenous (āgantu).
Of these two, the first is caused by the [vitiated] humors (doṣas), while the other arises from wounds inflicted by weapons and the like.

A wound arising from wind (vāta) is stiff, hard to the touch, with scanty discharge and great pain; it throbs, becomes dark-colored, and is accompanied by thirst, delusion, fever, moisture, burning, corruption, and tearing.
It is characterized by thirst, delusion, fever, moistening, burning, putrefaction, and laceration.

One should recognize a wound caused by *pitta* by its foul odors and putrid discharges. A wound caused by *kapha* is characterized by abundant mucus, heaviness, oiliness, numbness, mild pain, a pale color, little moisture, and a slow healing process.

A wound caused by blood, characterized by the discharge of blood, arises from two or three origins; it is curable through its own natural course when located in the skin and flesh, in a favorable region, in a young person, and when free from complications.
A fresh wound in a wise patient, occurring at an auspicious time and in a favorable location, heals easily.
A wound deficient in any of these qualities is considered difficult to heal.
One that is devoid of all of them should be known as incurable, accompanied by many complications, putrid, discharging pus and highly corrupted blood, having cavities, and persisting for a long time.
A malignant ulcer is characterized by excessive foul odor and other such signs, which are the opposites of the symptoms of purification;
whereas an ulcer that is as soft as the surface of the tongue, smooth, glossy, minimally painful,
well-organized, and free from discharge is known as purified.

One should declare that a wound is healing when its interior has the color of a pigeon, is free from moisture, firm, and covered with pustules; likewise, a wound that is healed, without a track, without a glandular swelling, and without pain is considered cured.

One should declare that the skin of those afflicted by leprosy (kuṣṭha), those poisoned by toxins, those suffering from consumption (śoṣa), and those with diabetes (madhumeha) has become the same color as healthy skin, level, and properly healed;
yet their ulcers are cured only with great difficulty, and ulcers may even appear upon existing ulcers.
A wound from which fat, marrow, bone-marrow, or brain matter flows is curable if it is of exogenous origin (āgantuja),
but it will not be cured if it arises from the bodily humors (doṣaja).
[It may be treated] with wine, aguru, ghee, jasmine, lotus, sandalwood, and campaka flowers.
The ulcers of those about to die are known to have a putrid odor or a divine fragrance; they are located in vital spots (marmans) yet produce excessive pain,
and while burning intensely within, they are cold on the outside.
They burn excessively on the outside while remaining cool within;
they are afflicted by the wasting of vital breath and flesh, dyspnea, cough, and loss of appetite;
and those whose ulcers, filled with increased pus and blood, are located in the vital organs (marmas). 15–16.
A physician, even while protecting his own reputation, should avoid treating those ulcers that do not heal despite being properly initiated with medical procedures.
(17) This concludes the diagnosis of fresh wounds (*sadyovraṇa*).
Now follows the diagnosis of fresh wounds (sadyovraṇa): Wounds of various shapes arise from weapons falling upon various locations through various types of openings; learn of them from me. 1.
Cut, split, pierced, wounded, crushed, and likewise the sixth, which they call rubbed— I shall describe their characteristics.
A wound that is cut obliquely or even straight, and which is long in extent—

The falling of a limb is designated as "cut" (chinna). When the internal cavity is struck by a spear, teeth, the tip of a sword, or horns, and whatever [fluid] flows out, that indeed is called the characteristic of "pierced" (bhinna).

The locations for undigested matter (āma), for what is cooked by the fire (the digested food), for urine, and for blood— the heart, the duṇḍuka, and the lungs— are designated as the "viscera" (koṣṭha).
When these are perforated and filled with blood, fever and a burning sensation arise.
Blood issues from the urinary tract, the anus, the mouth, and the nose; there is fainting, labored breathing, thirst, abdominal distension, loss of appetite,
obstruction of feces, urine, and flatus, perspiration, and redness of the eyes.
There is a metallic taste in the mouth, foul odor of the body, and pain in the heart as well as in the sides; hear now my specific description of this condition:
when the blood is located in the stomach (āmāśaya), one vomits blood.
There is excessive distension and extremely severe colic;
when it has reached the colon (pakvāśaya), there is pain and heaviness,
and specifically, a coldness occurs here in the lower part of the body.

When a limb is struck by a fine-tipped shaft (śalya) without reaching the internal cavity (āśaya), or when it is protruding or has emerged [through the skin], one should designate that as "pierced" (viddha). That which is neither excessively cut nor excessively torn, yet possesses the characteristics of both, is so described.
An uneven wound on the body is designated as *kṣata*. However, that part of the body which has become swollen due to a blow or pressure,
containing bone and drenched with marrow and blood, should be known as *piccita*.

That part of the body which, due to rubbing or injury, has its skin stripped away and is accompanied by heat and discharge, is designated as *ghṛṣṭa* (friction-injury). [14] That which is dark-brown, slightly swollen, covered with pustules, and repeatedly discharging blood is called *vidagdha*.
They say that a wound which has risen up softly like a bubble, containing flesh and accompanied by pain, is one with a foreign body (śalya).

A foreign body, having passed through the skin, pierced the vessels and other structures, or bypassed them, and become established in the abdominal cavity (koṣṭha), produces the aforementioned complications. 15–16.

In that case, one should avoid [a patient] whose internal blood [is depleted], whose feet, hands, and face are pale and cold, whose breath is cold, whose eyes are bloodshot, and who is emaciated (17).
Furthermore, there is dizziness, delirium, falling down, fainting, convulsions, exhaustion, and fever.
A sense of the limbs being washed away, fainting, upward-moving wind (ūrdhvavāta), and various other pains caused by Vāta;

blood resembling meat-washings flows out, and likewise there is a cessation of the functions of all the sense organs—this, in general, is said to be the symptom when the five [types of] vital spots (marmas) are injured. 18–19.
When the veins are pierced or injured, blood flows profusely like that of a king of elephants or a cow, and the Vāyu produces various diseases as previously described;
furthermore, there occurs hunchbackedness, a general debility of the limbs, incapacity for action, and intense pains.

One should diagnose a man as having a ligament pierced when a wound heals only after a long time (21). An increase in swelling, intense pain, loss of strength, swelling occurring on all sides of both stable and unstable joints, and the cessation of all bodily functions are the signs [of a ligament injury] (22).

A wise physician who has mastered the aphorisms and understands their meaning should diagnose that man as one whose bones have been pierced by an arrow, whose terrible pains do not find relief day or night and in all conditions.
Furthermore, he should recognize these specific signs when the vital points (*marmans*) have been struck according to their respective locations.
One who is pale and discolored, who does not feel touch, and who suffers when the vital points (marman) of the flesh are pressed; 24.
erysipelas, hemiplegia, stiffness of the vessels, facial paralysis, delusion, insanity, pain from ulcers, fever, thirst, and lockjaw; 25.

Cough, vomiting, diarrhea, hiccup, dyspnea accompanied by trembling—these sixteen are declared by those who contemplate wounds to be the complications (upadrava) of wounds. 26. Diagnosis of Fractures (Bhagna-nidāna).
Now, regarding the etiology of fractures:

fracture, in brief, O Fire-god, is of two types—of the shaft (long bone) and of the joint. Among these, that of the joint is of six kinds: crushed, separated, displaced, obliquely situated, dislocated, and downward-displaced.

Painful extension, contraction, and twisting, along with an aversion to touch—this is said to be the general symptom of a dislocation. In a crushed joint (utpiṣṭa-sandhi), there is swelling on all sides; specifically, in a case of a separated joint (viśliṣṭa), there is pain occurring at night, as well as constant pain in both types.
When the bone is twisted, there is intense pain in the sides; when it has gone askew, there is severe pain [in those locations]. 3.
Furthermore, in the shaft-like (kāṇḍa) fracture types, there are the karkaṭaka, aśvakarṇa, vicūrṇita, piccita, asthi-challikā, 4.
as well as the broken-in-the-shaft (kāṇḍeṣu-bhagna), the completely displaced (atipātita), the marrow-reaching (majjāgata), and the cracked (sphuṭita) and crooked (vakra).
The fracture is either split in two or even in twelve ways; there is drooping of the limbs, swelling, and excessive pain.
When the bone is pressed, a sound is produced here, along with intolerance to touch, throbbing, pricking, and piercing pains.
In all stages, there is no attainment of comfort; indeed, these are the signs of a fractured bone.
A fracture that splits into many pieces at its midpoint is, in brief, equivalent to a severed bone in terms of its name.
A fracture in a person who eats little, lacks self-control, is of a windy temperament, or is afflicted by complications, is cured only with great difficulty.
A wise physician should indeed avoid one whose skull is fractured at the waist, or likewise displaced from its joint, or whose hips are crushed;
as well as one whose skull bones on the forehead are not joined together or are pulverized.
One should avoid fractures in the region between the breasts, on the back, at the temple, or on the head (10).
Even a bone that has been properly set should be avoided if it undergoes displacement due to improper positioning, binding, or agitation (11).

The young bones bend, the marrow-cords (nalaka) break, the cranial plates (kapāla) split apart, and the collarbones (rucaka) burst; this is the etiology of sinus ulcers (nāḍīvraṇa). 12. Nāḍīvraṇanidāna.
Now, the etiology of sinus ulcers (nāḍīvraṇa):
An ignorant person who neglects an inflammatory swelling while it is immature or even when it has reached suppuration, or one of improper conduct who neglects an ulcer containing abundant pus;
Having split open its previously established locations, it enters within; then,
because that pus travels excessively far, its movement is so designated.
Because it carries [substances] like a tube (nāḍī), it is considered a "tube" (nāḍī);
it arises from the three doṣas either individually, combined together, or due to other causes such as a foreign body (śalya). 2.
Among these, that caused by wind (vāta) has a rough, narrow opening and discharges a large amount of frothy discharge accompanied by pain during the nights;
that caused by bile (pitta) produces thirst and fever and is characterized by a burning sensation.

Yellow pus flows excessively and with great heat even during the day; it should be known as arising from phlegm (kapha), being thick, white, slimy, and flowing, and is stiff, itchy, painful, and increases at night.
One should designate that [fever]— in which burning heat, dyspnea, fainting, and dryness of the mouth occur,
as well as the aforementioned symptoms— as the terrible night of Time, which causes the destruction of life through the provocation of wind, bile, and phlegm.
When the arrowhead has been lost, it quickly reveals its path by some means through the aforementioned locations;
[the wound] becomes frothy, churned, hot, and mixed with blood.

If it causes sudden discharge and is constantly painful, the sinus originating from the three *doṣas* is incurable; indeed, the remaining four types are curable with effort. (6) [The Diagnosis of Fistula-in-Anus]
Now, the etiology of fistula-in-ano:
a very painful abscess that has burst on either side within a two-aṅgula area of the anus is known as bhagaṇḍara; it is considered to be of five types. 1.
When the Vāyu is excessively provoked by astringent and parching substances, it produces a carbuncle (piḍakā) in the region of the anus;

through neglect, this undergoes a severe suppuration, and when burst, it discharges reddish frothy matter. In that condition, where urine, feces, and semen emerge through numerous openings, one should call it Śataponaka.
Pitta, excessively provoked by aggravating factors, produces a red pustule located in the anus;
when that quickly suppurates and discharges cold, putrid matter, one should call it Bhagandara (fistula-in-ano), specifically the type resembling the head and neck of a camel.
It is characterized by itching, thick discharge, hardness, and mild pain.

The *bhagandara* (fistula-in-ano) born of *kapha* has a white appearance and discharges [fluid]. That which has multicolored pain and discharge, with a swelling resembling a cow's udder, and possesses a channel (*nāḍī*) shaped like the whorl of a snail shell, is considered *śambūkāvartaka*. 5–6.

When the wound becomes an opening for the passage of feces, it increases through neglect; worms arise there, and having torn it apart, they create many paths through various openings in the ulcer. One should call this "bhagandara" (fistula-in-ano), which is a downward-pathing disease. All types of bhagandara are terrible, difficult to cure, and painful.
Among these, the types arising from the three *doṣas* and especially that born of injury (*kṣataja*) are incurable.
Furthermore, worms (*krimayaḥ*) discharging wind, urine, feces,
and semen through the fistula destroy that patient.
Now, the causes of upadaṃśa (venereal disease) are:
from striking with the hand, from injury by nails or teeth, from [sexual] intercourse with a woman, or from excessive indulgence.
Due to disorders of the female reproductive tract (*yonipradoṣa*), five types of venereal sores (*upadaṃśa*) arise in the penis, which are to be diagnosed through various treatments:
one should identify a sore caused by *vāta* by its throbbing, piercing pain, twitching, and blackish vesicles;
that caused by *pitta* by its yellow color, excessive discharge, and burning sensation; and that caused by blood (*rakta*) by its appearance resembling raw flesh.
They declare that ulcer caused by the three *doshas* (*trimalopadaṃśa*)— which exudes blood with black vesicles, possesses the characteristics of *pitta*,
and is characterized by *kapha* with large, white, thick, and discharging eruptions accompanied by itching and swelling— is incurable when it is afflicted with various types of discharges and pain.
One should avoid [the patient] whose flesh has fallen away, who is devoured by worms, and whose only remaining parts are the testicles.
That foolish man, addicted to sensual objects, who does not perform the [prescribed] treatment as soon as [the disease] arises,
dies because his penis is destroyed by time through swelling, worms, burning, and suppuration.
Like sprouts gathered together and situated one above the other,
it gradually becomes a wick resembling the crest of a cock;
whether within the sheath at its junction or extending to all the joints.
Accompanied by pain, slimy, and difficult to treat, this condition arising from the three doṣas is known as liṅgavarti;
others call it liṅgārśas. This concludes the diagnosis of the defects of the penis (śūkadoṣa).
Now, the etiology of the disorders of the *śūka* (penile spines):
That fool-minded man who, out of sequence, desires the enlargement of the penis develops eighteen diseases born of the *śūka*. 1.

A pustule shaped like a white mustard seed (*gaurasarṣapa*), caused by the bending of awns and arising from phlegm and wind, is to be known as *sarṣapikā*. A hard, unevenly bent [pustule] produced by wind is *aṣṭhīlikā*.
That which is constantly filled with spikes and knotted together is known to arise from *kapha*.
The *kumbhikā* arises from blood and bile (*raktapitta*); it resembles the bone of a jambu fruit and is inauspicious.
A wise physician should recognize *alajī*, which has similar characteristics, as described previously.
That which is crushed, oppressed, or agitated by the provocation of Vāta,
and when excessively rubbed with the hands, becomes a *saṃmūḍhapiḍakā*.
Those numerous long pustules which burst in the middle are likewise [known as such].

That *adhimantha*, caused by *kapha* and blood, produces pain and horripilation. A swelling covered with pustules, arising from *pitta* and blood and shaped like the pericarp of a lotus, should be known as *puṣkarikā*.
Blood vitiated by *śūka* (hair-like particles) causes a loss of sensation;
that which is red, resembling mung beans or black gram, and arises from *rakta-pitta*,
is the disease named *uttamā*, caused by the undigested state of *śūka*.
That disease which is known as Śataponaka should be recognized by a swelling covered on all sides with small openings like the mouths of needles, arising from Vāta and blood.
Skin-pāka (tvakpāka), caused by Vāta and Pitta, should be known to produce fever and burning sensations.

That which is afflicted with black vesicles and reddish pustules, and in which there is severe pain in the seat of the disease, should be known as *śoṇitār-buda* (blood-tumor). One should recognize a tumor arising from flesh (*māṃsa-sambhava-arbuda*) by its being caused by a disorder of the flesh.

The physician should recognize that condition as *māṃsapāka* (flesh-cooking), caused by all the *doṣas*, when the flesh wastes away and all sensations [of pain] are present; one should designate it as a *vidradhi* (abscess) produced by the combination of all three humors (*sannipāta*), as previously described. 12–13.
Black, variegated, or even poisonous bristles, when struck, quickly cook the penis of a living being without exception; having become black, his flesh withers away. 14.
One should know that those *tilakālaka* (mole-like spots) arise from the combination of all three *doṣas*.
Among them, the *māṃsārbuda* (flesh tumor), that which is known as *māṃsapāka* (flesh suppuration),
*vidradhi* (abscess), and those *tilakālaka* spots do not succeed in being cured.
Now, the etiology of skin diseases (kuṣṭha): incompatible foods and drinks, as well as those that are liquid, unctuous, and heavy.
For those who indulge in vomiting, or suppress other natural urges;
for those who engage in excessive physical exercise, excessive heat, or overeating; and for those afflicted by the fear of heat and fatigue while consuming cold water—[cold water is harmful].

For those who eat while suffering from indigestion, those who overeat, those who practice the five purificatory therapies (pañcakarma) improperly, those who consume fresh grain, curd, fish, sesame, salt, and sour substances,
and those who eat black gram, radish, flour-based foods, sesame, milk, and molasses.
For those who engage in sexual intercourse during indigestion, those who indulge in sleep during the day,
those who insult Brahmins and gurus, and those who perform sinful deeds,
the three humors— vāta and the others— become deranged, affecting the skin, blood, flesh, and fluids.
These seven groups of substances vitiate [the body],
and from them arise the seven and eleven types of skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
Skin diseases are of seven kinds, arising from the humors (doṣas) individually, in pairs, or combined together.
In all cases of the three doṣas, the designation is according to whichever one is predominant.

(7) There is excessive smoothness or roughness to the touch, perspiration or lack thereof, discoloration of the skin, burning sensation, itching, numbness, pricking pain, elevation of urticarial patches (koṭha), and vertigo. (8)
An excessive number of ulcers, rapid formation, long-term persistence, dryness even when healed, and provocation by even slight causes— these,
along with horripilation and a blackish discoloration of the blood, are the premonitory signs of leprosy (kuṣṭha).
That leprosy which has the appearance of a blackish-red skull, is rough and thin,
and is characterized by intense piercing pain, is known as the difficult-to-cure *kāpāla* type;
it is surrounded by pain, burning, redness, and itching, and its hair becomes tawny.
One should call the *audumbara* leprosy that which resembles the fruit of the *udumbara* tree;
it is white, red, firm, thick, unctuous, and has elevated circular patches.
When these are combined with other types, this difficult-to-cure leprosy is called *maṇḍala*.
That which is rough, red at the edges, dark brown within, and painful is called Ṛṣyajihva; that which is white, red at the edges, and resembles the petal of a lotus is called Puṇḍarīka. 13–14.
That which is elevated and reddish is called a *puṇḍarīka*;
it is white and copper-colored, and when rubbed, it sheds fine dust. For the most part, that on the chest resembles the *sidhma* [disease], the *alābu* gourd, or a flower. 15.
That leprosy which has the color of a *kākaṇantikā* seed, accompanied by suppuration and intense pain, exhibiting the symptoms of all three *doṣas*, is called *kākaṇa*; it is indeed incurable.
That which is non-sudorific, extensive in area, and resembles the scales of a fish [is also incurable]. (16–17)
That which is a single type of leprosy called *carmākhya*, thick like an elephant's hide,
dark-brown, with a rough and callous touch, and coarse, is known as *kiṭibha*.
That which affects the feet (*vaipādika*) causes cracking of the hands and feet and is characterized by intense pain.
Alasaka is characterized by eruptions covered with itching and red patches;
Dadru-maṇḍala is raised, accompanied by itching, redness, and pustules;
and Rakta is red, painful, itchy, marked by eruptions, and even oozing.
That is called Carmadala; it is said to be unable to endure touch.
Numerous fine pustules that are exuding, itchy, and accompanied by burning sensations are called Pāmā.
That same condition, when accompanied by eruptions and severe burning, should be known as *kacchū* (scabies), affecting the hands and the buttocks.
Eruptions that are dark-red in appearance and have thin skin are called *visphoṭa*.
Rakta-śatāru is reddish-brown, accompanied by burning and pain, and characterized by many ulcers (22).
Vicarcikā consists of itchy, dark-brown pustules with excessive discharge.
Kuṣṭha caused by Vāta is rough, dark-brown or reddish, dry, and painful (23).
From pitta, it is considered to be boiled, accompanied by burning, redness, and discharge; from kapha, it is moist, thick, unctuous, and characterized by itching, coldness, and heaviness.
Kuṣṭha born from two [doṣas] possesses two symptoms, while that born from all three [doṣas] possesses three symptoms.
When Kuṣṭha is located in the skin, discoloration and roughness arise in the limbs (25).
When Kuṣṭha is situated in the blood, there occurs numbness of the skin, horripilation, excessive perspiration, itching, and suppuration (26).
Excessive thickness, dryness of the mouth, roughness, the eruption of pustules, pricking pain, vesicles, and firmness occur when Kuṣṭha has taken refuge in the muscle tissue (māṃsa).
When it reaches the tendons and ligaments, there is deformity of the hands, loss of movement, splitting pain in the limbs, and the spreading of ulcers.
When [the vitiated humors] have reached the locations [of the sense organs], the symptoms are as previously described;
furthermore, there occurs a distortion of the nose, redness of the eyes, the appearance of worms in wounds, and impairment of the voice when [the vitiation] has reached the bones and marrow. (28–29)
The offspring born of a husband and wife who both suffer from an abundance of leprosy (kuṣṭha) due to corrupted blood and semen should be known as likewise afflicted by leprosy. However,
that which resides in the skin, blood, and flesh, and in which vāta and śleṣman predominate, is curable.
That which arises from fat is palliable; that which resides in the marrow and bones must be rejected.

That which is born of the three doṣas, accompanied by worms, thirst, burning sensations, and weak digestion, as well as that which is cracked, with leaking limbs, red eyes, and a lost voice, should be abandoned. (31–32)
Transcending the five qualities of action, it destroys leprosy (kuṣṭha) in a person here;
Kāpāla leprosy arises from Vāta, Audumbara from Pitta,
and from Kapha arise those called Maṇḍala and Vicarcī, while that called Ṛṣya is born from Vāta and Pitta.
Carma-kuṣṭha, kiṭibha, sidhma, alasa, and vipādikā arise from vāta and śleṣman;
dadru, śatārus, puṇḍarīka along with visphoṭa, pāmā, and likewise carmadala arise from śleṣman and pitta. (34–35)
From all [the seven types of kuṣṭha] together, kākaṇaka arises; with the first three, dadru occurs along with kākaṇa.
Puṇḍarīka, ṛṣyajihva, and the others—these are the seven great kuṣṭhas (mahākuṣṭha).
Śvitra, kilāsa, and vāruṇa arise from a single cause, namely kuṣṭha.
It has been described as non-exuding, arising from and dependent upon the three *dhātus*:

from *vāta* it is rough, reddish, and coppery like a lotus leaf, accompanied by burning and hair loss; from *pitta* it is coppery like a lotus leaf, with burning and loss of body hair; from *kapha* it is white, thick, and heavy. (37–38)
One should recognize [the disease] as being accompanied by itching (kaṇḍū) in the skin, and sequentially in the blood, flesh, and fat;
by its color alone, both types are thus characterized, and each subsequent one is more difficult to treat.
[A healthy area is] one where the hair is not white, is not sparse, is not matted together, and is fresh.
Leucoderma that has not been burnt by fire is curable; otherwise, it is to be avoided.
Even if it is recent, leucoderma appearing on the private parts, the palms of the hands, or the lips must be especially avoided by one who desires success. (40–41)
Through incidental contact of the body, through breath, through eating together,
through sharing a bed or a seat, and through the use of clothing, garlands, and ointments— leprosy, fever, consumption, and indeed inflammation of the eyes [are transmitted].

And contagious diseases (aupasargika-roga) are transmitted from person to person. 43. Now follows the diagnosis of cold-pitta (śītapitta), urticaria (udarda), and skin eruptions (koṭha). Now follows the diagnosis of cold-pitta, urticaria, and skin eruptions.
Due to contact with cold winds, the deranged *kapha* and *vāta*, having combined with *pitta*, spread both externally and internally;
[this is accompanied by] thirst, anorexia, nausea, exhaustion of the body, and heaviness of the limbs.
Redness of the eyes is a characteristic sign of its premonitory stage. A swelling arises externally at the site bitten by a *varaṭī* (wasp),
accompanied by itching and frequent pricking pain, as well as vomiting, fever, and a burning sensation.
One should know that as *udarda*; others, however, call it *śītapitta*.
*Śītapitta* is characterized by a predominance of *vāta*, whereas *udarda* has a predominance of *kapha*.
It is characterized by circular patches (*maṇḍala*) that are elevated, reddish, and itchy.

The disease arising from phlegm (kapha) in the cold season is known as udarda. It is caused by improper administration of emetics, the provocation of pitta and phlegm, and the suppression of natural urges; it manifests as numerous circular patches that are itchy and reddish.
Utkoṭha, when accompanied by its sequelae, is designated as Koṭha. Now begins the diagnosis of Amlapitta (acid dyspepsia).
6. Diagnosis of Amlapitta.

The virtuous declare that *amlapitta* (acid bile) is that bile which was previously accumulated through its own causes by one who consumes incompatible, corrupted, sour, burning, and pitta-aggravating drinks and foods; it becomes "digested" (vidagdha) [as a morbid transformation]. It is characterized by indigestion, exhaustion, nausea, bitter and sour eructations, and heaviness.

The physician should declare *amlapitta* (acid bile) by the presence of burning in the heart and throat, and loss of appetite; it causes thirst, burning sensations, fainting, giddiness, and delusion. Sometimes it moves downward in various forms, producing nausea, urticaria-like rashes, fever, exhaustion, horripilation, perspiration, and yellowness of the skin.
Vomited matter that is green, yellow, blue, black, reddish, or blood-like in appearance, extremely sour, resembling meat-washings, very slimy, clear, and arising from phlegm with various tastes—
this, produced after eating or even when fasting, sometimes causes vomiting that is bitter and sour.
Such vomiting produces a burning sensation in the throat, heart, and belly, as well as pain in the head;

it causes a burning sensation in the hands and feet, great heat, severe loss of appetite, and fever; and it generates phlegm and bile, resulting in a mass of diseases such as itching, circular rashes, pustules, coughs, and afflictions that cover the limbs.
This disease called *amlapitta* is successfully treated with effort when it is recent;
if it has arisen long ago, it becomes palliable, and for some, it is difficult to cure.
One should recognize whether it is associated with *vāta*, or with *vāta* and *kapha*, or with *kapha*.
A wise physician [should diagnose] by means of the symptoms of the doshas, for that [condition] causes delusion:
trembling, delirium, fainting, twitching, exhaustion of the limbs, and piercing pain;
from the provocation of Vata arise the vision of darkness, confusion, bewilderment, and excessive joy. (8–9)

Expectoration of phlegm, heaviness, dullness, loss of appetite, coldness, exhaustion, a sense of being smeared, burning sensation, loss of strength, itching, and excessive sleep are the signs when [the disease] is associated with *kapha*. Both these sets of symptoms occur together when it arises from both *vāta* and *kapha*. 10. In the case of *amla-pitta*, these very same signs appear.
Bitterness, acidity, and pungency; eructation; burning sensations in the heart, abdomen, and throat;
vertigo, fainting, loss of appetite, vomiting, lethargy, headache, salivation, and sweetness in the mouth—these are the symptoms of *śleṣmapitta*. 11–12.
Now, the etiology of visarpa: it arises from the provocation of the doṣas due to the excessive consumption of salty, sour, pungent, and hot substances.
Visarpa (erysipelas) is to be known as sevenfold, because it spreads in every direction:
three types arise from each of the [three] doshas individually, one from all three combined, and three from the combinations of two doshas;
namely, the vātika, the paittika, the kaphaja, and the sānnipātika.

These four types of visarpa will be described; three are born from the combination of two doshas: that caused by vāta and pitta is called āgneya, while the one known as granthi is born from kapha and vāta.
That which is the terrible kardamaka arises from pitta and kapha.

Blood, lymph, skin, and flesh are the corrupted tissues (dūṣyas), while the three humors (doṣas) are the impurities (malas). These seven constituents should be known as the origin of visarpa (erysipelas).
Among them, that visarpa arising from vāta has symptoms identical to those of vāta-fever.
Accompanied by swelling, throbbing, piercing pain, tearing sensations,

exhaustion, distress, and horripilation, moving rapidly due to pitta, characterized by the symptoms of pitta-fever, and extremely red; from kapha, it is associated with itching, is unctuous, and has a pain similar to that of kapha-fever.

That which arises from the combination [of all three humors] (sannipāta) is endowed with all the symptoms. From wind and bile (vātapitta), it is accompanied by fever, vomiting, fainting, diarrhea, thirst, giddiness, breaking pain in the joints, loss of digestive fire, exhaustion, darkness before the eyes, and anorexia.
It makes every limb appear as if strewn with glowing embers;
whatever region the erysipelas (visarpa) spreads to,
that very place quickly becomes black like extinguished coals, or blue, or red, and swells up.

Due to its rapid movement, that excessively powerful Vāta spreads quickly like a fire, following the vital points (marmas) and appearing as eruptions resembling burns; it causes pain in the limbs, robs one of consciousness and sleep, and excites labored breathing.
And having fallen into such a state, he suffers from hiccups; no one anywhere, seized by a craving for pleasure, finds rest on the ground, in beds, or on seats.
Thus, struggling and distressed, he experiences a delusion of both mind and body.
One who is difficult to awaken from sleep suffers from what is called agnivisarpa (fire-like erysipelas).

When the wind (vāyu), obstructed by phlegm (kapha), breaks through that phlegm in many ways, it reaches the skin, vessels, ligaments, and flesh— either the phlegm itself or the blood in one whose blood is increased.
Having corrupted [the blood], it produces a chain of knots that are long, small, round, thick, and rough in nature, accompanied by redness, intense pain, and fever;
[this condition is further characterized] by dyspnea, cough, diarrhea, wasting of the face, hiccups, vomiting, and vertigo.
Accompanied by delusion, discoloration, fainting, breaking pain in the limbs, and loss of digestive fire— this is Granthivīsarpa, arising from the provocation of Kapha and Vāta.
From Kapha and Pitta arise fever, stiffness, drowsiness, lethargy, and headache.

Lassitude of the limbs, restlessness, coating of the mouth, anorexia, vertigo, fainting, loss of digestive fire, breaking pain in the bones, thirst, heaviness of the sense organs, the passage of undigested stool, and a coating of the channels— this [dosha] spreads throughout the body. 18.
Generally, it affects the stomach (āmāśaya) and involves only one region without excessive pain; it is covered with eruptions that are extremely yellow, reddish, or pale-white,
is unctuous, blackish-blue, dirty-looking, swollen, and heavy.
Deep-seated in its maturation, intensely hot, and becoming moist upon contact,
it sloughs off like mud; with its flesh shattered and its network of tendons and veins clearly exposed,
smelling like a corpse— this spreading disease (visarpa) is called Kardama.
Provoked by injury from an external cause, the wind (vāyu), agitating the blood and bile (pitta), produces erysipelas (vīsarpa) characterized by eruptions resembling horse-gram (kulattha),
abounding in swelling, fever, pain, and burning, and marked by a dusky-red discoloration. (22–23)
Fever, diarrhea, vomiting, a tearing sensation in the skin and flesh, exhaustion, anorexia, and indigestion are the complications of visarpa.
Visarpas caused by vāta, kapha, and pitta become chronic (sidhmanti).
That which is caused by injury to all [tissues] does not reach success;
that which consists of pitta and has the appearance of an ointment is incurable; indeed, all those occurring in the vital spots (marmans) are difficult to treat. 25
Now, the etiology of visphoṭa: it arises from pungent, sour, sharp, hot, burning, dry, and alkaline substances, as well as from indigestion, overeating, and exposure to the sun.
Likewise, due to the disorder of the seasons and through their mutual aggravation, the humors such as wind (pavana) and the others become provoked;
having taken refuge in the skin and corrupted the blood, flesh, and bones, they produce all the terrible eruptions (visphoṭa), preceded by fever.
Eruptions resembling burnt flesh, accompanied by fever and arising from blood and bile (*raktapitta*),
occurring either in some parts or throughout the entire body, are known as *visphoṭa*.
Headache, intense piercing pain, fever, thirst, and a breaking sensation in the joints [are its symptoms].
The presence of a blackish color is a characteristic of wind-type eruptions (vātavisphoṭa).
Accompanied by fever, burning sensations, pain, discharge, suppuration, and thirst,
and having a yellowish or reddish color, are the characteristics of bile-type eruptions (pittavisphoṭa).
Accompanied by vomiting, anorexia, and lassitude, characterized by itching, hardness, and pallor,
maturing slowly and without pain, that eruptive ulcer is of the nature of phlegm (kaphaja).
However, that which is produced by wind and bile (vātapittaja) causes intense pain.
One should recognize the Kapha-Vata type by itching, numbness, and heaviness (7).
The Kapha-Pitta type is characterized by itching, burning, fever, and vomiting;
it is depressed in the center, elevated at the edges, hard, and slow to suppurate (8).
Burning sensation, thirst, delusion, vomiting, fainting, pain, fever, delirium, trembling, and drowsiness— this [fever] born of the three doṣas is incurable.
Those [eruptions] arising from blood are red, resembling guñjā seeds or coral.

It should be understood that those [afflictions] caused by blood and by bile do not reach success even through hundreds of perfected yogas. One arising from a single humor is curable; one born from two humors is difficult to cure.
Arising from all the [three] doshas, it is terrible, incurable, and accompanied by many complications. 11.
The Diagnosis of Masūrikā (Smallpox).
Now follows the diagnosis of Masūrikā.
Through the consumption of pungent, sour, salty, alkaline, incompatible, or over-eaten foods; through spoiled *niṣpāva* beans, leafy vegetables, and the like; through corrupted winds and waters;
and even from the gaze of malefic planets, the bodily humors (*doṣas*) become aggravated within the body.

When combined with vitiated blood, they produce eruptions on this body shaped like lentils; these are known as *masūrikā*. Prior to their appearance, there is fever, itching, a breaking sensation in the limbs, restlessness, and vertigo.
In the skin-type, swelling accompanied by discoloration and redness of the eyes arises;
eruptions that are dusky-red, dry, and associated with intense pain,
being hard and slow to suppurate, occur when they are born from Vāyu.
There is a splitting sensation in the joints, bones, and limbs; coughing, trembling, restlessness, and exhaustion;
dryness of the palate, lips, and tongue; thirst accompanied by loss of appetite;
and red, yellow, or white eruptions that are burning and intensely painful.
They ripen quickly and arise from the provocation of pitta;
there is diarrhea, body ache, burning sensation, thirst, and likewise loss of appetite,
as well as inflammation of the mouth, redness of the eyes, and a fever that is intense and most dreadful.
In the case of [diseases] born from blood, these disorders characterized by pitta occur:
excessive salivation of phlegm, a sense of stiffness, headache, heaviness of the limbs,
nausea with loss of appetite, drowsiness, and lassitude accompanied by lethargy.
White, glossy, very large, intensely itchy, and mildly painful eruptions arising from phlegm (kapha) are proclaimed to be masūrikā, which take a long time to heal.
Blue, flattened and wide, depressed in the center, and accompanied by great pain—
These carbuncles known as *carma* are slow to suppurate, discharge pus, are abundant, and arise from all three *doṣas*.
Accompanied by obstruction of the throat, loss of appetite, stiffness, delirium, and aversion to food, they are declared to be difficult to treat. (11–12)

Those arising from phlegm and bile (kapha-pitta) are characterized by elevations at the hair follicles, are accompanied by cough and loss of appetite, have hairs at their edges, and are preceded by fever;
those located in the skin (tvag-gata) resemble water bubbles and are known as masūrikā. 13.
When they are slightly afflicted, they develop with little pain; when incised, they exude water.
Those located in the blood are red in appearance, suppurate quickly, have thin skin, are curable if not excessively vitiated, and when incised, they bleed. 14–15.
Those born from the flesh are hard, unctuous, slow to suppurate, and have thick skin;
they are accompanied by body aches, thirst, itching, fever, and restlessness.
Those born from fat are circular in shape, soft, and slightly elevated.

Those [ulcers] that are afflicted by severe fever, large, glossy, and painful, accompanied by delusion, aversion, and burning heat—only rarely can one emerge from them. Those that are small, equal in size to the body part, rough, flattened, or slightly elevated [are of a different nature]. 17–18.
Arising from the marrow and joined with intense delusion, pain, and distress, they indeed sever the vital points (*marman*) and swiftly carry away the life-breaths;
they cause the bones to throb all over as if pierced by bees. (19)
In Masūrikā born from semen (śukra), there indeed appear pustules that are ripe-looking, unctuous, small, and extremely painful,
accompanied by numbness, restlessness, delusion, burning sensation, and insanity. (20–21)
Only the mere sign is indicated here, but not the actual life-force;

however, these seven types, when mixed with the humors (doṣas), should be observed by the characteristics of those humors. (22) They are: those located in the skin, those born from blood, those born from bile (pitta), and likewise those born from phlegm (śleṣman).
Measles caused by phlegm (kapha) and bile (pitta) are easily curable.
Those born from wind (vāta), those arising from wind and bile, and those caused by phlegm and wind are most difficult to cure; therefore, one should treat them with great effort.
Those arising from the derangement of the three humors (sannipāta) are incurable; I shall describe their symptoms:
some resemble coral, some are like the jambū fruit, some are like a net of iron, and some are similar to the atasī seed.
From the various distinctions of these defects, many kinds of symptoms arise:
cough, hiccup, urinary disorder, and severe, most dreadful fever;
delirium, restlessness, fainting, thirst, burning sensation, and excessive giddiness. (26–27)
Blood may flow from the mouth, as well as from the nose and the eyes;
making a rattling sound in the throat, the patient breathes with extreme pain—these are the signs of one overcome by *masūrikā* (smallpox), according to the best of physicians. 28.
If the characteristic signs are observed, one should not administer medicine in this case.
He who is overcome by smallpox and breathes heavily through the nose, being afflicted by thirst and corrupted by wind, loses his life completely. (29–30)

Following the smallpox (masūrikā), there may be swelling at the elbow, the wrist, and also on the shoulder-blade; it is difficult to treat and very severe. (31) [End of] the Diagnosis of Minor Diseases (kṣudraroga-nidāna).

Now, regarding the diagnosis of minor diseases: those that are unctuous, of the same color as the skin, knotted, painless, resembling mung beans, and arising from kapha and vāta are known as ajagallikās in children. (1)
A hard, knotted pustule, shaped like barley and embedded in the flesh,
caused by phlegm and wind, is called *yavaprakhya*.
A thick, straight, elevated, and circular pustule [is likewise described].
One should know that *antrālajī*, which has little pus, arises from *kapha* and *vāta*.
One should know that the circular ulcer called *vivṛtā*, which has a wide opening, causes great burning, and resembles a ripe *udumbara* fruit, arises from *pitta*. 3–4.
Five or six hard pustules, resembling tortoises and clustered together,
arising from the derangement of phlegm (kapha) and wind (vāyu), are known by the wise as *kacchapikā*.
They occur in the region of the neck, shoulders, armpits, hands, or feet, at joints, or in the throat, due to all three humors (doṣas).

That knot (*granthi*), like an anthill (*valmīka*), having arisen through the lack of treatment, gradually increases in size. Physicians call this disorder *valmīka*, which spreads with many openings that cause a pricking sensation like a stream of ants, with elevated tips, resembling a creeping eruption (*visarpa*); it is particularly characterized by being chronic and lacking any counteractive remedy.
The physician should recognize that as Indra-viddhā when it is covered with pustules in its center like the pericarp of a lotus, and arises from Vāta and Pitta;
it is circular, elevated, reddish, and strewn with pustules.
One should know that Gardabhikā, which causes pain, arises from Vāta and Pitta (9).
A swelling arising from Vāta and Kapha at the joint of the jaw,
which is firm, slightly painful, and oily, is to be known as Pāṣāṇagardabha (10).
One should know that *panasikā* is a firm, intensely painful pustule arising within the ear, produced by the provocation of Vāta and Kapha.
That swelling which spreads like erysipelas (*visarpa*), being thin and non-suppurating, is also [known as] *panasikā*.

That which causes a burning fever due to pitta should be known as *jālagardabha*. One should recognize *irivellikā* as a circular pustule located on the head, accompanied by severe pain and fever, possessing the nature of all [doshas] and exhibiting all their symptoms.
One should designate as *kakṣā* a painful, black vesicle arising from the provocation of *pitta* on the arms, sides, shoulders, or armpits;
having observed such a single pustule resembling a vesicle [in these locations].
They declare that when there is an eruption of the skin due to the provocation of bile (*pitta*), it is called *gandhamālā*.
Those pustules which arise in the armpits, tearing the flesh, causing internal burning and fever, and resembling a blazing fire, [are known by this name].
Within seven days, ten days, or a fortnight, it destroys the man;
one should know that as Agnirōhiṇī, born from all the doṣas and incurable.
(17) Vāyu and pitta, having taken hold of the nails and flesh of embodied beings, [cause this disease].
If these two produce burning and suppuration, one should designate that disease as *cippa*. One should call that very same condition *kunakha* when the humors (*doṣas*) are even more diminished.
[One should recognize] a [growth] that is deep-seated, with little swelling, similar in color to the surrounding skin, and situated on the surface.
One should know that this [type of tumor] is latent within the discourse; it ripens internally.
Vidārikā occurs at the joints of the armpits, the groins, and the knees, shaped like the tuber of the vidārī plant;
it is red when born from blood, and possesses all symptoms when born from all [doshas]. 20–21.
Having reached the flesh, vessels, and ligaments, the phlegm, fat, and likewise the wind produce a glandular swelling; when this is incised, it exudes a discharge resembling marrow,
clarified butter, or muscle-fat, as the wind there increases once again.
Having dried up the flesh, it then produces knotted gravel;
thereafter, the veins suddenly discharge blood that is foul-smelling, excessively moist, and multicolored— one should know that to be *śarkarārbuda*.
In one who habitually walks about, the wind produces a cracking of the feet that are excessively dry; this condition one should designate as *pādadārī*.
[This occurs] when the foot is bruised by pebbles or wounded by thorns and the like.
A knot that arises as elevated like a jujube fruit is indeed called *kadara*.
When the spaces between the toes of the feet are moist, accompanied by itching,
burning, and pain, one should identify that as *alasa* resulting from contact with foul mud.
The pitta, following the hair follicles and combined with vāta,
causes the hairs to fall out; thereafter, the kapha along with blood obstructs the hair follicles, and consequently, no further growth occurs.
That which is known as *lupta* (alopecia) or *khālitya* (baldness), and is characterized by the word *ruhya* (growing), is perceived thus:
when the scalp becomes harsh, itchy, and rough, and begins to flake due to the provocation of *kapha* and *vāta*, one should know that condition as *dāruṇaka*. 29–30.
One should recognize *aruṣikā* as sores on the head characterized by many openings and much exudation, caused in men by the provocation of phlegm, blood, and parasites (verse 31).
The bodily heat produced by anger, grief, and fatigue, when it reaches the head—
Pitta also digests the hair; by that [digestion], they arise.
32 Resembling the thorns of the *śālmalī* tree, born from phlegm, wind, and blood, these are to be known as *yuvānapiḍakā*, which defile the faces of the young. 33
A circular patch covered with thorns, pale and itchy, resembling the thorns of a lotus plant, is called *padminīkaṇṭaka*; it arises from phlegm and wind.
A uniform, elevated, painless circular patch arises from phlegm and blood.
According to some, the *lakṣma* is innate, while that which is a mole (*jatumaṇi*) is the object characterized by it.
That which appears on a limb as painless and stable, black like a bean and raised up, is a *maṣaka* caused by wind (*anila*). 35–36.

One should recognize as *tilakālaka* those black spots, the size of sesame seeds, which are painless and uniform, resulting from the drying up of wind, bile, and phlegm. Whether large or small, whether brownish-black or black— (37)
A painless circular patch on the body is designated as *nyaccha*.
Vāyu, aggravated by anger and exertion and combined with pitta, suddenly reaches the face and thereby discharges this circular patch. 38–39.
One should designate as *vyaṅga* a dark, thin, and painless discoloration on the face;
likewise, one that is black with these same qualities on the body or face is known as *nīlikā*. [This occurs] from excessive rubbing, pressing, or even from injury.
When the wind, moving everywhere, affects the skin of the penis, then,
due to being afflicted by the wind, that skin turns back;
and beneath the glans, the sheath hangs down in the form of a knot.
One should know that painful condition arising from Vāta as Parivartikā;
when that same condition is accompanied by itching and hardness, it is produced by Śleṣman.
When a man, due to sexual excitement or force, approaches a woman who has very little vaginal discharge, [the resulting condition is known as Putrighnī].
Or even from a blow with the hand, when the prepuce is forcibly turned upward;
one should know that condition in which the skin is split open as *avapāṭikā*.
When the penis is afflicted by Vāta, the skin retracts over the glans.

When the glans penis is constricted by a leather thong, it obstructs the urinary stream; when that [stream] is blocked, urine flows out with a weak stream and without pain, yet the glans does not open. 46.
Urine flows from the person, but the glans penis does not dilate.
One should know that [the condition] characterized by obstructed discharge and pain is caused by Vāta.
Due to the suppression of natural urges, the Vāyu becomes obstructed and, residing in the rectum, blocks the large intestine and causes its opening to become narrow. 47–48.
Due to the subtlety of the passage, his feces pass with difficulty;
one should recognize this as the extremely dreadful disease known as sanniruddhaguda.
In an infant, it occurs when the anus is not washed and is covered with a mixture of feces and urine.
Whether the patient has sweated or is not being bathed, an itching arises from the provocation of blood and phlegm (50).
From scratching that, pustules and discharge quickly appear;
when these have coalesced into a terrible ulcer, one should recognize it as *ahipūtana* (51).

When the filth located at the testicles of one who has neglected bathing and massage becomes moistened by sweat, it then produces itching (kaṇḍū). From scratching that [itching], eruptions (sphoṭa) and discharge quickly arise. 52.52–53ab.
They call that condition vṛṣaṇakacchū, which arises from the provocation of phlegm and blood.
When the anus protrudes externally due to straining or diarrhea in a person whose body is dry and weak, one should designate that as gudabhraṃśa (prolapse of the rectum). 53–54.
Accompanied by burning, with red margins, characterized by suppuration of the skin, intense pain, itching, and causing fever— that is *śūkaradaṃṣṭraka*.
(55) [This concludes] the diagnosis of diseases of the mouth.
Now, the etiology of diseases of the mouth:
Through excessive consumption of the meat of marshy animals, milk, curd, and fish, the aggravated *doṣas*, with *kapha* predominant, produce diseases within the mouth. (1)

Due to the provocation of the wind (māruta), the lips become rough, harsh, and stiff, afflicted by the pain of the wind; they are split and cracked. Furthermore, they are covered all over with painful pustules.

Due to Pitta, the lips have burning, suppuration, and eruptions, and they appear yellowish (3). Due to Kapha, the lips are covered with eruptions that match their own color, and they are painless, slimy, cold, and heavy (4).
Those [ears] which are once black, once yellow, and likewise once white,
should be known as resulting from a combination of the humors (sannipāta) and covered with many pustules; they are oppressed by pustules having the color of dates (kharjūra-phala).
When afflicted by rakta (blood), the eyes flow with blood and have a reddish luster;
