when afflicted by guru (phlegm) or sthūla (fat), they are heavy and large, protruding like a lump of flesh,
and living beings swarm there from both sides of the man's face.
Resembling the scum of clarified butter, itching, heavy, and due to an excess of fat,
they discharge a clear exudate resembling crystal profusely. Their ulcer does not heal, nor does it attain softness.
The two lips become blood-red, they crack and split due to trauma; likewise, the lips may become knotted and accompanied by itching,
and blood flows suddenly from the gums.
When the gums become foul-smelling, blackish, moist, and soft, and they wither away and ulcerate one another,
that disease arising from phlegm and blood is called Śītāda.
When a great swelling arises on the three [anterior] teeth, that disease is called Dantapuppuṭaka; it is born from phlegm and blood (12). Pus and blood flow out, and the teeth become loose.
That which arises from vitiated blood at the gums should be known as *dantaveṣṭa*.
A swelling at the roots of the teeth accompanied by pain, born of phlegm and blood,
and characterized by the discharge of saliva, should be known by the name *śaiṣira*.
In that condition where the teeth loosen from their sockets and the palate is also torn,
it is the disease born of all [three humors], known by the name Mahāśauṣira (15).
In that [condition] where the gums wither away and one spits blood, [it is called Dantaśarkarā].

That disease arising from bile, blood, and phlegm should be known as paridara (bleeding gums). That disorder caused by bile and blood, in which there is burning and suppuration in the gums and the teeth become loose, is named upakuśa.
When the gums are rubbed, a great swelling arises and the teeth become loose; this is the Vaidarbha disease, born from injury. When aggravated by Vāta, a tooth becomes excessively painful.
This condition known as Khalivardhana causes pain upon its appearance, which then subsides;
gradually, the wind residing in the teeth produces long and deformed teeth, and this Karāla disease is not curable. 19–20.

A large swelling with great pain on the posterior molar tooth, characterized by salivation and caused by kapha, should be known as *adhimāṃsaka*. Five types of sinus tracts (*nāḍī*) located at the roots of the teeth should be understood as previously described. 21.

That disease which arises in the teeth as if they were being torn apart by pain, known as *dālana*, is caused by the movement of the *sadāgati* (Vāyu). It is characterized by black cavities, mobility, discharge, inflammation, and great pain.
A toothache arising from wind (vāta) without any visible cause should be known as *krimidantaka* (23).
That disease caused by phlegm (kapha) and wind (vāta), in which the mouth becomes crooked and the breaking of teeth occurs, is designated as *bhañjanaka* (24).
O twice-born ones, when the teeth cannot endure cold, dry, windy,
or sour sensations due to the provocation of pitta and vāta, that condition is known by the name *dantaharṣa* (trembling of the teeth).
Furthermore, the dental plaque (*mala*) located on the teeth which has been dried up by pitta and vāta—

That which has a rough touch like sugar is to be known as *danta-śarkarā* (tooth-tartar). When the teeth crack as if they were potsherds, that very tartar is to be recognized as *kapālikā*, which constantly destroys the teeth.
That tooth which has been completely scorched by bloodless bile and has become either dark-brown or blue is called *śyāvadantaka*.
When there is a heavy swelling, both internal and external, in the gums caused by impurities mixed with blood, it is [known as] *danta-puppuṭaka*. (28)
When burst open, it constantly discharges pus and blood; this is *dantavidradhi* (tooth abscess).
(29) The tongue, due to *vāta*, becomes cracked and numb, appearing like the leaf of a *śāka* plant.
Due to *pitta*, it burns and swells with long, reddish thorns.
Due to *kapha*, [the tongue] becomes heavy, thickly coated, and covered with elevations of flesh resembling the thorns of the *śālmalī* tree (30).
That deep-seated swelling on the underside of the tongue, which consists of *kapha* and blood, is known as *alāsa*;
when it has increased, it stiffens the tongue, and the base of the tongue undergoes severe suppuration (31).

A swelling in the form of a protuberance at the tip of the tongue, arising from the root of phlegm and blood, which causes salivation, is accompanied by itching and a burning sensation; that is designated as *upajihvā* (ranula) by physicians. (32) A long swelling at the base of the palate, increased by phlegm and blood, resembling an inflated bladder— [is known as *galagaṇḍa*].
Physicians call that disease which is caused by thirst, dryness, and dyspnea "kaṇṭhaśuṇḍī" by name.
A large swelling accompanied by pricking pain, burning, and suppuration is considered *tuṇḍikerī*, arising from the two previously mentioned causes;
however, a soft, red swelling arising from blood, accompanied by fever and intense pain, is known as *adhruṣa*. 33–34.
A painless disease that arises slowly with a protuberance like a tortoise shell due to phlegm (kapha) should be known as *kacchapa*.

One should recognize a swelling in the middle of the palate that is shaped like a lotus and caused by blood as *arvuda*, possessing the symptoms previously described. A painless, swollen mass of flesh in the middle of the palate caused by phlegm is called *māṃsasaṃghāta*.
Due to Kapha associated with fat (medas), there occurs a swelling the size of a jujube fruit that remains painless in the region of the palate; this is called Puppuṭa.
Furthermore, due to Vāta, there is excessive dryness and the palate is even torn, accompanied by severe labored breathing; this is Tāluśoṣa.
Pitta causes a most terrible suppuration in the palate itself; thus they call it Tālupāka. (36–37)

When the wind (vāyu), along with the pitta and kapha, become aggravated and congealed, they corrupt the flesh and likewise the blood; by means of sprouts that cause obstruction in the throat, this disease destroys the vital breaths—this indeed is Rohiṇī.
Those fleshy sprouts which grow all around the tongue and obstruct the throat are accompanied by intense pain.
That which is caused by Vāta is designated as Rohiṇī; it is characterized by complications arising from the nature of Vāta.
That which arises from Pitta has rapid onset, rapid burning and suppuration, and is accompanied by intense fever.
That which originates from Kapha obstructs the channels, rises steadily, and possesses firm protrusions. 39–40.

That which has deep-seated ripening, irresistible power, the symptoms of the three *doṣas*, and arises from all three; which is covered with eruptions and has symptoms identical to those of *pitta*—this blood-born (*rudhirātmikā*) [tumor] is declared curable.
(41) That which is produced by *kapha*, the size of a peg or a bone, appearing like a thorn or a bristle in the throat, is a *granthi*.
A hard, stable swelling, curable by the application of surgical instruments, they call *kaṇṭhaśālūka*. 42.

A swelling shaped like the tip of a tongue, arising from phlegm mixed with blood above the tongue, is to be known as the disease *adhijihva*; one should avoid treating it once suppuration has set in. 43.
Valāsa produces a long and elevated swelling by obstructing the passage of food;

because its power is entirely irresistible, physicians declare it to be fatal and must be avoided. When Kapha and Vāta are aggravated, they produce a swelling in the throat accompanied by the affliction of dyspnea.
Experts call this condition "Balāsaka," which cuts into the vital points (marmans), is difficult to cure, and is characterized by swelling;

it is known as a single disease produced from both *balāsa* (phlegm) and *kṣataja* (blood), being circular and elevated in the center, accompanied by burning, itching, non-suppurating, soft, and heavy. 45–46.
They describe *vṛnda* as being elevated, circular, intensely burning, and characterized by severe fever;

it should be known to arise from the provocation of *pitta* and blood (*kṣataja*), while that which is accompanied by pricking pain (*sātoda*) is of the nature of *vāta*. A thick, throat-obstructing plug (*varti*) covered excessively with fleshy growths is also [a form of this].

The *anekaruk* is known to be fatal due to the three *doṣas*, while the *śataghnī* has the appearance of a *śataghnī* weapon. A hard, extremely painful knot in the throat, the size of an *āmalaka* stone, which is a manifestation of *kapha* and blood and makes food appear as if stuck, is called *galāyu*; it is curable by surgical means. 48–49.

The swelling that arises pervading the entire throat, wherein all types of pain are present due to all the *doṣas*, is indeed the *galavidradhi* (throat abscess), which is identical to the *sarvaja* (arising from all causes) type. This swelling is massive, obstructing food and water, accompanied by intense fever, and it destroys the movement of the vital air (*vāyu*).
That which arises in the throat from phlegm combined with blood is proclaimed as *galauigha*.
However, when one who is fainting breathes incessantly, with a broken voice and a parched, loosened throat,
while the channels of wind are smeared with phlegm— that disease should be known as *svaraghna* (loss of voice) due to labored breathing.
That swelling which is spreading, extremely painful, and gradually causes obstruction of the throat is called *māṃsatāna*; it is a life-threatening disorder caused by all [three] doṣas.
A swelling within the throat that is accompanied by constant burning and piercing pain, is deep copper-colored, and has putrid, sloughing flesh— [is known as *vidārī*].

One should recognize *vidārī* by its presence in the face due to *pitta*; however, it is specifically located on that side where the patient lies. That which is covered all over the face with pricking eruptions (*sphoṭa*) is from *vāta*.
That which is covered with thin, reddish-yellow eruptions accompanied by burning is from the provocation of *pitta*.
That which is covered with painless, itchy, and skin-colored [eruptions] is indeed caused by phlegm (kapha).
Among the afflictions of the lips, those born of muscle-tissue (māṃsa), blood (rakta), or the three humors (tridoṣa) are to be rejected;
likewise, among the diseases of the roots of the teeth, those characterized by the three symptoms (triliṅga) and those involving sinus-like cavities (śauṣira) are to be rejected.
In diseases of the teeth, Śyāva-dāla and Nabhañjana do not succeed; likewise, in diseases of the tongue, Balāśa occurs, and in those of the palate, Arbuda.
Svaraghna, Valaya, Vṛnda, Balāśa, and Vidārikā [are also found there]. 57
Galaugha, māṃsatāna, śataghnī, and rohiṇī in the throat—
these nine diseases are declared to be incurable; regarding them, the physician should perform treatment only after having declared the case hopeless.
The Diagnosis of Ear Diseases:
Now follows the diagnosis of ear diseases.
When the wind (vāyu) has entered the ear and moves in an abnormal manner, it causes excessive pain throughout both ears.
When [the wind] is obstructed by its respective humors (doṣas), it causes pain; this is described as Karṇaśūla (earache), which is difficult to treat.
When the wind is located in the ear canal, one hears various sounds such as those of kettledrums, clay drums, and conchs; that is called Karṇanāda (tinnitus).
When the pure wind, or that which is associated with phlegm, remains obstructing the channel that carries sound, deafness is produced by that;
when the wind is joined with bile and other humors, it produces a sound resembling the resonance of a bamboo flute.

That which produces a whirring sound in the ears is called *karṇakṣveḍa*. Alternatively, when pus flows from the ear due to a head injury, or from immersion in water, or even from suppuration or an abscess caused by the provoked wind (*vāta*), it is proclaimed as *karṇasaṃsrāva*.
Vata combined with Kapha causes itching in the ear;
and Kapha, dried by the heat of Pitta, produces earwax (karṇagūthaka). When that earwax reaches a liquid state and becomes dissolved, it flows into the nostrils and the mouth.
Then that disorder, constricted by the ear-wax, becomes a cause of splitting pain in the lower part of the head. When living organisms multiply or when flies produce their offspring therein,
because it manifests with such characteristics, the ancient physicians designate this disease as *krimikarṇaka* (ear-worm).
Indeed, when moths and centipedes enter the ear canal, they cause intense restlessness, agitation, and pain;
his ear is pierced as if by needles and throbbed with a tingling sensation. 9.108.9–10ab.

When a worm moves within it, there is intense pain; when it is motionless, the pain is mild. Furthermore, an abscess (vidradhi) may arise from a wound or injury, as well as another type caused by the humors (doṣas).
This latter type discharges blood that is reddish-yellow or crimson, and is characterized by pricking pain, a sensation of fuming, burning, and sucking pain.
Karṇapāka (ear-inflammation) is caused by pitta and produces suppuration and moistening;
it arises either from the suppuration of karṇavidradhi (ear-abscess) or from filling the ear with water. When it discharges foul pus, it should be known as pūtikarṇaka (foul-smelling ear).
One should recognize ear-swelling, tumors, and hemorrhoids by their previously described characteristics.
(13) From Vāta arise ringing in the ears, excessive pain, dryness of the earwax, thin discharge, and loss of hearing;
from Pitta arise swelling with redness, tearing pain, a burning sensation, and the discharge of yellowish, putrid fluid. (14)

From Kapha, there is discharge that is audible, itching, firm, swollen, white, and unctuous, with little pain; from Sannipāta (the combination of all three humors), all these symptoms appear, and the discharge has the color of the predominant humor. Due to tenderness, when the condition is neglected for a long time or suddenly aggravated, [it becomes severe].

An ear swelling that occurs on the lobe, being painful, fissured, resembling black or reddish-brown in color, and rigid, is known as *paripoṭaka* caused by Vāta (16). It may also arise from the contact of heavy ornaments, from being struck, or even from friction.
A dark swelling may occur at the earlobe, accompanied by burning, suppuration, and pain;
or it may be red due to the provocation of blood and bile—this disorder is known as Utpāta.
Furthermore, in one who forcibly stretches the ear, the Vāyu becomes aggravated in the lobe. (17–18)
Having seized the *kapha*, it produces a stiff, painless swelling;
this disorder, born of *kapha* and *vāta*, is called *unmanthaka*, characterized by itching.
When a wound is improperly incised and continues to enlarge, it becomes accompanied by itching, suppuration, and pain.
Swelling and suppuration occur, increasing suffering through the aggravation of all three doṣas.
When kapha, blood, and worms are provoked, they produce spreading eruptions (visarpa) on the margin resembling mustard seeds, accompanied by itching, burning, and pain. 20–21.
Arising from phlegm, blood, and parasites, it spreads here and there; licking the palate and the corners of the mouth, it is known as *parilehī*. (22) [The Diagnosis of Diseases of the Nose]
Now, the etiology of diseases of the nose:
when the nose becomes constricted, dries up, becomes excessively moist, or emits a foul odor,
and the person no longer perceives smells or tastes, one should determine that the individual is afflicted by apīnasa (chronic rhinitis).

One should describe that disorder arising from wind and phlegm as having symptoms identical to those of chronic catarrh (pratiśyāya). When the wind, having become concentrated at the root of the throat and palate due to the vitiated humors,
exits foul-smelling from both the mouth and the nostrils, they call that disease putrid rhinitis (pūtinasya).

One should diagnose as *nāsikāpāka* (inflammation of the nose) that disorder in which bile residing in the olfactory region produces ulcers and intense suppuration, or where there is excessive moistening and sloughing; or when,
due to the provoked humors (*doṣas*) or by various injuries to the forehead of a person, [these symptoms arise].
When pus mixed with blood flows from the nose, they call that disease *pūyarakta* (pus-blood).

When the wind (*vāyu*), vitiated and accompanied by phlegm (*kapha*), issues repeatedly and excessively with a loud sound through the nostrils due to the affliction of a vital point (*marman*) located in the nose, those who know the medical rules call that disease *kṣavathu* (sneezing).

From the application of pungent substances, from smelling pungent things, from gazing at the sun, or from the discharge of tears and other fluids when a fresh bone or vital point (*marman*) is opened, another type of rhinitis (*kṣavathu*) emerges;
furthermore, for one whose thick, burnt, and salty *kapha* is discharged through the nose...
Accumulated previously and heated by the sun at the crown of the head, they call that falling disease *bhraṃśathu*.
When the nose is intensely accompanied by a burning sensation, the wind issues forth here like smoke;
when a living being's nose seems as if ablaze, they call that disease *dīpta*.
When phlegm along with wind obstructs the passage of exhalation, one should call that condition *pratīnāha*.
When a thick, yellow, white, or thin discharge flows from the nose due to the humors (*doṣa*), one should call that *srāva*.
When the nasal channels are severely inflamed and dried up by wind located within the nose...

When a person breathes with difficulty both upwards and downwards, that condition is called *nāsāpariśoṣa* (drying of the nose). Heavier head, loss of appetite, nasal discharge, a weak voice, emaciation,
and frequent spitting are the symptoms of *āmapīnasa*.
Kapha, accompanied by the symptoms of undigested matter (āma), becomes thick and sinks into the channels;

the purification of voice and complexion is the characteristic of its being fully digested. [12] [Kapha is provoked] by suppression of natural urges, indigestion, dust, excessive talking, anger, seasonal irregularities, and heat in the head.

When the humors have become stagnant in the head due to staying awake at night, excessive sleep, cold water, exposure to frost, sexual intercourse, tears, and smoke, the aggravated Vāyu (wind) brings about catarrh (pratiśyāya).
Likewise, when Vāyu and the other doshas— either individually or combined— have accumulated in the head, as does the blood, they produce the same condition.
When provoked by various aggravating factors, they indeed become the cause of catarrh (pratiśyāya).
The onset of sneezing, a sense of fullness in the head, stiffness, body ache, horripilation,
and other diverse complications are known to precede catarrh in human beings.
The nose is stuffed and obstructed, with thin nasal discharge and trickling;
there is dryness of the throat, palate, and lips, as well as a piercing pain in the temples (16), excessive sneezing, and a bad taste in the mouth.
In the case of a vāta-type coryza, there may be impairment of the voice;
in the pitta-type, a warm, yellowish discharge flows from the nose. The patient becomes emaciated, excessively pale, feverish, and oppressed by heat.

That person suddenly seems to vomit smoke from his breath; due to the disorder of phlegm, cold, pale, and copious phlegm flows from the nose with a whitish appearance; the man’s eyes become white, and he feels as though his head is heavy. 19.
When catarrh (pratiśyāya), having repeatedly afflicted the throat, palate, lips, and head with itching, suddenly subsides—
whether it has reached maturity or remains immature— it is known as "arising from all [causes]. (20)

Furthermore, the nose becomes moistened and then dries up again; it may likewise contract or expand. Moreover, the breath becomes exceedingly foul-smelling, and the person no longer perceives odors. (21–22)
Thus one should recognize malignant coryza as being difficult to cure.
In the case of blood-born coryza, however, a discharge of blood occurs;
the person's eyes become copper-colored, and he is afflicted by a constriction of the chest. (23)
With his breath smelling foul, he no longer perceives even fragrances.
All types of catarrh in a man who fails to seek treatment eventually turn malignant, and at that time they indeed become incurable. (24–25)
Furthermore, white, glossy, and minute worms multiply therein;
the symptoms of this condition are identical to those of a disease caused by worms (krimi), such as deafness, blindness, loss of smell, and severe ocular disorders. (26)
When provoked, these nasal catarrhs (pīnasa) cause swelling, loss of digestive fire, and cough.

There are seven types of tumors (arbuda), four types of swellings (śotha), and four varieties of hemorrhage (raktapitta); those who know the tradition understand that these same [four] varieties also occur in the nose.
The Diagnosis of Eye Diseases:
Now, regarding the diagnosis of eye diseases, men should at all times exert effort in the protection of their eyes as long as they desire life.
This world is futile for men who are blind to the truth, even though wealth exists and days and nights are equal;

for they enter water when scorched by heat, look far off, and suffer from the distortions of dreams, as well as from being drenched in sweat, exposure to dust and smoke, the suppression of vomiting, and excessive emesis.

Likewise, from consuming food at night, from the suppression of the natural urges of feces, urine, and flatus, from excessive crying, anger, and grief, from injury to the head, and from the excessive drinking of wine;
as well as from the reversal of the seasons, from affliction by distress, and from excessive sexual indulgence.
Due to the suppression of tears and from close scrutiny, the humors (doṣas) produce abnormalities in the eyes.
Abhiṣyanda is fourfold—arising from vāta, pitta, kapha, and rakta; it is generally a terrible condition that serves as the source of all eye diseases.
When the eyes are afflicted by Vāta, there occurs pricking pain, stiffness, horripilation, a sensation of friction, roughness, headache, dryness,
and cold lacrimation. When afflicted by Pitta,
there is burning, suppuration, a longing for cold things, a sensation of smoking, and an excess of tears.
When the eyes are afflicted by *pitta*, they become hot to the touch, yellowish in color, and yellow-eyed (6).
When the eyes are afflicted by *kapha*, there is a craving for heat, heaviness, swelling, itching, discharge, excessive coldness, and frequent slimy secretions (7).
Reddish discoloration of the ears, redness of the eyes, and veins that are excessively red all around—
these, as well as whatever symptoms belong to pitta, occur when the eyes are affected by blood.
These aforementioned abhiṣyandas, when aggravated, afflict men who fail to take treatment.
There may be as many types of Adhimantha as there are [causes], characterized by intense pain in the eyes;
one should recognize Adhimantha by its specific symptoms, such as the eye feeling as if it were being excessively pulled out or churned, and likewise [pain] below the head. 9–10.

The *adhimanthu* caused by phlegm destroys vision within seven nights; that born of blood, within five nights; and that caused by wind, within six nights. However, the one caused by bile destroys it immediately through improper conduct. An eye with aggravated pain, accompanied by redness and swelling, [is incurable].

They know that an eye affected by *āma* (undigested humors) is characterized by rubbing, pricking pain, aching, lacrimation, and swelling. One should recognize that the *doṣa* has reached full suppuration (*saṃpakva*) when there is mild pain, itching, subsiding of the inflammation and lacrimation, and a healthy coloration of the eyes.
That which is accompanied by itching, exudation, and tearing, resembling a ripe udumbara fruit, and characterized by inflammation and suppuration, is netrapāka born of swelling (śothaja).
In the case of netrapāka not born of swelling (aśothaja), the symptoms are present but devoid of swelling. 14.
When the wind-natured Adhimantha, due to neglect,
forcibly afflicts the eyes with intense pains, this incurable disease is indeed known as Hatādhimantha. Furthermore, the wind repeatedly moves about in the eyebrows and the eyes.

When there are various intense pains, that should be known as *vātaparyaya*. When the eyelid is contracted, harsh and dry, when it burns and vision is blurred, and when the eye is extremely painful upon opening—such an eye is afflicted by *śuṣkākṣipāka* (dry ophthalmia). 16–17.
When the *vāyu* located in the hollow of the ear, the head, the jaw, the neck, or elsewhere causes pain in the eyebrows and the eyes, they call that condition *anyatovāta*.
The entire eye becomes dark-brown with red margins and undergoes suppuration.
Accompanied by constant burning, swelling, and discharge, and aggravated by sour substances due to their acidity;
or whether it is painless or painful, when the vessels of the eye become copper-colored and repeatedly lose their color, such a disease is designated as *sirotpāta*. 19–20.
If the sirōtpāta is neglected due to delusion, the disease known as sirāpraharṣa arises;
it discharges a deep red blood profusely, and likewise, the patient is unable to see clearly. Indeed, objects appear as if submerged in blackness, as if pierced by a needle.
That which discharges an excessively warm secretion is called *savraṇa-śukla* (ulcerated leucoderma) by physicians.
That which is located near the eye, which is not deep-seated, does not discharge, is painless, and is not double or white—that too may sometimes attain success [through treatment]. 22–23.

They say that a swelling which is characterized by discharge, located in the dark parts of the body, accompanied by burning, resembling a conch shell, the moon, or a jasmine flower, appearing like a thin cloud in the sky, and being without ulcers, is most easily curable.
They further state that one which is deep-seated, extensive, white, and long-standing is difficult to treat.

That which has a severed middle, or is covered with flesh, or is mobile, or has fine vessels that are invisible, or is located between two layers of skin, or is red at its edges, or has been present for a long time— this too must be rejected. (25) Furthermore, that eye in which there is a fall of hot tears, pustules, and a white portion resembling a mung bean [must be rejected].

Some declare that even this is incurable, as is any other [eye disease] which resembles the wing of a partridge (tittiri). When a white [film] spreads from all sides over the eye that has a black circle,
they say that this eye disease, known as akṣipākātyaya, involving the entire [organ], must be abandoned as incurable.
Resembling the dung of a goat, painful, reddish, with blood that is red and slimy,
and forming a black accumulation when scraped away— one should determine that to be *ajakājāta*.
(28) This occurs when the humors (*doṣas*) are situated in the first layer (*paṭala*) of the vision.
Then, at times, one sees forms that are unmanifest;
when the second layer [of the eye] is affected, vision becomes greatly disturbed, and one sees flies, gnats, and even cobwebs. (29–30)
He perceives mandalas, banners, rays of light, earrings, various flickering objects, rain, clouds, and darkness as being close at hand, even though they are situated at a distance.
31. He considers forms that are far away to be nearby.
Due to the confusion of the visual field, things nearby and those far away appear as if at a distance;
even one who exerts extreme effort does not see the eye-lash, and when [the disorder] has reached the third layer (paṭala), one sees what is above but not what is below. (32–33)
Even great forms appear as if covered by veils;
one sees them as if mutilated, lacking ears, nose, and eyes.
Furthermore, the vision becomes attached according to the specific defect when that defect is predominant. (34)

When the defect is situated below, one sees what is nearby; when it is situated above, one sees what is far away. Likewise, when the defect is situated at the side, one does not see what is at the side. When the defect is situated all around, one sees things as if they were crowded together.
When the defect is situated in the center of the vision, one sees what is large as small;
when it is divided into two, one sees things as double; and when it is unstable, one sees them as manifold. When the defect rests upon the side of the vision, one perceives a single object as double.

That defect known as *timira*, having reached the fourth layer (*paṭala*), obstructs vision on all sides; beyond this is *liṅganāśa*. Even in this great disease, when it has become darkened but is not yet fully advanced, [there is a chance for recovery]. 38–39.
When one sees the moon and the sun along with the stars, as well as lightning in the sky and stainless, radiant lights—
that indeed is the destruction of the visual faculty (*liṅganāśa*), known by the names *nīlikā* and *kāca*.
Due to wind (vāta), moreover, a person sees forms as if they were spinning;
they appear turbid, reddish, and as if distorted.
Due to bile (pitta), one perceives the sun, fireflies, Indra’s bow (the rainbow), and lightning. 41–42.
One who sees everything as blue and like a dancing peacock sees through phlegm; one would see forms that are glossy and white,
extremely subtle, and as if there were a cloudless deluge of clouds.
A person would perceive various kinds of darkness as if drenched in water, appearing reddened by blood; likewise,
that person would see even white things as black and yellow.
Due to a derangement of the humors (*sannipāta*), one sees all things as variegated and as if disordered;
they appear manifold and even doubled on every side, and frequently with missing or extra limbs, as do the celestial bodies. 45–46.

When the *pitta* is exhausted and then intensified by the fiery heat of *pitta*, it causes the directions to appear yellow; one perceives fireflies and even the sun as if they were scattered fireflies, or trees as if they were ablaze with light. (47)
Hereafter, I shall describe the sixfold destruction of the *liṅga* caused by passion (*rāga*).

Passion born of wind (*māruta*) is reddish and inflamed; that from bile (*pitta*) is withered and likewise blue; that from phlegm (*kapha*) is white; that born of blood (*śoṇita*) is bloody-red; and that arising from all the humors combined is variegated.

When the disease is subsiding, one may see a reddish circle in the vision with a thick, glass-like red luster; however, when the disease is fading away, the circle becomes bluish. Due to the depletion of the humors (*doṣa*), vision may sometimes occur there spontaneously.
From wind (vāta), the disc is reddish, flickering, and rough;
from bile (pitta), the disc is bluish-black, resembling the luster of bell-metal, or yellow;
from phlegm (śleṣman), it is abundant, yellow, and as white as a conch shell, a kunda flower, or the moon.
Situated upon the trembling petals of the eyes, it is like a white drop of water;
and when the eyes are being scorched, that circle spreads forth—a circle consisting of blood, with the luster of coral and lotus petals. (53)
There may be various types of affection for vision (dṛṣṭirāga) when the destruction of the visual axis (liṅganāśa) is caused by the three doṣas;
indeed, the specific symptoms of each respective doṣa appear in all of them.
There are six types of liṅganāśa, and these six diseases have the visual axis as their substratum; thus, exactly six [types] are to be described.

When the *pitta* is constantly vitiated, the vision of a man becomes yellow; he sees all forms as yellow, for that man indeed has a vision impaired by *pitta*. When the disorder reaches the third layer (*paṭala*), he does not see by day but sees at night.

And at night, a person whose vision is assisted by coldness may see those [colors] even due to the diminished state of bile (pitta); likewise, one whose vision is corrupted by phlegm (śleṣman) perceives those very same things as white. When the disorder resides in the three inner layers [of the eye], it forcibly brings about night-blindness (naktāndhya).
By day, his vision being favored by the sun, he perceives forms due to the deficiency of phlegm (kapha). 58.
That man whose vision is afflicted by grief, fever, fatigue, or pains in the head, and who consequently sees all things as smoky, is designated as one with "smoky-vision" (dhūmadarśin). 59.
He who is dull-witted and slow, and by whom short forms are seen with difficulty during the day,
and whose vision flashes like that of a mongoose when afflicted by the humors— that man sees variegated forms during the day; this indeed is the disorder known as *nakulāndhya*.
The vision becomes distorted, and when afflicted by wind, it undergoes contraction from within;
this deep-seated pain is called Gambhīrikā by those who know the disease.
Furthermore, two external types are prescribed here: that caused by a specific cause and that which is without a specific cause.
In that case, it should be known as caused by a specific sign (nimitta) when there is a headache; it is characterized by excessive lacrimation (abhiṣyanda).

Furthermore, the vision of a person may be destroyed even by the sight of gods, sages, gandharvas, great serpents (mahoragas), or the sun; this is called liṅganāśa without a discernible cause (animittasaṃjña).

Therein, the eye appears as if very clear, and the vision is stainless and of the color of lapis lazuli (vaiḍūrya). (64) A thin, spread-out film (arma) that is dark-brown, reddish, or white on the sclera, and pale-white and soft, is known as śuklārma; it grows slowly upon the white part. (65)

That which has the luster of a lotus and is soft is *raktārma*; that fleshy growth which accumulates on the white part (*śuklabhāga*) and is broad and soft is *adhimāṃsārma*; that which is thick, liver-like, firm, spreading, and rich in flesh is *piśitārma*; and the fifth is *snāyvarma*, which is dry. 66.
Those spots which are dark-brown and resemble flesh,
or those that have the luster of a pearl-oyster shell and are fixedly white, are designated as *śukti*; likewise,
there is one type of spot which resembles the blood of a rabbit.
That which is located in the *śukla* (the white part of the eye) they call *arjuna*.
Know that when the *śleṣman* (phlegm) and *vāyu* (wind) are provoked, a raised growth like dough appears on the *śukla*, resembling a mirror smeared with impurities; this is called *piṣṭaka*. 67–68.

A large, web-like growth with a hard surface and reddish hue is known here as *jāla* (the web); white pustules located on the white parts of the eye, covered by vessels and arising near the black part, one should call *sirājā* (vein-born).

That which has the luster of bell-metal, is not soft, and resembles water droplets in the white of the eye should be known as *balāsaka*. A suppurated swelling arising at a joint that is accompanied by piercing pain and discharges putrid pus is called *pūyālasa*.
A small, non-suppurating, itchy, and painless swelling at the junction of the eyelids is called *upanāha*.
(70) When the humors reach the joints via the path of the lacrimal canal, they produce discharges (*srāva*) characterized by their own specific symptoms;
some call this discharge *netranāḍī*, and I shall describe its fourfold signs. (71)
That disease which exudes pus from a joint due to suppuration is known as *pūyāsrāva* (pus-discharge), and it arises from all [three] doshas.

That disorder which exudes white, thick, and slimy fluid is considered *śleṣmāsrāva* (phlegm-discharge). The disorder arising from blood is *raktaśrāva* (blood-discharge), wherein vitiated blood flows in abundance.
A discharge resembling turmeric, yellow, hot, and watery flows from the middle of the joint due to Pitta (73).

A thin, copper-colored swelling accompanied by burning and pain, occurring at a joint between the black and white parts of the eye, should be known as *parvaṇī* arising from blood; it is circular and its appearance is heralded by the same symptoms previously described for *alajī* (74).

Worms born at the junction of the eyelid and the eyelashes cause itching; appearing in various forms, they move within the junction of the eyelid and the white of the eye, vitiating the interior of the eye.
That [condition] which has its opening inward, is copper-colored, and extends from the exterior of the eyelid—
A swelling with elevated pustules occurring on all parts of the eye, accompanied by thick itching, is [sthūlakaṇḍurā].

Pustules that are swollen at the edge of the eyelid, which burst and discharge fluid, resembling the seeds of the *kumbhīkā* plant, are *kumbhīkā*, born from the derangement of all three humors (*sannipāta*). 76–77.
Pustules that are exuding, itchy, heavy, resembling red mustard seeds, and painful are known as *pothakī*.
A pustule that is rough, large, and covered with small [pustules] is also [known as such]. (78)
The disease known as *śarkarā* (gravel) is located in the eyelid and vitiates the eyelid. 79.
Small, slightly painful pustules, resembling the seeds of a cucumber (*ervāru*), which are either smooth or rough and situated on the eyelid, are declared to be *vartmārśa* (eyelid polyp). 80.
Long, hard, rigid, harsh, and arising from within—

the disease well-known by the name of *śuṣkārśas* (dry hemorrhoid) is thus described. A copper-colored pustule accompanied by burning and pricking sensations, arising at the eyelid margin, [is another form].
That which is soft, slightly painful, and subtle should be known as *añjananāmikā*.
When the eyelid is covered all over with pustules that are similar in color to the skin and firm, one should know that to be *bahulavartman*.

The person whose eye is covered by a swelling of the eyelid that is itchy, slightly painful, and copper-colored, with soft and mild symptoms, is one for whom this Vartmabandhaka [condition] exists. (84) Mad-vartma is likewise even and characterized by slight pain and a copper hue.
When the eyelid suddenly becomes red, the experts know that as *kliṣṭavartman*.
Furthermore, when blood mixed with *pitta* causes inflammation,
and it subsequently reaches a state of moistness, it is called *vartmakardama*.
Those expert in the diseases of the eyelids call that condition *śyāvavartma*, wherein the eyelid is dark-brown both externally and internally, swollen, and painful. Furthermore,
when a person's eyelid is swollen on the outside but free from pain—
One should know that as *praklinna-vartma* when the eyelids are excessively moistened at their edges (verse 88).
When the eyelids, whether washed or unwashed, repeatedly become adhered together while remaining unripened, one should know that as *aklinna-vartma* (verse 89).
One who examines the eyes should recognize this as *vātaha-ta-vartma* (wind-destroyed eyelid), wherein the joints are loosened, the eyelid is motionless, and it does not close.
An irregular, painless growth situated within the eyelid that has become nodular [is also to be known].
One should call *arbuda* that which is reddish and occurs without delay.
When the wind enters the blinking vessels located at the joints and causes the eyelids to tremble,
the experts know that condition as *nimeṣa*.
That which is situated in the middle of the eyelid, red and soft like a sprout, is the blood-born *śoṇitārśas*; once cut, it grows back again and again.
A painless, non-suppurating, hard, and thick glandular swelling arising from the eyelid [is called a *granthi*].

That disease is proclaimed by its symptoms as *lagaṇa*. When the three *doṣas* produce an external swelling and perforations on the eyelids that exude water from within like lotus stalks, that is *visavartma*. 94–95.

When the humors, such as wind (vāta) and others, cause the contraction of the eyelids, one is then unable to see; that condition is known as *kuñcana*. Indeed, when the eyelashes are displaced by the wind, they enter into the eye.
The eyes rub repeatedly and cause intense irritation;
even from the root-follicles, lashes fall upon both the dark and white portions.
This disease, known as *pakṣmakopa*, should be recognized as extremely severe. 97–98.

Pitta located in the eyelid and the follicles of the lashes causes the falling out of the lashes and produces itching and burning; one should designate that condition as Pakṣmaśāta (falling of the lashes).
There are nine types [of diseases] based on the joints, while twenty-one arise from the eyelids.
There are eleven [diseases] arising from the bright half, four born from the dark half,
seventeen residing in all [parts], and twelve indeed arising from vision;
two external diseases are declared to be most terrible.
The Diagnosis of Head Diseases:
Now follows the diagnosis of head diseases;
indeed, head diseases arise from the three—vāta, pitta, and kapha.
Due to the combination of humors (sannipāta), blood disorders, depletion, or parasites,
as well as by sūryāvarta, ānanta-vāta, ardha-avabhedaka, and śaṅkhaka,
there arise intense headaches without apparent cause, which become excessive during the night.

1. Where there is relief from binding and fomentation, that headache is caused by Vāta. 2. That headache which is as hot as if covered with glowing coals, where the head and the eyes burn, and which finds relief at night through cold applications, arises from the provocation of Pitta.
That person whose head is smeared with phlegm (kapha), feels heavy and stiff, and is cold,
and whose eye-sockets and face are swollen— that is headache caused by the provocation of phlegm.
When headache arises from the involvement of all three [humors], all the symptoms manifest together.
That which is characterized by blood has symptoms identical to those of pitta, and there is an inability to bear touch;
furthermore, due to the depletion here of the blood, muscle-fat, phlegm, and wind located in the head,
a headache arising from wasting occurs, which is painful, severe, and exceedingly intense.
It increases through fomentation, emesis, fumigation, nasal medication, and bloodletting.
When one's head is excessively pricked, as if being devoured, and seems to throb within,
and water mixed with pus flows from the nose, that is the terrible Śirobhitāpa caused by worms.
That most painful disorder which, upon the rising of the sun, slowly and steadily approaches the eyes and eyebrows,
becomes intense and increases along with the sun's rays, and subsides entirely when the sun sets—
they call that "Sūryāpavarta."
When the three vitiated *doṣas* afflict the *manyā* (the neck muscles) and the *ghāṭās*, they produce extremely intense pain,
especially in the eyes, eyebrows, and the region of the temples; moreover,
they cause trembling on the side of the cheek, lockjaw, and diseases of the eyes.
They describe that disorder of the head arising from the three *doṣas* as *anantavāta*.
Vata, aggravated by the consumption of dry food, overeating, exposure to the morning wind, suppression of natural urges, sexual intercourse, and physical exertion, becomes provoked. (10–11)
When the powerful [Vāyu], either alone or accompanied by Kapha, seizes the head from below,
it causes intense pain in the neck, eyebrows, temples, ears, eyes, and half the forehead—
pain resembling the stroke of a weapon or a fire-drill; this is Adhāvabhedaka.
Or else, being excessively advanced, it may destroy the eyes or the ears.
When blood, bile, and wind are vitiated and concentrated in the region of the temples, they indeed produce a severe, painful swelling characterized by burning and redness. 13–14.

That [disease] called Śaṅkhaka, possessing the force of poison, quickly obstructs the head and likewise the throat; it destroys life after three nights. Beyond that, one may live for three days; having renounced medical treatment, one should perform [the prescribed rites]. 15.
Now,
the etiology of menorrhagia:
it arises from incompatible foods, wine, overeating, indigestion, miscarriage, and excessive sexual intercourse.
Due to excessive strain from vehicles, travel, or grief, and from the impact of heavy loads or sleeping during the day,

physicians describe this disorder as *pradara* (menorrhagia), which is of four types arising from the combination of *kapha*, *pitta*, *vāta*, or all three; it may also manifest as *asṛgdara* (metrorrhagia), accompanied by aching in the limbs and pain throughout.
Upon its excessive passage, there occurs weakness, vertigo, fainting, intoxication, thirst,

burning sensations, delirium, pallor, drowsiness, and diseases born of Vāta. Due to Kapha, however, the stool is undigested (āma), resembling slimy mucus, pale, and like the water used for washing rice-grains.
3. Hot, accompanied by the pain of *pitta*, yellowish, bluish, blackish, or red, with great force—this [urine] arises from *pitta*. 4.
Dry, reddish, frothy, scanty, and occurring in small amounts—this arises from *vāta* and the pain of *vāta*.
Resembling meat-washings, mixed with honey, the color of yellow orpiment (*haritāla*), or resembling marrow—this "corpse-like" (*kuṇapa*) urine arises from all three *doṣas*.
Experts declare that condition to be incurable; therefore, the physician should not undertake its treatment.
One should designate as incurable a case where the discharge flows incessantly, accompanied by thirst, burning sensations, and fever, and where the blood is depleted and the patient is weak. (5)

One should declare the menstrual flow (*ārtava*) pure when it is free from sliminess, burning, or pain for a month, does not persist for more than five nights, and is neither excessive nor too scanty;
that which resembles the blood of a rabbit or the juice of lac.
They praise that menstrual blood which does not become discolored in water;
this is the cause of the disorders of the female reproductive tract.
Now follows the diagnosis of the disorders of the female reproductive tract.
Twenty disorders of the womb have been specified in the compendium of diseases;
they arise in women from improper conduct, from vitiated menstrual flow, from defects of the seed, and from destiny. Listen now to them individually.
She discharges frothy menses with upward movement (udāvarta) and with great difficulty;
one should recognize her as *vandhyā* (barren) if she has lost her menses, and as *viplutā* if she suffers from constant pain.
In the case of *pariplutā*, there is intense pain during sexual intercourse.

In all four of these [disorders], there occur pains caused by Vāyu (wind), characterized by being windy, rough, stiff, and afflicted with piercing and aching sensations. That [condition] in which blood diminishes accompanied by burning is called Lohitakṣaya (blood-depletion).
The *savāta* woman emits the seed mixed with blood;

the *vāminī* vomits it; the *prasraṃsinī* discharges it when agitated; the *duṣprajāyinī* destroys every embryo that has been established; and the *putraghnī* [destroys the fetus] due to the loss of blood.
The excessively bilious (pittala) vagina is characterized by burning, suppuration, and fever;
furthermore, in all four of the first [types], there is an aggravation of the symptoms of pitta. The "excessively joyful" (atyānandā) woman does not reach satisfaction through sexual intercourse.
In the *karṇinī* type, a fleshy protuberance (*karṇikā*) arises at the vulva due to phlegm and blood. In the *acaraṇā* type, [the woman] previously exceeds the man in sexual intercourse;
in the *aticaraṇā* type, she does so excessively, and [consequently] their seed does not find its way [to conception]. 8–9.
The *śleṣmalā* (kapha-type) vagina is slimy, afflicted with itching, and extremely cold;
in all four of these [types], there is an increase of the symptoms of *śleṣman* (phlegm).
The *anārtavā* (menstruation-less), *astanī* (breastless), *ṣaṇḍī* (eunuch-like), and *kharasparśā* (rough-to-the-touch) types are characterized by lack of sexual desire during intercourse.
In a young woman who has conceived a fetus of excessive size, the vulva becomes fissured;
it remains wide open yet is extremely constricted at the opening like the point of a needle,
resulting in the emergence of all types of genitalia and arising from the provocation of all the bodily humors.

In all four of these initial types, there is an elevation of all the genitalia; five types of *yoni* (vaginal disorders) here are incurable, arising from all three *doṣas*. This concludes the diagnosis of the root of *yoni* disorders.
Now, regarding the etiology of *yonikanda*:
when the *vāta* and other [doshas] are provoked by daytime sleep, excessive anger, physical exertion, excessive sexual intercourse, and injury from nails, teeth, and so forth; (1)
When it is produced in the womb resembling pus and blood and shaped like a *nikuca* fruit, it is called *kanda*; that which is born from the womb is known as *yonija*.
One should diagnose that which is dry, discolored, or cracked as being caused by *vāta*.

One should know that which is accompanied by burning, redness, and fever to be of the nature of pitta (3). That which resembles a blue flower and is characterized by itching is of the nature of kapha;
that which is endowed with all the symptoms is known as being of the nature of sannipāta (4).
Now,
regarding the condition of a fetus in distress:
[the fetus] is fully endowed with all its limbs and possessed of mind, intellect, and the other faculties.
One who is bewildered by a defective downward breath (*apāna*) is called a "confused fetus" (*mūḍhagarbha*).
Due to fear, trauma, or the consumption of sharp and hot drinks and foods, the fetus falls from its place; there occurs the appearance of blood accompanied by pain.

From the fourth month onwards, there occurs a discharge of the embryo; thereafter, from the fifth or sixth month, there is a miscarriage of the one whose body has become firm. Due to trauma, the consumption of unwholesome food, pressure, and so forth, the embryo falls instantly like a ripe fruit from a tree.

Indeed, the wind (vāyu), when deranged, produces a malpositioned fetus (mūḍhagarbha) and causes colic in the vagina, the abdomen, and other regions, as well as retention of urine. Then, that fetus, having exceeded its [normal] proportions, enters the birth canal in various ways due to the vitiated wind:
one blocks the opening with its head, another with its abdomen, and some have their bodies twisted or bent by the displacement of the limbs.

One [goes] with one [leg], another with both arms, one goes sideways, another with face downward, and yet another with a sidelong turning gait; thus this eightfold gait is described, and another fourfold [gait]:
*saṃkīlaka*, *pratikhura*, *parigha*, and *bīja*; among these, [the practitioner enters] the womb with upraised arms and feet, and with the head.

He who is attached like a stake is a "stake" (kīla); for he goes with visible hooves, each hoof being joined by a nail (kāyu), and having two arms and a head, he is called "seed-like" (bījaka) when situated in the womb, resembling a club (parigha).
But she whose head is cast down, whose limbs are cold, and who is shameless—[is another].
When blue veins protrude, it kills the fetus, and the fetus likewise kills her.
When the fetus is dead, there will be an absence of fetal movement, loss of the labor pains (āvīnā), a dark-yellowish pallor, fetid breath, and swelling.

The embryo perishes in the womb when it is afflicted by mental and adventitious distresses of the mother, or when it is oppressed by diseases; likewise, there is obstruction due to the constriction of the birth canal, attachment, and even the presence of makkalla (fetal excrement) within the womb. 9.
The woman may die from a dead fetus, as well as from the complications (upadrava) already described.
Furthermore, the aggravated Vāyu, obstructing the flowing blood, causes pain in the heart, head, and bladder of the woman who has recently given birth; this condition is known as Makkalla.
Now, regarding the etiology of puerperal diseases:
bodily aching,
fever, tremors, thirst, and heaviness of the limbs [are the symptoms].

Swelling, colic, and diarrhea are the symptoms of puerperal diseases (sūtikā-roga). Those terrible diseases which arise in a woman after childbirth due to improper care, distress, or the consumption of irregular and undigested food [are known as such]. 1–2.
Fever, diarrhea, swelling, colic, abdominal distension,

wasting, drowsiness, loss of appetite, excessive salivation, and other such diseases arising from the disorders of phlegm and wind are indeed difficult to cure when the patient's flesh, strength, and digestive fire are diminished.
All those diseases are designated by the name *sūtikā* (puerperal disorders), as well as their complications. Now begins the diagnosis of breast diseases (*stanaroga*).
Whether the breasts contain milk or are without milk, when the *doṣas* of a woman become aggravated upon reaching them, they corrupt the flesh and blood, leading to breast diseases;
for among those five types [of breast disease], all except the one born of blood (*raktaja*) are [caused by the *doṣas*].
The symptoms are identical to those of external poisoning. Now follows the diagnosis of corrupted breast milk (*stanyaduṣṭi*). The diagnosis of corrupted breast milk.
Even when the limbs are dissected, semen is not seen;
nevertheless, because it is supported by the entire body, it is described as having the body as its characteristic.
And that very [semen] arises from seeing a young woman, or even from remembering her.
It proceeds from hearing sounds, from touch, and from exhilaration;
in that state of exhilaration, the mind becomes perfectly serene, and that exhilaration is said to be the cause.
Likewise, the breast milk of women has its origin in the essence of food.
That very affection, through contact with offspring, as well as through seeing, remembering,
and even grasping the body, flows forth continuously like semen; therein, it is said that the cause for this outflow is uninterrupted attachment.

The mother’s milk, vitiated by various heavy foods and corrupted by the humors (doṣas), leads to manifold diseases in the child. When the milk is astringent, diluted with water, and corrupted by the wind (vāta), [it causes similar ailments].
That which is pungent, sour, and salty, and marked with yellow streaks, is designated as Pitta-type.
That which is thick, sinks in water, and is slimy is Kapha-corrupted.
One should know that which possesses two symptoms is born from two humors (Dvandvaja), and that which possesses all symptoms is born from all three humors (Tridoṣaja).
When not spoiled, water poured into it becomes uniform, pale, sweet, and uncolored; that which is clear is praised. (8) This concludes the diagnosis of diseases of children.
Now, the diagnosis of diseases of children:
A child drinking breast milk vitiated by *vāta* becomes afflicted with wind-born ailments;
he has a weak voice, emaciated limbs, and his feces, urine, and flatus become obstructed. (1)
A child who has been sweated and whose impurities have been expelled, yet suffers from jaundice,
bilious diseases, thirst, and heat throughout the entire body, drinks milk that is vitiated by *pitta*.
One who drinks milk vitiated by *kapha* suffers from excessive salivation and diseases of phlegm.
One afflicted by *śiśu* [fever] is drowsy, dull, has swollen face and eyes, and vomits.
In *dvandvaja* [fever], the symptoms are those of two combined types; in *sarvaja* [fever], all symptoms are present.
One should discern whether the child's pain is intense or mild from its crying.
One should know that pain exists in whatever part of the body he touches intensely, or in that place where he is unable to bear the touch; likewise,
one should know there is pain in the head from the closing of the eyes,
and in the abdominal cavity (koṣṭha) from constipation, flatulence, pain in the breasts, and gurgling in the intestines.

One should also observe the distension of the abdomen, the bending of the back, and the protrusion of the belly; furthermore, due to the retention of feces and urine, fear, and looking toward the cardinal directions, one should diligently examine the channels, the limbs, and the joints again and again.
Kukūṇaka arises in the eyelids of infants due to defects in the breast milk;
because of it, that eye becomes itchy and discharges repeatedly, and the infant rubs the forehead, the orbital region, the nose, and the lower lip. (8)
A child in the womb of a pregnant mother is generally unable to see the light of the sun, nor is he capable of opening his eyes; even while drinking breast milk,
he is afflicted by cough, loss of digestive fire, vomiting, drowsiness, emaciation, loss of appetite, and vertigo.

When there is enlargement of the uvula, they call that disease *pārigarbhika* (congenital) or *paribhava*; in such a case, one should employ treatments that stimulate the digestive fire (*agni-dīpana*).
When phlegm (*kapha*) is provoked in the flesh of the palate, it produces *tālukaṇṭaka* (palatal thorn).
By that, a depression occurs at the top of the palate;
there is falling of the palate, aversion to the breast, difficult drinking, vomiting of feces, thirst, pain in the eyes, throat, and mouth, stiffness of the neck, and nausea. 12–13.
Visarpa (erysipelas) occurring in an infant, arising from the head of the bladder, known as Padmavarṇa or Mahāpadma, originates from the three doṣas;
it spreads from the temples to the heart, or from the heart it may proceed to the rectum. (14)
When minor diseases such as *tvak*, *jālagardabha*, and *ahipūtanā* are mentioned [in the context of children],
all the ailments beginning with fever that were previously described for adults should always be understood by the skilled [physicians] to be likewise present in the bodies of children. 15–16.
In one moment the infant is agitated; in another moment he trembles and weeps;
he tears at his nurse with his nails and teeth, or even at himself. He gazes upward, gnaws at his teeth, coos, and yawns.
He clenches his teeth against his lips, repeatedly spitting foam;
he is excessively emaciated, keeps awake at night, has swollen eyes, and his stool and voice are altered; he smells of flesh and blood, and does not eat as he did before.
The general characteristics of those possessed by grahas have been fully described:
there is discharge from one eye, twitching and trembling of the limbs, looking upward with the gaze, having a distorted face, and smelling of blood. 20.
Terrified, he gnashes his teeth and takes no pleasure at all in the breast-milk. Those seized by Skanda-graha weep only slightly;
one whose consciousness is lost vomits froth, while one who has regained consciousness cries out excessively.
The smell of pus and blood is the characteristic of Skanda and Apasmāra (22).
With drooping limbs, terrified by fear, smelling of birds,
he is tormented on all sides by wounds with discharging matter.
A child whose body is covered with eruptions accompanied by constant burning and suppuration should be known as afflicted by Śakunī (23).
One whose limbs are strewn with boils, who exudes a foul, mud-like odor and blood, and who suffers from diarrhea,
fever, and burning sensations, exhibits the symptoms of the Revatī graha (24).
Diarrhea, fever, thirst, sidelong glances,
crying, loss of sleep, and agitation— such a child is seized by Pūtanā.
(25) Vomiting, cough, fever, thirst, a smell of fat, and excessive crying [indicate seizure by Śītapūtanā].
Aversion to breast milk and diarrhea occur due to Andhapūtanā (26).
The infant trembles, coughs, becomes emaciated, suffers from eye disease, foul odor, vomiting, and diarrhea due to Śītapūtanā (27).
One whose complexion and face are bright, who is covered with visible veins, who smells of urine, who eats excessively, and who suffers from stomatitis (mukhamaṇḍikā) [is afflicted by this disease].
Vomiting, thirst, dryness of the throat and mouth, fainting, and foul odor [are its symptoms]. 28.1–2.
If one sees [the child] looking upward and gnashing its teeth, one should declare it to be the possession by the Naigameṣa Graha.
If the eyes are fixed, the child has a hatred for the breast, and faints repeatedly and incessantly,
that Graha, possessing all the full symptoms, kills the child before long.
The Diagnosis of Poisonous Diseases:
Now follows the diagnosis of poisonous diseases;
poison is said to be of two kinds: stationary (sthāvara) and mobile (jaṅgama).
The first [type of poison] consists of roots and the like, while the second arises from snakes and other such sources.
This mobile poison causes sleep, lethargy, exhaustion, burning sensations, indigestion, horripilation,
swelling, and diarrhea.
It causes chronic fever, hiccups, sensitivity of the teeth, throat obstruction, excessive vomiting of foam, loss of appetite, labored breathing, and fainting;
it perceives the inner intentions of men through distortions of speech, gestures, and facial expressions.
A wise person should recognize the giver of poison by these signs:
when questioned, he does not give an answer; though desiring to speak, he falls into confusion;
and he speaks much that is meaningless and incoherent, like a fool.
He laughs suddenly, snaps his fingers, scratches the ground,
and experiences trembling; he looks about in fear at one another,
his face becomes pale and darkened, and he even cuts himself slightly with his nails.
A dejected person may clutch at his seat or pull at his hair with his hand; one who has ingested poison becomes senseless and behaves in a contrary manner.
Furthermore, there is convulsing from root-poisons, as well as delirium and even fainting.
Yawning, trembling, labored breathing, and delusion result from leaf-poison;
swelling of the scrotum from fruit-poisons, as well as burning sensations and aversion to food;
and vomiting, flatulence, and dyspnea result from flower-poisons. (9)
Indeed, by the use of poisons derived from tree bark,
sap, or exudations, there occur foul breath, roughness of the skin, headache, and discharge of phlegm; with milk-based poisons, there is the appearance of froth, diarrhea, and heaviness of the limbs.
Pain in the heart, poisoning of the bodily tissues (dhātus), fainting, and a burning sensation in the palate—
these should generally be diagnosed as poisons that cause death in a short time. In a person whose fresh wound suppurates and from which blood flows and repeatedly suppurates, [death is imminent].
One should determine that a man whose flesh from a wound has turned black, become moist, and is excessively putrid, and even sloughs away;
and who suffers from thirst, fainting, fever, and burning sensations—that man has been struck by poisoned [weapons].
These very same symptoms would also occur if poison were administered to one's wound by enemies through negligence.
One who passes yellowish feces resembling the smoke of a house-fire,
and also vomits froth, should be declared as having drunk poison.
Serpents are of the nature of wind, bile, and phlegm, and are classified as *bhogin*, *maṇḍalin*, and *rājila*.
In their respective order, those occurring between the two [groups] are described as having dual characteristics:
a bite caused by a *bhogin* is black and produces all types of wind disorders (*vāta-vikāra*);
a bite from one born in a circle (*maṇḍalin*) is yellow, characterized by swelling, and possesses the disorders of bile (*pitta*). (16–17)

A bite originating from a *rājila* [snake] results in a stable swelling that is slimy, pale, and unctuous; it produces very thick blood and causes all disorders of *kapha*. [Bites occurring] at the *aśvattha* tree, temples, cremation grounds, anthills, during the twilights, or at crossroads— 18.
[The bite of a *rājila* snake] results in a stable swelling that is slimy, pale, and unctuous; it produces very thick blood and causes all disorders of *kapha*.
[Bites occurring] at the *aśvattha* tree, temples, cremation grounds, anthills, during the twilights, or at crossroads—
Those bitten in the southern quarter (Yāmya) should be avoided, as well as those bitten in the constellations (ṛkṣa) or in the vital veins and joints (sirā-marma).

The venom of hooded snakes (darvīkara) acts swiftly; moreover, all poisons are doubled in potency during the heat, and in those afflicted by indigestion, bile, or exposure to the sun, as well as in children, the elderly, and the hungry.
One should avoid treating a person who is emaciated, suffering from ulcers, delirious, afflicted with leprosy, dehydrated, weak, or pregnant;
likewise one who has no bleeding from a surgical wound, whose skin does not break out in streaks or eruptions,
whose body hair does not stand on end when touched by cold water, or one who is overwhelmed by poison.

One whose face is distorted, whose hair falls out, whose nose collapses, and who suffers a break in the voice; one whose bite site is blackish-red and swollen, and whose jaws become rigid—such a patient should be abandoned. One from whose mouth a thick wick-like substance emerges, and from whom blood flows both upward and downward, [should also be abandoned].

The physician should also avoid one whose four fangs have fallen out; likewise, he should not perform medical treatment for a man who is excessively insane, severely afflicted, has a weak voice, or is discolored (24),
or who is known to have fatal signs (ariṣṭa) and lacks natural vitality.
Poison that has become old, or has been neutralized by anti-poisonous herbs, or dried up by forest fires, wind, or heat,

or which is naturally devoid of its potency, attains the state of *dūṣīviṣa* (latent poison); because of its diminished power, it does not cause immediate death, but being associated with *kapha*, it persists for many years.

Afflicted by that [vitiated wind], with the color of excrement, accompanied by foul odor and a bad taste in the mouth, thirsty, suffering from fainting, vertigo, stammering speech, vomiting, and convulsive movements, he may experience restlessness.
When located in the stomach (āmāśaya), it causes diseases of kapha and vāta; when located in the large intestine (pakvāśaya), it causes diseases of vāta and pitta.
His hair and limbs become disheveled, like a bird whose wings have been plucked;
or else, when situated in the fluids and other tissues, it produces the aforementioned disorders arising from the bodily constituents (dhātus).
It quickly falls into a state of agitation during cold winds and foul weather; first, hear its symptoms. 28–29.

It causes drowsiness, heaviness, yawning, or a sense of looseness and exhilaration, as well as body aches; thereafter, it produces indigestion from overeating, loss of appetite, and the appearance of circular patches (maṇḍala) and urticaria (koṭha),
along with wasting of the flesh, swelling of the feet and hands, fainting, vomiting, and diarrhea.

Dūṣīviṣa causes dyspnea, thirst, fever, and even the enlargement of the abdomen (jaṭhara). Another [type] produces insanity (unmāda), another causes constipation (ānāha), and another destroys semen (śukra). Yet another causes stammering (gādgadya), leprosy (kuṣṭha), and various other disorders of many kinds.

Because it repeatedly vitiates the bodily constituents (dhātus) by being corrupted through place, time, food, and frequent daytime sleep, it is known as *dūṣīviṣa* (corrosive poison). It is curable for one who possesses self-control, and it becomes manageable (yāpya) when it has persisted for a year.
Dūṣīviṣa poison becomes incurable in one who is emaciated and who indulges in unwholesome things.
(34) For the sake of securing good fortune, women may provide sweat, menstrual blood, impurities from various parts of the body, or even poisons administered by enemies, mixed with food. (35)
By these [causes], one becomes pale, emaciated, and has weak digestion;
moreover, vomiting arises in him, along with the swelling of the vital points (marman), distension, and edema in the hands.
Abdominal enlargement (jaṭhara), disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī-doṣa), consumption (yakṣmā), abdominal tumors (gulma), wasting (kṣaya), and fever [also result].
One should observe the symptoms of this and other such diseases.
Because drops of perspiration from the Sage fell upon the grass that had been cut, they are called *lūtās*; by number, there are sixteen of them. (37–38)

When bitten by them, there occurs swelling at the site of the bite, discharge of blood, fever, burning sensation, diarrhea, and diseases born of the three doṣas; furthermore, various types of pustules and large circular patches appear. (39)
The swellings are large, soft, red, dusky, and unstable;
this is the general characteristic of the bite of all spiders.
However, that which is black or dusky in the center of the bite and covered with a web-like membrane [is specific].
One should identify a bite by spiders (*lūtā*) with *dūṣīviṣa* venom as being characterized by an upward-spreading, intense inflammation accompanied by moisture, swelling, and fever (verse 42).
There is swelling, and white, pale, red, or yellow pustules appear, along with fever.
Life-threatening conditions arise, such as labored breathing, hiccups, and stiffness of the head (43).
In one afflicted by the poison of a rat (*ākhu*), there occurs blood-letting from the bite site, pale spots, fever, loss of appetite, horripilation, and a burning sensation (44).

Fainting, swelling of the limbs, discoloration, discharge, loss of hearing, fever, heaviness of the head, and vomiting of saliva and blood are the symptoms of being bitten by an incurable *mūṣika* (mouse/rat);
furthermore, there may be blackness, a dark-brown hue, or even various other colors.
In the case of being bitten by a *kṛkalāsaka*, there occurs delusion and a discharge of feces (46).
The venom of a scorpion first burns like fire and quickly pierces upward; it moves through the site of the bite and subsequently remains there (47).
A person bitten [by this] is incurable; if the heart, nose, or tongue is afflicted, and the flesh falls off excessively, the man, tormented by pain, gives up his life.
There is also spreading inflammation, swelling, colic, fever, and vomiting.
The symptoms of a bite by a *kaṇabha* spider are that the bite site itself becomes suppurated;
when bitten by an *ucciṭiṅga*, the body hair stands on end, the penis becomes rigid, and there is intense pain, such that the person feels as if his limbs have been sprinkled with cold water. (49–50)
Bitten by poisonous frogs, the symptoms are swelling from a single fang, pain, yellowness, thirst, vomiting, and drowsiness (51). Poisonous fish, however, cause burning, swelling, and likewise pain.
Poisonous leeches cause itching, swelling, fever, and fainting (52).
A house-lizard causes a burning sensation, swelling, pricking pain, and sweating at the site of the bite;
the venom of a centipede produces sweating, pain, and a burning sensation (53).
An itchy eruption caused by mosquitoes is slightly swollen and mildly painful; a wound from an insect bite resembling that of an incurable insect is likewise incurable.
A wound from a mosquito is characterized by immediate exudation, a darkish discoloration, and is accompanied by burning sensations, fainting, and fever.
A boil resulting from a fly sting is called *sthagikā*, which is harmful;
furthermore, the poison from the claws or teeth of quadrupeds and bipeds causes swelling, suppuration, discharge, and even fever. (55–56)

When the wind, vitiated by phlegm and localized in the channels that carry consciousness, robs dogs, jackals, hyenas, bears, tigers, and other such animals of their consciousness, then they have their tails, fingers, jaws, and shoulders drooping and are excessively salivating. (57)
Invisible, deaf, and blind, he runs toward one another;
one among them, utterly deluded, runs about devouring [the others], while another is bitten by that mad, venomous fanged creature. 58–59.
Drowsiness arises at the site of the bite, and black blood flows excessively;
he is generally characterized by the symptoms of one pierced by a poisoned [arrow].
Furthermore, a man may exhibit the behavior or cry out like the creature by which he was bitten.

One who attempts many remedies but lacks the proper ritual action perishes. If one bitten by a fanged creature sees its form in water or in the reflection of a mirror, one should declare that the bite has occurred.
One who trembles repeatedly and unexpectedly upon seeing or even touching water should be known as *jalatrāsa*; that too is declared to be a defect.
One who suffers from *jalatrāsa*, whether bitten by a snake or not, does not succeed in any way whatsoever.
Whether asleep or awake, healthy or terrified, one does not attain success [in treatment].

A physician should recognize a person as being free from poison when their humors (doṣas) are pacified, the bodily constituents (dhātus) are in their natural state, there is no craving for food, and the stool and urine are normal; and when the complexion, senses, mind, and physical movements are clear and serene. Minor ailments, worms, ear, nose, eye, and head diseases, those caused by women and children, and poison— this is declared to be the summary of the *Rugviniścaya*.
Whatever well-spoken [medical knowledge] exists anywhere has all been diligently compiled here as one.

Whatever merit has been gained by the illustrious Mādhava, the son of Indukara, through this *Rugviniścaya* composed for the definitive determination of all the ailments of men— by that merit, may all living beings forever be freed from the continuous succession of diseases. (10–11)
